1.title: Upland oakwood
1.key_data: There are approximately 1516ha of upland oak woodland in the Peak District, which has been identified in all Landscape Character Areas but is largely absent from the White Peak due to the underlying ecology. Seven Sites of Special Scientific Interest in the Peak District have Upland Oak Woodland as one of their designated features. Of these, one is in favourable condition, two in unfavourable but recovering condition, one unfavourable but with no change and the remaining two have no data available.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

1.description:
Upland oakwoods grow on soils that are acidic in nature, and are the most abundant type of priority woodland in the Peak District. These woodlands are less diverse than upland mixed ashwoods, as they possess denser canopies, which allow less light to reach the ground below. The most common species of tree found in this habitat is the sessile oak (Quercus petraea), with species such as birches (Betula), rowan (Sorbus aucuparia), hazel (Corylus avellana) and holly (Ilex aquifolium) making up the rest of the canopy. Within the ground flora species include: wood anemone (Anemonoides nemorosa), cowberry (Vaccinium vitis-idaea), common cow-wheat (Melampyrum pratense), wood sorrel (Oxalis acetosella) and bluebells (Hyacinthoides non-scripta). Upland oakwoods can support a number of important birds – for example pied flycatchers (Ficedula hypoleuca) and wood warblers (Phylloscopus sibilatrix) – as well as invertebrates like the purple hair-streak butterfly (Favonius quercus).

Even though this is the most dominant priority woodland type in the National Park, areas of this habitat tend to be small and isolated. However, despite this, upland oakwood is a vital habitat and part of the reason the South Pennine Special Area of Conservation (SAC) was designated as such. Beyond sites protected in this location, other areas of oakwood are protected within Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs). Oakwoods in the Peak District have cultural and historical value, as well as ecological, for example in relation to charcoal pits and the tanning industry. The makeup of species within each area of woodland often depends on the acidity of the soil, as well as grazing from livestock. Overgrazing can prevent regeneration, especially in more newly planted forests. Climate change and the likely introduction of new and invasive species will affect this habitat in years to come. However, projects such as the Clough Woodland Project - part of Moors for the Future Partnership - aim to increase semi-natural woodlands (including oakwood) in the Peak District, with a view to increasing habitat network connectivity and buffering against impacts from climate change.

Although there have been many projects aimed on clough conservation and restoration – including the Clough Woodland Project, ‘Slowing the Flow’ Project, and Churnet Valley Landscape Partnership Project’ – upland oakwoods are still vulnerable to land management practices and a changing climate. The pressures that many SSSIs in the Peak District face often fall under land management practices, especially over and under grazing. New woodlands can struggle to grow if there is a lack of deer management, as they often eat young saplings; but with no grazing at all the ground cover can become too dense and shade out certain species. Climate change will impact the species abundance and diversity of this habitat as the weather becomes more erratic, and those with a low adaptive capacity, such as some lichens and fungi, will especially struggle.

65.distribution:
There are about 1516ha of upland oak woodland in the Peak District. As this habitat type grows on acidic soils, it is largely absent from the limestone-rich geology of the White Peak but can be seen in all the other landscape character areas. Larger areas can be found within the larger Dark Peak and South West Peak regions, which are formed on more acidic rock types. Although individual stretches of upland oak woods tend to be small, concentrations can be found in and around Padley Gorge and towards Wincle in the west of the National Park[158],[159].

Example site: Padley Gorge

These woodlands are located in the east of the Peak District near Grindleford, and form part of the Yarncliff Wood Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI). As well as the ancient oaks and birches that make up the woods, many bird species are found in this protected site, including: hawfinches, pied flycatchers and wood warblers[165].

2.title: Upland mixed ashwood
2.key_data: There are approximately 820ha of upland mixed ash woodland in the Peak District. The SSSI condition data available are very poor quality and cannot be used to understand the condition of this habitat type. However, in places 99% of ash trees are infected with ash dieback disease, which indicates that this habitat type will be in severe decline in the immediate future.

family.description: Ecological and geological features

25.description:
Upland mixed ashwood grows on alkaline soils and in the Peak District is almost all located within the White Peak, due to the geology of the area. The ash-dominated nature of the woodland creates a thin canopy with abundant light reaching the ground floor, leading to a species rich environment with flora and fauna of nationally recognised importance. In these woodlands, in addition to ash (Fraxinus excelsior), species of tree such as wych elm (Ulmus glabra), hazel (Corylus avellana), rowan (Sorbus aucuparia), downy birch (Betula pubescens) and sycamore (Acer pseudoplatanus) can be found. Beyond trees, this priority habitat hosts a wide diversity of plants, with notable ones including lily-of-the-valley (Convallaria majalis), pink-flowered bush mezereon (Daphne mezereum) and fingered sedge (Carex digitata). The invertebrate species encompass species such as: barred toothed-strip moth (Trichopteryx polycommata), white-spotted pinion moth (Cosmia diffinis) and lemon slug (Malacolimax tenellus).

Upland mixed ashwoods have faced many issues with invasive diseases over the decades, as many wych elms were lost as a result of Dutch elm disease in the 1980s. More recently, ash dieback has had drastic impacts on these woods, with 60-90% of ash trees expected to die and in many places safety works taking place to remove trees before they drop limbs. This will also greatly affect species associated with ash as a food plant, roost or nest site, host or substrate. As a result, the habitat in areas which are currently upland mixed ash woodlands is expected to change greatly over a short timescale. This will have knock on impacts on ash a timber crop, and upland mixed ash woods as places for leisure and recreation for people in prominent White Peak locations, such as Dovedale.

67.condition:
Due to the fragmentation of upland mixed ashwood in the Peak District, condition can vary quite significantly between sites. Over 80% of this habitat is protected within SSSIs in the Peak District, but not every site has had a condition assessment carried out. From the 12 SSSI sites that have upland mixed ash woodland as a feature, eight do not have a condition record with another three having low or no confidence associated with their condition rating. Therefore, SSSI data gives little to no insight into the condition of upland mixed ash woodlands[160].

However, the progression of ash dieback disease and the threat it poses to upland mixed ash woodlands would indicate that the overall condition of this habitat is likely to be declining. Action is being taken to support the areas where this habitat type is currently prevalent. For example, in the limestone ravines of the White Peak where 99% of ash trees are infected, the “Life in the Ravines” project is seeking to diversify woodland species through tree planting. While this will alter the habitat type, such projects hope to support the continued ecological functionality of these areas[167].

66.distribution:
There are an estimated 820ha of upland mixed ashwoods in the Peak District, almost exclusively found in the limestone rich area of the White Peak, however it is also recorded in the Derwent Valley, Derbyshire Peak Fringe and Southwest Peak[158],[159]. This habitat is more fragmented than it was historically, and will further decrease in extent as ash dieback changes the species composition of this habitat, especially in areas where the canopy is over 90% ash. Notable places where this woodland type can be seen include: Cressbrook Dale, Chee Dale and in the woods along the River Dove in the south of the National Park.

Example site - Cressbrook

This area is protected both as a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and as part of the Derbyshire Dales National Nature Reserve (NNR). As well as the ash-dominated canopy, wych elm, small-leaved lime, rowan, hazel and rock whitebeam can be found. Underneath the tree canopy, many other species of flora are present, with dog’s mercury, lily of the valley and guelder rose being just a few. Many woodland bird species can be seen, such as redstarts, with grey wagtails and dippers being found closer to the streams[166].

3.title: Wet woodland
3.key_data: There are approximately 99ha of wet woodland in the Peak District, which is highly fragmented into small patches mostly under 10ha. Wet woodland is a feature in eight SSSI sites, with five of these recorded as being in favourable or unfavourable but recovering condition which suggests this habitat type is in relatively good condition, although the data are limited.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

26.description:
Wet woodlands are found on waterlogged soils that are either seasonally or permanently wet with poor drainage. Located along stream edges, floodplains and cloughs, this is a very rare habitat within the Peak District, and often seen in mosaics with other types of woodlands and wetlands. Wet woodland is characterised by willows (Salix), downy birch (Betula pubescens) and alders (Alnus spp.). These woodlands are vital because they host species not typically found in other habitats, such as marsh marigolds (Caltha palustris) and greater tussock sedge (Carex paniculata), as well as rare birds like the willow tit (Poecile montanus). Beyond this lichen, fungi, craneflies, hoverflies and moths can be found.

Wet woodland is one of the smaller areas of priority habitat in the National Park, partly due to the specific abiotic conditions needed for it to occur and also as a result of historic land management practices, such as drainage. These practices, along with others such as intensive forestry, continue to occur and can dry out these woodlands and lead to habitat loss, while grazing can affect species composition. Wet woodlands are vulnerable to climatic changes due to their fragmented nature, especially hotter, drier summers which reduce the water table and lead to desiccation. They are also vulnerable to invasive species including Himalayan balsam (Impatiens glandulifera).

68.condition:
Wet woodland is a feature of eight Sites of Special Scientific Interest, with condition records available for five sites. At these, two are in favourable condition and three are in unfavourable but recovering, suggesting that the condition of wet woodland as revealed by this limited sample if relatively good and trending upwards[160].

The isolated and fragmented nature of wet woodland throughout the Peak District may mean it is more vulnerable to factors such as climate change and land use management. Further fragmentation of this habitat could occur with ongoing drainage of land through agriculture and forestry. Agricultural techniques which result in nutrient run off and pollution can also easily impact these habitats, due to where they grow along waterways which provide transport for pollutants. Beyond land management practices, climate change and ecological change pose the greatest threats to wet woodlands, as changing weather patterns could lead to fluctuations in the water table and desiccation of these habitats, as well as the introduction of new and invasive species, which may outcompete native ones.

67.distribution: There are only 99ha of wet woodland in the whole Peak District which is highly fragmented into small often isolated patches. While pockets can be found across the whole National Park, it is located mostly in the South West Peak and Dark Peak. As heavily saturated soils are needed for wet woodland to form, it is usually found near rivers and streams, reservoirs and on floodplains. This habitat can usually be seen forming a mosaic with other woodland types, but some distinct areas of wet woodlands can be seen in the Eastern Moors, particularly around Foxlane Plantation and Ramsley Moor[158],[159].

4.title: Wood pasture and parkland
4.key_data: There are approximately 645ha of wood pasture and parkland in the Peak District concentrated in small number of sites typically associated with country houses and stately homes. There are not SSSIs in the Peak District where wood pasture and parkland is a designated feature. The Chatsworth Old Park SSSI could be used as an indicator, however, with five of its six invertebrate and lichen features reported to be in favourable condition.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

27.description:
Wood pasture and parkland is a habitat type defined not by a specific ecological make up, but instead by its mosaic structure of mixed-age trees that are dispersed through parkland. Most often found on acidic, nutrient-poor soils where the land is less suitable for cultivation, this habitat is maintained by grazing and active management and associated with country houses and stately homes. Due to the long-term historical management of these areas, they can be of immense ecological value. For example, at Chatsworth Park alone there has been recordings of four red data book species and 13 nationally scarce species amongst others. Wood pasture and parkland is also important for ancient and veteran trees which can be biodiversity hotspots, with each tree having the potential to host thousands of different species. These areas tend to be of cultural significant locally and internationally, attracting many visitors. This significance is discussed further on the estate lands, parks and gardens page.

As a result of the nature of these habitats, they are very vulnerable to land management decisions, in particular grazing levels. Too little grazing can result in the succession to more dense and closed woodland canopies, whereas overgrazing can open up the area to heathland or grassland. The resilience of this woodland type to climate change depends on the proportion of older and veteran trees, as these can be more resilient than their younger counterparts, as well as their ability to host a wider range of vertebrate and invertebrate species. However, veteran trees are more vulnerable to droughts and storms in the open structure of wood pastures – as opposed to being more sheltered in a denser woodland – and so to increase the resilience of this habitat type it is imperative to protect younger individuals (as well as the older ones), so they have the opportunity to ‘veteranize’.

69.condition:
As wood pasture and parkland is not a habitat type which is designated as a feature of any SSSIs in the Peak District, there is no overall SSSI condition data that can be used as a proxy to indicate the condition of the habitat across the National Park. However, the Chatsworth Old Park SSSI could be used an example site. This site is designated as a SSSI for its lichen and invertebrate assemblages, which in this instance could be taken as an indicator of good quality wood pasture and parkland. The condition of five of the six features in this SSSI is recorded as favourable, with the other feature in unfavourable but recovering condition[160]. Therefore, in this site the wood pasture and parkland appears to be in good condition. However, Chatsworth may not be typical for this habitat type due to its high profile and significant resources to manage the site compared to other smaller estates.

The condition of wood pasture and parkland does not often change rapidly or dramatically due to the nature of how the habitat is formed. Many locations of this habitat – especially within the Peak District – are found in and around estate land. This means they are typically in planned management, with practices including grazing, mowing and pollarding used to maintain the structure and species composition seen at each individual site. It may only be as a result of land ownership changes that dramatic changing occur, as a result of differing preferences in how the land is managed.

Examples like the wood pastures and parklands at Chatsworth are the example of hundreds of years of cultivation and management, with flocks of sheep and herds of fallow and red deer used to graze the parklands and keep their traditional structure. Deer, in particular, eat young saplings, but have little effect on established trees, and so help to reinforce the more veteran and ancient trees in grassland structure. However, veteran trees are threatened by invasive diseases, notably ash dieback in the National Park. If these die, they cannot be replaced and so greatly biodiverse habitats will be lost. Therefore, for the resilience of the habitat in the future new saplings must be planted – and protected from grazing – so they can establish and eventually become veteran trees themselves.

68.distribution:
There are roughly 645ha of wood pasture and parkland across the National Park. Their distribution is uneven, with fairly large areas of the habitat associated with estates which occur primarily on the eastern and western fringes of the National Park, for example Longshaw in the East and Lyme Park in the West[158],[159].

 Example site - Chatsworth

Perhaps the most well-known estate in the Peak District, Chatsworth is located near Bakewell and along the banks of the River Derwent. Much of the area is open to the public and contains formal gardens near Chatsworth House, in addition to the wood pasture and parkland. This landscape has been heavily designed and managed for over 500 years, which has shaped the parkland as it exists today. The Old Park Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI), which is closed to the public, contains a concentration of ancient pollarded oaks (Quercus spp.), which may once have formed the western edge of Sherwood Forest[168].

5.title: Lowland mixed deciduous woodland
5.key_data: There are roughly 645ha of lowland mixed deciduous woodland across the National Park, widely distributed across all Landscape Character Areas. There is very limited SSSI data for this habitat type which, while it indicates one site is in relatively good condition, cannot support conclusions about this habitat type overall in the Peak District.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

28.description:
Lowland mixed deciduous woodland is a broad term that covers many different woodland types that can grow on a wide range of different soil types. They also cover the whole spectrum of ancient, semi-natural and plantation woodlands, as areas of this priority habitat can fall into each of these three categories. The species composition of this habitat can differ dramatically depending on the soil and geology conditions, as well as other factors. Sites are typically fragmented and small, and often form a mosaic with other woodland types.

As a result of the diverse species and woodland types found within this broader category, this habitat is impacted by many factors, but, as with other woodland habitats, the primary drivers of change are often climate change, land management practices and ecological change. The fragmented and isolated nature of sites means that they have less resilience against changing average temperatures and weather patterns, as well as invasive species and agricultural practices. However, due to the range of woodland sites under this category, even though individual areas are vulnerable, the overall habitat is more resilient than others. Overgrazing poses a threat as this reduces the ground diversity and prevents sapling growth. Woodlands near agricultural land are at risk of run off from fertilisers and nitrogen pollution.

70.condition:
The range of species-assemblages that can be included within this habitat designation can mean that condition varies greatly and is difficult to compare between sites. Only two Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) in the Peak District have lowland mixed deciduous woodland as a designated feature, with condition data only available for one of these. This lists the condition as unfavourable but recovering, which indicates a reasonably good condition at this site however this is not sufficient data to extrapolate to indicate condition across the whole National Park[160].

The condition of these woodlands is impacted by multiple factors, especially as it has a broader definition than other kinds of woodland. This has both positive and negative implications, as the broader category means that there are more factors this habitat as a whole is susceptible to, but at the same time the diversity in this woodland type means it has a higher degree of resilience overall. For example, increasing pests and diseases will pose an increasingly high risk, as climatic conditions change and mass species migration occurs, but as many different species can be found in lowland mixed deciduous woods – depending on the underlying geology – even if some species and sites are lost, the habitat as a whole is less vulnerable than more specialised woodland types. However, the small size, and fragmentation, of sites in the Peak District increases this habitat’s vulnerability to the effects of climate change and changes in land management practices.

69.distribution:
Lowland mixed deciduous woodland can be found in all the landscape character areas of the Peak District, with the most northern parts having the scarcest amounts. There are roughly 645ha of this habitat in the National Park in total[158],[159]. Its widespread nature is due to the fact that they can grow in a wide range of soil types, and so can be found in the calcareous regions of the White Peak as well as the more acidic geology of the Dark Peak in the north. Although generally these woods are found in small patches alongside other woodland types, there are some slightly larger examples around the Rivelin Reservoirs and on Stanton Moor.

 Example site - Stanton Moor

This area hosts a diversity of habitats including great swathes of common heather (Calluna vulgaris) and bilberry (Vaccinium myrrtillus) moorland, stretches of bracken, and other woodland types, alongside its lowland mixed deciduous woods dominated by oak (Quercus spp.) and birch (Betula spp.). It is an area of rich biological diversity, but also cultural and historical significance, as multiple heritage features are found here, in particular the Nine Ladies stone circle. This monument is sacred to many, and visited often, with thousands of people coming to celebrate the summer and winter solstices here every year[9].

6.title: Trees outside woodlands
6.key_data: There are over 225,000 records of trees outside of woodlands in the Peak District, with a total area greater than that of all other woodland types. By nature, these trees are fragmented across the geography. Whilst trees outside of woodlands are a common landscape feature, there is almost no condition data relating to this feature.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

29.description:
Trees outside woodlands are defined as any tree over three meters tall with a five-meter square area of canopy which exists outside the woodlands mapped in the National Forest Inventory. This includes many trees in open fields, parks and gardens, and alongside roads, where they can be highly ecological significant, especially those ancient and veteran trees which support a wide range of species of invertebrates, fungi, lichen, bats and birds, including rare and priority species. These oldest trees take hundreds of years to reach this life stage and provide huge ecological benefit as well as cultural significance; a single tree can support over a thousand other species!

Subject to the same factors as trees with woodlands, trees outside woodland have some unique pressures as a result of their isolated nature. They may be subject to greater environmental stresses, such as heat and drought exacerbated by climate change, as they aren’t in the more regulated environment created by a woodland. Additionally, human-induced pressure could be greater, with the risk of individual trees being removed for development or either intentionally or accidentally damaged. Often significant lone trees, such as ancient and veteran trees, are protected under planning policy through mechanisms such as Tree Preservation Orders. Due to the huge length of time it takes to reach this ancient life stage, it is vital that younger trees are also protected, as well as planting trees and allowing natural recruitment outside of woodlands to ensure the future of ancient trees.

71.condition:
There is very little condition data relating to trees outside woodlands. The National Trees Outside Woodlands dataset maps out lone trees and groups of trees but has no condition data associated with it12. The Ancient Tree Inventory is an open-sourced map of notable, veteran and ancient trees which does indicate if the tree is alive or dead and standing or fallen, however these are not a good indicator of condition in this instance as the standing deadwood of an ancient tree can be as or more ecologically significant than a living tree[22].

The extent of trees outside woodlands in the Peak District does indicate that this habitat type is relatively common. This could be an indicator of good condition, however this needs to be considered in a relative sense against other woodland habitat types. While increasing the cover of lone trees in the open country may be ecological beneficial, doing so at the expense of other woodland types, or even other priority habitat types, could not be. However, trees outside woodlands are a vital habitat type for mobile species moving through the landscape, especially where they form corridors connecting other woodland habitats, and as such their management should be supported.

70.distribution: Trees outside of woodlands occur in every Landscape Character Area of the Peak District but are least concentrated in the Dark Peak and are most concentrated in parts of the Southwest and White Peaks, and the Derwent Valley. They tend to fill in gaps between other woodland types areas where the trees do not grow densely enough to form a woodland. They can also often be seen to follow river valleys and roads as well as sometimes tracing the outlines of field boundaries. There are over 225,000 records of lone trees or groups of trees under 1000m2 in the Peak District, with a total area of 2032ha, giving them the largest areas of all other woodland types but by nature being completed fragmented[169].

10.introduction:
The Peak District is notable for its scarcity of woodlands, however the priority woodland habitats that are present in the National Park make a significant ecological and cultural contribution to its character. From the upland oakwoods of the Dark Peak that cling to clough-sides below the high moorlands, to the wood pasture and parklands intrinsically linked to the Peak Districts estate lands, parks and gardens. Where woodlands remain in the National Park, it tells a story about how the land has been managed for the last 10,000 years. Woodlands play a vital role in providing benefits within the National Park and to its surrounding communities. Wooded valleys slow the flow of water, providing flood protection to communities downstream. Trees outside woodlands can be some of the most culturally significant ecological features in the landscape, with people travel to visit just a single tree.

As priority habitats, the woodlands discussed in this report are often within protected sites, including Sites of Special Scientific Interest, Special Areas of Conservation or Special Protected Areas. This gives them some protection as well as helping to reveal the condition of these habitats through survey data. However, these habitats are still at risk from a number of factors. Ash dieback disease is a significant factor in the Peak District which is already leading to the rapid decline of the White Peaks’ characteristic ash woodlands. Novel pests and diseases could further impact the Peak District’s woodlands, especially as climate change further threatens trees, making them more vulnerable. Land management practices can have both positive and negative impacts on woodlands, with historic land management one of the most significant factors on the current state and extent of the Peak District’s woodlands.

17.distribution: Woodlands are highly fragmented and scattered across the Peak District, which makes preserving the current extent of priority woodlands vitally important. The character of woodland across the Peak District’s Landscape Character Areas (LCAs) varies significantly; the Eastern Moors is largely unwooded, while the Derwent Valley has some of the largest extents of upland oak woodland. The White Peak contains the Peak District’s upland mixed ash woodlands as well as a high density of trees outside of woodlands. The gritstone areas of the Southwest and Dark Peak LCAs are also largely unwooded, with some patches of upland oak woodland in their cloughs and valleys, as well as occasional wood pastures such as surrounding the historic Lyme Park in Cheshire.

8.importance:
While priority woodland habitats are themselves often small and fragmented, in connection with their wider ecosystem they play a vital role in the provision of ecological and social benefits in the National Park. This includes contributing to the provision of clean and plentiful water and flood protection, by slowing the flow of water off the upland moors. Woodlands also support the quality of soil, by holding soils together and controlling erosion.

The wooded valleys, cloughs and dales of the Peak District also have important social and cultural value, with visitors and residents feeling a sense of connection to the landscape in wooded landscapes. This contributes to the health and wellbeing of people who take time to find leisure and recreation in these woodlands.

1.quality: • Relying on SSSI condition data to understand the condition of these habitats will only give a partial picture as it does not account for sites outside of protected areas. Additionally, SSSI condition data is very often out of data, with many records not having been updated for 10-20 years or more. This means that the condition assumptions presented in this report are of very low certainty.

1.likelihood_text: It is almost certain that the combined effects of these factors will lead to the death of some trees and damage of others. The death of trees is a natural part of their life cycle, however this impact reflects anthropogenic causes which are increasing the likelihood of this. An example would be the death of the Major Oak in Sherwood Forest in the summer of 2026, which was linked to climate change.
1.severity:
Over the next 10 years this impact is likely to be moderate, increasing to devastating in places. This higher rating is largely due to the impact of ash dieback disease which is spreading across the ashwoods of the White Peak and will have devastating consequences in this area, with whole woodland ecosystems potentially being lost.

In other areas it is more likely to be individual trees that could be impacted, with less widespread impact. However, the overall impact across the National Park is likely to become increasingly severe over time, as a result of climate change and increased likelihood and severity of drought conditions occurring.

3.impact:
Climate change has compound impacts on other factors. These are briefly laid out below with more detail on each of the relevant factor pages.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Due to climate change having unequal impacts globally, as a result of both physical and socio-economic conditions, international migration of people may increase the UK population and/or change the character of the UK population as a whole. Additionally, there may be increased demand for housing in rural areas as a result of disproportionate population growth and warming in urban areas. As a result, the Peak District may experience changes to the demographic character of both its residents and its visitors due to global and local population changes. There is little research into exactly what these changes may look like, however projections do indicate that current migration trends are likely to be amplified as a result of climate change[64].

Ecological change

The projected impacts of climate change are intrinsically linked to potential ecological changes. As the physical conditions which define species’ niches shift, both spatially and temporally, species distribution and phenology (timing of biological events) will change.

Cooke et al. (2026) model biodiversity change in the UK under a range of climate scenarios up to 2080[61]. They project “extensive community reorganisation” under any scenario with “the disappearance of current bioclimates and emergence of novel ones”. In the Peak District, this is likely to contribute to the local extinction of species, colonisation by novel species, changes to composition of biological communities, increase likelihood of invasive alien species and increased likelihood of pathogens.

Formulating and setting habitat and species targets, as has been the practice for many years, will need to be carefully re-examined as an approach.

Land management practices

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

5.impact:
Climate change

Change in ecological communities could alter the potential for carbon storage in biomass, which will impact the possibility for land-based mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions as is accounted for in net zero targets. For example, changes to blanket bog communities could result in less accumulation of peat soil, reducing carbon storage potential, and in the possible release of additional carbon from soil due to runoff, resulting in enhanced climate change. Ecological communities may also experience non-linear shifts, for example a sudden collapse in function in single biome, which could in turn provoke non-linear climatic impacts due to the impact on water, carbon and nutrient cycling.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Ecological change could impact on the demography and sociocultural practices of both residents and visitors to the Peak District due to the connections between people and their wider ecologies. Shifts in ecological communities could invoke changes to the composition of rural communities, as the possibility for agricultural livelihoods changes and people’s connection to and sense of belonging in the landscape shifts. Additionally, visitors to the Peak District come in part to interact with the ecology of the landscape, from foraging to taking in the view. Changes to these communities may result in different people visiting in different ways.

Land management practices

Land management practices take place in relation to the underlying ecological communities. Therefore, changes to this ecology are likely to result in changed land management practices. Pollution

The potential destabilisation of moorland soils as a result of changes to upland vegetation communities could resulting in the wash out of heavy metal pollution stored in these soils from industrial revolution. This would have downstream consequences as this pollution is spread, potentially having further ecological impacts as well as impacting agricultural land and drinking water.

7.impact:
Climate change

Demographic and sociocultural change

Where land management and ownership change, this could have consequences for the demographics of rural and farming communities, based on who is able to live and work in the Peak District. If land is consolidated under fewer ownership, this could mean that fewer people live and work on the land. However, changes to farming or conservation land management practices may result in more rural jobs. Therefore, it is difficult to make projections about exactly what these changes may look like.

Pollution

Certain land management practices can either result in or reduce pollution. Fertiliser run off from agricultural land can cause polluting effects in freshwater systems, and therefore moving toward lower input agricultural land management can reduce this pollution. Land management practices which stabilise soils, for example peatland restoration, can result in reduced top soil runoff and therefore less sediment contaminated with pollutants from industrial air pollution ending up downstream.

Visitation and access

The Peak District is widely known among visitors for its landscapes under their current management regimes, which promote people to visit the area and participate in different recreational activities. If land was managed differently, this could change people’s perception of the landscape and alter their visiting behaviour, as well as possible changes to access infrastructure which would need to adapt around changing land use.  This could be in the direction of reduced access and declining visitation, for example under agriculture intensification, or it could be increased visitation through ecotourism.

8.impact:
Climate change

Particulate pollution can contribute towards climate change as a result of airborne particulates absorbing heat and light, contributing to atmospheric warming and cloud formation[118].

Ecological changes

Water pollution alters the chemical environment for aquatic life, impacting species’ abilities to reproduce. Excess nutrients or changes to pH cause imbalance with some species thriving at the expense of others, resulting changes to the diversity and composition of aquatic ecosystems. This can also have knock on impacts on terrestrial ecosystems which interact with polluted water sources[119].

Nitrogen air pollution alters lichen community composition, with some species being nitrogen-tolerant and others nitrogen-sensitive. In this was lichens can be used as indicators of nitrogen air pollution[120].

Climate change has compound impacts on other factors. These are briefly laid out below with more detail on each of the relevant factor pages.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Due to climate change having unequal impacts globally, as a result of both physical and socio-economic conditions, international migration of people may increase the UK population and/or change the character of the UK population as a whole. Additionally, there may be increased demand for housing in rural areas as a result of disproportionate population growth and warming in urban areas. As a result, the Peak District may experience changes to the demographic character of both its residents and its visitors due to global and local population changes. There is little research into exactly what these changes may look like, however projections do indicate that current migration trends are likely to be amplified as a result of climate change[64].

Ecological change

The projected impacts of climate change are intrinsically linked to potential ecological changes. As the physical conditions which define species’ niches shift, both spatially and temporally, species distribution and phenology (timing of biological events) will change.

Cooke et al. (2026) model biodiversity change in the UK under a range of climate scenarios up to 2080[61]. They project “extensive community reorganisation” under any scenario with “the disappearance of current bioclimates and emergence of novel ones”. In the Peak District, this is likely to contribute to the local extinction of species, colonisation by novel species, changes to composition of biological communities, increase likelihood of invasive alien species and increased likelihood of pathogens.

Formulating and setting habitat and species targets, as has been the practice for many years, will need to be carefully re-examined as an approach.

Land management practices

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

5.impact:
Climate change

Change in ecological communities could alter the potential for carbon storage in biomass, which will impact the possibility for land-based mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions as is accounted for in net zero targets. For example, changes to blanket bog communities could result in less accumulation of peat soil, reducing carbon storage potential, and in the possible release of additional carbon from soil due to runoff, resulting in enhanced climate change. Ecological communities may also experience non-linear shifts, for example a sudden collapse in function in single biome, which could in turn provoke non-linear climatic impacts due to the impact on water, carbon and nutrient cycling.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Ecological change could impact on the demography and sociocultural practices of both residents and visitors to the Peak District due to the connections between people and their wider ecologies. Shifts in ecological communities could invoke changes to the composition of rural communities, as the possibility for agricultural livelihoods changes and people’s connection to and sense of belonging in the landscape shifts. Additionally, visitors to the Peak District come in part to interact with the ecology of the landscape, from foraging to taking in the view. Changes to these communities may result in different people visiting in different ways.

Land management practices

Land management practices take place in relation to the underlying ecological communities. Therefore, changes to this ecology are likely to result in changed land management practices. For example, in the Peak District, uplands currently managed for grouse moors may be managed differently if the red grouse experiences population decline and the composition upland moorland habitats shift to make this form of moorland management no longer sustainable. Similarly, agricultural practices may have to change if different compositions of agri-ecological systems emerge, pests and diseases impact on crops and livestock, etc.

Pollution

The potential destabilisation of moorland soils as a result of changes to upland vegetation communities could resulting in the wash out of heavy metal pollution stored in these soils from industrial revolution. This would have downstream consequences as this pollution is spread, potentially having further ecological impacts as well as impacting agricultural land and drinking water.

7.impact:
Climate change

As described above, land can be managed to mitigate the impacts of climate change by sequestering or preventing the further emission of fossil fuels. If the Peak District was managed to maximise this, it could help remove CO2 from the atmosphere to slow future climate change. However, on the scale of the Peak District this would have a relatively small impact on global climate change.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Where land management and ownership change, this could have consequences for the demographics of rural and farming communities, based on who is able to live and work in the Peak District. If land is consolidated under fewer ownership, this could mean that fewer people live and work on the land. However, changes to farming or conservation land management practices may result in more rural jobs. Therefore, it is difficult to make projections about exactly what these changes may look like.

Pollution

Certain land management practices can either result in or reduce pollution. Fertiliser run off from agricultural land can cause polluting effects in freshwater systems, and therefore moving toward lower input agricultural land management can reduce this pollution. Land management practices which stabilise soils, for example peatland restoration, can result in reduced top soil runoff and therefore less sediment contaminated with pollutants from industrial air pollution ending up downstream.

Visitation and access

The Peak District is widely known among visitors for its landscapes under their current management regimes, which promote people to visit the area and participate in different recreational activities. If land was managed differently, this could change people’s perception of the landscape and alter their visiting behaviour, as well as possible changes to access infrastructure which would need to adapt around changing land use.  This could be in the direction of reduced access and declining visitation, for example under agriculture intensification, or it could be increased visitation through ecotourism.

23.likelihood_text:
This impact is likely, partly as a result of the wide range of causes that may lead to it. Shifts in species composition in habitats is a feature of ongoing background ecological change, but this is likely be exacerbated by anthropogenic causes. Climate change, in combination and related to other factors such as changes in land management practices, will further this as the underlying conditions on which species assemblages are constructed continue to move further away from the baseline.

In ash woodlands this is almost certain as a result of ash dieback.
23.severity: This impact may only be minor over the next ten years, but will become increasingly severe over time as the impacts of climate change develop. It is also possible that the negative consequences of this impact could be mitigated, for example by managing changes in species composition to support the continuation of the overall functioning of ecosystems, so that benefits like clean water or climatic regulation continue to be provided. This would reduce the overall severity of the impact in some ways.

6.impact:
Governance and legislation have the potential to impact all other factors due to the legislation and governance frameworks that underlie all action carried out in the UK. This could be drawn together in an almost infinite number of links, however certainty about what impacts are likely is very low, and many relevant ways in which governance and legislation impacts other factors have already been outlined above. Therefore, these are briefly summarised below with some additional impacts that have not yet been noted.

Factor

Possible impacts from governance and legislation

Climate change

Stronger commitments to emissions reduction and carbon sequestration and storage could help to reduce likelihood of global climate change impacts, e.g. changes to the Climate Change Act 2008 or additional global agreements.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Impacts on communities from changes to planning regulation (NFFP, local plan making process etc) could alter housing development in communities, potential knock-on impact to composition of communities.

Ecological change

Possibility for strengthened or weakened environmental protections, e.g. through BNG and biodiversity credits, changes to National Park legislation and governance, etc. Land use framework, LNRSs and 30x30 target may introduce stronger requirements and spatial planning for land to be managed for ecology.

Economy and industry

Changes to farm subsidy schemes may positively or negatively impact he viability of farm businesses. More NSIPs to support low carbon energy and transport infrastructure could support construction and operation jobs.

Land management practices

Farm subsidies and land management grants may incentivise changes to land uses and management actions. Land use framework may change how land use is determined. Changes to land ownership resulting in changed land management may result from enhance community right to buy to England[98].

Possible changes to legislation relating to driven grouse shooting, including further changes to moorland burning regulation about and an ongoing campaign to ban on driven grouse shooting[99], may result to changes in moorland management.

Changes to the regulation of sewage waste outflow into freshwater would reduce freshwater pollution. Legislation relating to land management outline above could change agricultural pollution e.g. lower input farming reducing nutrient pollution.

8.impact:
Climate change

Particulate pollution can contribute towards climate change as a result of airborne particulates absorbing heat and light, contributing to atmospheric warming and cloud formation[118].

Ecological changes

Water pollution alters the chemical environment for aquatic life, impacting species’ abilities to reproduce. Excess nutrients or changes to pH cause imbalance with some species thriving at the expense of others, resulting changes to the diversity and composition of aquatic ecosystems. This can also have knock on impacts on terrestrial ecosystems which interact with polluted water sources[119].

8.title: Calaminarian grassland
8.key_data: There are approximately 195ha of calaminarian grasslands in the Peak District, predominantly in the White Peak LCA. Eight of the total 13 calaminarian grassland features in SSSIs in the National Park are in either favourable or unfavourable but recovering condition.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

30.description:
Calaminarian grasslands are fairly unique which occur where tolerant plant species grow on soils containing high levels of heavy metals, for example, lead, chromium and copper. These can occur naturally, but in the Peak District commonly are found near mine works, spoil heaps and lead rakes. Due to the slightly toxic nature of the underlying substrate, calaminarian grasslands are often species poor and fragmented, and often form mosaics with other grassland habitats. However, the species that can survive in these conditions are rare and can be unique to each site. Some of the metal tolerant plants that exist in the Peak District are spring sandwort (Sabulina verna) – also known as leadwort – moonwort (Botrychium lunaria), and some orchid species (Orchidaceae spp.). Calaminarian grasslands also host a variety of insects and the mine workings they grow on can provide homes for bats and amphibians.

As these are such unique habitats, both as a grassland category and individually from site to site, they are very vulnerable and can be hard to manage. Each area of calaminarian grassland forms through a particular combination of environmental, historical and land management factors, and as a result are considered near impossible to recreate; once a site is lost it is unlikely to ever return. Due to many sites being part of mosaics with other habitats it can be difficult to manage and protect the calaminarian grasslands specifically. Grazing is sometimes used to control scrub and prevent succession, but calaminarian grasses are less likely to succeed to woodland than other grasslands due to the toxic substrate beneath.

72.condition:
Calaminarian grassland is recorded as two separate feature-types in the Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) record for the Peak District:

  • Calaminarian grassland and serpentine heath (upland)
  • Lowland calaminarian grasslands (OV37)

There are 13 of these features recorded across 11 sites in the National Park, which can be used to indicate the condition of this feature. One condition rating has complete confidence in its assessment, which was carried out in 2025. This monitored feature is located in the Cressbrook Dale SSSI. Four assessments had a medium confidence rating and eight assessments had low or no confidence. This includes four SSSIs where there is no condition data for the feature[160].

A summary of these condition assessments shows that over half are either in favourable or unfavourable but recovering condition, with one declining[160]. This could indicate that where there is data, this indicates that the condition of calaminarian grasslands is relatively good. However, these sites can easily be disturbed due to land management practices, for example ploughing or removal of lead-mining features such as spoil heaps. This could immediately and irrevocably damage these features and if their condition record if not regularly updated, this could have happened without it being reflected in the available data.

The condition of calaminarian grasslands in the Peak District is difficult to manage, due to each specific site needing distinct handling as a result of the combination of historical and ecological conditions that created the habitat in the first place. These sites often form mosaics with other habitats and grassland types, which makes this even more complex. Governance over the nearby mining areas also has huge impacts on the amount and quality of the calaminarian grasses found, especially depending on whether the mines are out of commission or still extracting minerals. Climate change and increasingly erratic weather patterns, in addition to likely hotter, drier summers will also affect the species composition at each site.

71.distribution:
There are approximately 195ha of calaminarian grassland in the Peak District, almost all of which is located in the White Peak, or on the border between the White Peak and Derwent Valley or Dark Peak Landscape Character Areas. Sites are scattered and located near mineral extraction sites, whether functional or disused[158],[159].

Example site - Lead mines around Castleton, Derbyshire

The Castleton Site of Special Scientific Interest contains a number of lead mines, such as Odin Mine, the surrounds of which support calaminarian grasslands. The area supports both a more sparse vegetation type (OV37a under the National Vegetation Classification) and the more closed OV37b representing the next successional stage of vegetation colonisation. Spring sandwort (S. verna) is present alongside calcareous herbs[170],[171].

9.title: Lowland calcareous grassland
9.key_data: There are roughly 2786ha of lowland calcareous grassland in the Peak District, predominately in the White Peak area due to its underlying limestone geology. Condition records are available for around half of lowland calcareous grassland features in SSSIs, however confidence in these condition assessments is generally low. This shows that roughly half of features are in favourable or unfavourable but recovering condition.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

31.description:
Lowland calcareous grasslands are found where the underlying geology is formed in limestone areas with the soil on top typically quite thin and well-draining. In the Peak District almost all lowland calcareous grassland is located in the White Peak, due its underlying geology. Calcareous grasslands throughout the UK are renowned for their high species richness, and the lowland calcareous grassland in the Peak District is no exception, being the most biodiverse habitat in the National Park. This habitat is home to many rare species, including the nationally scarce spring cinquefoil (Potentilla neumanniana), as well as pyramidal orchid (Anacamptis pyramidalis) and Jacob’s ladder (Polemonium). These grasslands are also host to a variety of invertebrates, such as the dingy skipper (Erynnis tages), dark green fritillary (Argynnis aglaja) and brown argus (Aricia agestis) butterflies.

In the Peak District areas of lowland calcareous grassland are fairly fragmented and have a limited extent, often being found on steep slopes. A significant proportion of calcareous grasslands are protected under designations including Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs), but knowledge of their condition is variable. Limestone grasslands are retained through grazing, and therefore lack of grazing management can lead to scrub encroachment and succession to woodlands, resulting in the loss of the grassland. Land management decisions including changes in the types of grazing livestock and intensity of grazing have and will continue to impact the extent and diversity of this grassland. Furthermore, climatic changes will result in changes in the species composition of calcareous grasslands, as weather patterns get hotter and drier.

73.condition:
Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) records in the Peak District record lowland calcareous grassland features as divided between five different feature classifications based on the National Vegetation Classification categories of CG1, CG2, CG3-5, CG6 and CG7. There are 35 of these features recorded across 19 SSSI in the Peak District, which can help to understand the condition of these sites, however just under half (16) do not have a current condition record. Of those which do, six sites are noted as having complete confidence in their condition assessments, all having been recorded in the past two years. These sites are located in the Long Dale, Chrome and Parkhouse Hills, and Cressbrook Dale SSSIs. The remaining 13 features have either low or no confidence in their condition record[160].

Where a condition record is available, just over half the features are in either a favourable or unfavourable but recovering condition. However, given that almost half of the lowland calcareous grassland in SSSIs has not been assessed, it makes it difficult to get an accurate idea of the wider condition of this habitat across the park[160].

The limestone grasslands in the Peak District – including lowland calcareous grasses – are increasingly fragmented due to being converted to improved grasslands through agricultural practices. The majority of sites are now found on steep slopes, where grazing maintains their structure. This is an issue for the future extent and quality of lowland calcareous grasslands in the Peak District as it reduces the ability for specialist species to colonise new areas. Additionally, land management practices can have great impacts on this habitat, due to the nature of its maintenance through livestock grazing. If overgrazed the habitat can struggle to maintain growth, and if under grazed scrub can encroach and lead to succession. Changing climatic patterns will also impact the species composition of lowland calcareous grassland, but the habitat type as a whole will be more resilient if fragmentation is reduced and isolated areas reconnected.

72.distribution:
There are approximately 2786ha of lowland calcareous grassland in the Peak District, primarly in the White Peak and occasionally just over the border into neighbouring Landscape Character areas. Rarely, this habitat type is also recorded where quarried limestone has been used to lay paths or roads and resulted in atypical vegetation for the true underlying geology[158],[159].

Example site - Cressbrook Dale

Cressbrook Dale is a SSSI and part of the Derbyshire Dales National Nature Reserve (NNR). The grasslands here are incredibly species rich, in turn hosting an abundance of insects and bryophyte diversity. Plants found here include: meadow oat (Avenula pratense) and carnation sedge (Carex flacca) – which are plentiful – as well rue-leaved saxifrage (Saxifraga tridactylites) and shining cranesbill (Geranium lucidum) on rocky outcrops[172].

10.title: Lowland dry acid grassland
10.key_data: Approximately 7823ha of lowland dry acid grassland can be found across all areas of the Peak District, but predominantly in areas with underlying gritstone geology. Where condition data is available for SSSI sites with lowland dry acid grassland, this indicates the feature-type is in reasonable condition with 15 of 23 sites with available condition data recorded as being in favourable or unfavourable but recovering condition.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

32.description:
Lowland dry acid grasslands grow in slightly acidic soils with poor nutrient content, typically located on acidic rock types, as well as superficial deposits including thin peat, sands and gravel. In the Peak District, this predominantly occurs on the gritstone geology of the Dark and Southwest Peak areas. This habitat is common in association with heathlands and blanket bogs and is often found in a mosaic with dwarf shrub heath. Acid grasslands contain grass species such as common bent (Agrostis capillaris) and sheep’s-fescue (Festuca ovina), as well as perennial herbs such as heath bedstraw (Gallium saxatile) and tormentil (Potentilla erecta), and can possess a high level of diversity where the grass is of good quality. This habitat can be host to a variety of fauna and is important for specialist invertebrates, especially ground-dwelling and burrowing species.

Stretches of species rich acid grassland have been lost historically due to agricultural improvement and afforestation, and what is left is still vulnerable to change. Just under half of all the acid grassland types in the Peak District are within Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs), which have their condition assessed. Acid grassland is maintained through cutting or grazing, and left unregulated is susceptible to bracken and scrub encroachment. Therefore, agricultural management and land owner decisions can have a great impact on future lowland dry acid grassland abundance and distribution. Climatic changes will also impact this habitat, either directly, for example through temperature changes and droughts, or indirectly by introducing invasive species into the area.

74.condition:
As there are many individual – as well as interconnected – sites of lowland dry acid grassland across the Peak District, the condition is very variable between locations, even more so in areas outside of protected designations. In the Around just under half of all acid grassland in the Peak District (including lowland dry acid) lies within Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs), with recorded feature-types divided according to National Vegetation Classification categories U1a, U4 and U4/20. There are 35 of these feature-types recorded across 23 SSSI sites in the National Park. As a result, there is condition assessment information available for these areas.

However, roughly one third (12) of these features do not have a current condition record available. Additionally, only five of those features which have been monitored have high or complete confidence in their condition assessment, with only four features having been monitored in the last five years (the remaining feature had its assessment in 2012). These five monitored acid grasslands are found within Bonsall Leys, Longstone Moor, Ballidon Dale, Cressbrook Dale, and Long Dale SSSIs. Overall, five feature assessments have high/complete confidence, four have medium confidence, and 14 have low/no confidence[160].

Where condition information is available, the majority of lowland dry acid features in SSSI sites are in either favourable or unfavourable or recovering condition. This indicates that the majority of this feature-type, where recorded, is in a reasonably good condition[160].

As acid grassland is maintained through grazing, land management and agricultural practices have incredibly significant impacts on the extent and quality of this habitat. In the Peak District agricultural improvement, afforestation and overgrazing have had and will continue to have effects on lowland dry acid grass. Bracken encroachment also poses threats, as this plant dominates and can easily outcompete other species. Atmospheric pollution and increased acidification have also been linked to decreases in floristic diversity.

73.distribution:
Lowland dry acid grassland is widespread across the Peak District, with approximately 7823ha across the National Park, making this the priority grassland habitat with the largest cumulative area. Due to the geology on which lowland dry acid grassland grows, much of this habitat is found to the north, east and southwest areas with underlying gritstone geology, but patches do occur in the White Peak especially in wetter areas[158],[159]. Variations in the size and structure of this habitat type occur between sites, but some high-quality examples can be found around the Longshaw Estate, alongside Errwood Reservoir and the Goyt Valley, and near Ladybower reservoir.

 Example site - Goyt Valley and Errwood Reservoir

This area lies along the River Goyt between Buxton and Macclesfield. Moorland, woodlands and reservoirs are found here and a large proportion of the Goyt Valley is designated as a SSSI. Sheep grazing and moorland management, including rotational heather burning and grouse management, are responsible for the acid grassland that can be found around Errwood reservoir. Plants such as heath bedstraw and tormentil can be spotted here, in addition to birds such as meadow pipits (Anthus pratensis), skylarks (Alauda arvensis), ring ouzels (Turdus torquatus) and whinchats (Saxicola rubetra)[173],[174].

11.title: Meadows
11.key_data: There are roughly 2388ha of meadows across the Peak District, in all Landscape Character areas but in small fragmented patches which are mostly concentrated in the White and Southwest Peak. Only three SSSI sites have meadow features, none of which are in favourable condition, two are unfavourable but recovering while the other is declining. The data certainty for these condition assessments is very low as they have not been updated since at least 2013.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

33.description:
Meadows are grasslands that are traditionally managed, usually cut for hay but also used as grazing pasture. They can also occur in non-agricultural settings for example churchyards or road verges which are mown infrequently. As a consequence of their low-intensity management, meaning they receive few nutrient inputs and soil fertility remains low, meadows are typically species rich, with many different types of grasses, broadleaved plants and wildflowers. Altitude impacts the species present, and while the vast majority of meadows in the Peak District are characteristics of the lowland type, there are a small number of examples of rarer upland hay meadows. These are considered together as one feature-type in this report. The diverse assemblages of grasses and forbs in meadows host a wide range of invertebrates, for example many types of butterflies and bees, including the dark green fritillary (Speyeria aglaja), and birds such as skylarks (Alauda arvensis) and twites (Linaria flavirostris). As well as being important for biodiversity, meadows also have great historical and cultural significance, being popular in local literature and folklore.

Throughout the UK, there has been a huge decline in species rich meadows over the last century, with the Peak District being no exception. Meadows are highly susceptible to changes in land management and human influence, with moves towards silage rather than hay-making greatly impacting their extent and the diversity in remaining sites. This process includes more frequent cutting, which allows certain grass types to dominate, rather than a mixture of species. Changes in livestock abundance, type and grazing schedule have also seen much of this habitat degraded. Land management practices will have an unrivalled effect on the distribution and quality of meadows in the future, with issues being exacerbated by a changing climate.

75.condition:
Meadows in the Peak District are highly fragmented and very few are within protected areas – only three Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) in the Peak District contain meadow-features, all lowland meadows. Those with no protection at all are at greater risk of degradation and fragmentation. Within the three SSSI sites where condition information is available, two are in unfavourable but recovering condition which the other is in unfavourable but declining condition. However, none of these condition assessments have been updated since at least 2013, giving medium to low confidence in these assessments[160].
