Land management practices have a massive impact on the condition and number of meadows both in the Peak District and the UK as a whole. Techniques, such as hay- or silage-making, determine the species richness of the habitat, and nutrient and fertiliser usage can result in the loss of less competitive species and allow plants like nettles (Urtica dioica), common hogweed (Heracleum sphondylium) and cow parsley (Anthriscus sylvestris) to spread and dominate. This reduces the biodiversity and has knock on effects on the invertebrate, mammal and bird populations. Climate change will also see alterations in the diversity of meadows, as species that cannot tolerate hotter, drier summers, or wetter winters will be lost. Furthermore, changes in plant and insect lifecycle stages might lead to imbalance in pollination timing. Sites may also be lost as food pressures increase as a result of crop failures – due to erratic weather patterns.

74.distribution:
There are approximately 2388ha of meadows across all Landscape Character Areas (LCAs) in the Peak District, however they are most highly concentrated within the White and Southwest Peak LCAs, where traditional hay-cutting and grazing regimes persist. Many meadows are fairly small in size and fragmented, commonly alongside semi-improved grassland in wider agricultural landscapes. Some larger examples are seen in and around Monyash, and there are some concentrations near Warslow, as well as around Stoney Middleton and Grindleford[158],[159].

Example site – Hard Rake

The fields at Hard Rake are cut in July or August and then grazed, which maintains a low soil fertility while allowing a long growing season into the summer. The hay is used for winter animal feed, while the meadow hosts species including ox-eye daisy (Leucanthemum vulgare), knapweed (Centaurea nigra), yellow-rattle (Rhinanthus minor) and meadow vetchling (Lathyrus pratensis), while skylarks nest in the unmown grasses and forbs[175].

13.title: Purple moor grass and rush pastures
13.key_data: There are roughly 745ha of this habitat type in the Peak District across all Landscape Character Areas but the only sizable patches are in the Southwest Peak. There is limited condition data available for this habitat type, but of the six sites with condition records these indicate that condition is very variable overall.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

34.description:
Purple moor grass and rush pasture is typically found in areas of poorly drained and therefore acidic, peaty soils, where the vegetation is grazed, cut or burned. This creates relatively species-rich assemblages where purple moor grass (Molinia caerulea) and sharp-flowered rush (Juncus acutiflorus) are abundant. Other key species include wavy St. Johns wort (Hypericum undulatum), whorled caraway (Carum verticillatum), and meadow thistle (Cirsium dissectum) which creates vital habitat for breeding waders including snipe (Gallinago gallinago) and lapwing (Vanellus vanellus). In the Peak District these habitats are found in the highest abundance in the Southwest Peak, with a few other more sizable patches on the Eastern Moors, where it forms mosaics with other grassland habitat types.

The fragmentation of purple moor grass and rush pasture habitats makes them more vulnerable to land management decisions and climate change. Large swathes of wet grassland were lost in the Peak District in the 20th century as a result of drainage and agricultural practices, with many now being dominated by purple moor grass, instead of a mixture of grass species, or just overall very species poor. As purple moor grass and rush pastures need a certain level of water in the ground, changes in the water table due to drainage and agricultural changes – as well as climate change leading to high frequencies of droughts – can greatly impact these habitats. Types of livestock also affect the abundance and distribution, as cattle can keep purple moor grass restrained, but as sheep do not like to eat this tough sward and prefer finer grasses, an increase in sheep and decrease in cattle leads to increased dominance of purple moor grass.

76.condition:
Two SSSI feature-types in the SSSI record for the Peak District have been grouped here to indicate the condition of purple moor grass and rush pasture; acid grassland (upland) and mire grassland and rush pasture (upland). While the SSSI classification of mire grassland and rush pasture maps clearly over to the UKBAP classification of purple moor grass and rush pasture (see Landscape page for details on classifications used), acid grassland (upland) could include some habitat types which are more dissimilar to purple moor grass and rush pasture. However, in the Peak District, acid grassland (upland) habitat types included within this classification are likely to share significant characteristics with purple moor grass and rush pasture due to the nature of the altitude and underlying geology, and as such this feature has been included in the review of the condition recorded below[177].

Across these two feature types there are 13 records in eight SSSIs in the Peak District. Condition records are only available for six of these features, with features in every condition category indicating that condition is variable across sites[160].

Agricultural improvement and inappropriate land management have resulted in the distribution and quality of purple moor grass and rush pasture that we see in the Peak District today. Drainage and unsuitable fertiliser usage have affected the species composition and impacted the water table, leading to loss of species-rich rush pasture. Additionally, livestock changes have impacted the abundance of purple moor grass, as a reduction in cattle – which keep the tough, tussocky grass in check – and increase in sheep has allowed this habitat to spread. Sheep prefer finer grasses and typically avoid grazing on purple moor grass, which allows it to end up dominating areas. Overgrazing can also be an issue. In the future, to improve their resilience, patches of rush pasture should be joined up to become more interconnected. Climate change is likely to have significant impacts on this habitat, as the most probable modelling scenarios indicate an increase in hotter, drier summers, which have already been shown to have notable, serious effects on water tables.

75.distribution:
Approximately 745ha of purple moor grass and rush pasture can be found across all Landscape Character Areas (LCAs) in the Peak District. In most places these are very small habitat fragments, but the highest concentration by far is in the Southwest Peak LCA between the Roaches and Warslow, in the Leek Moors Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI). This is due to the underlying geology found here, as well as land management decisions and grazing in the area.[158],[159],[176].

Example site – Leek Moors

The Leek Moors SSSI covers an area of 3970ha in the Southwest Peak with underlying gritstone geology. It contains a mosaic of moorland and grassland habitat types resulting from fragmented land use. The purple moor grass and rush pastures in this area contribute towards its high density of breeding golden plover (Pluvialis apricaria) and snipe[176].

14.title: Upland calcareous grassland
14.key_data: There may be up to 219ha of upland calcareous grassland across the Peak District, however this is uncertain as location records for both upland and lowland calcareous grasslands overlap in some places. There are only three sites with condition records for this habitat type, two of which are favourable and the other unfavourable but no change.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

35.description:
Upland calcareous grasslands grow on fairly shallow and thin soils in limestone areas of the Peak District, general over 300 metres above sea level. As a result, this habitat is almost exclusively limited to the White Peak. Upland calcareous grasslands are typically much more species rich than upland acidic grassland habitats, and the calcareous grasslands in the Peak District are the most biodiverse habitats in the park. Often upland calcareous grasslands grow on soils that are more nutrient poor than their lowland counterpart, which results in a different species assemblage. This includes common bent (Agrostis capillaris), sheep’s fescue (Festuca ovina) and tormentil (Potentilla erecta) – are sometimes seen here.

The few patches of upland calcareous grasslands in the Peak District are scattered, fragmented and found as parts of habitat mosaics. A high proportion of limestone grasslands in the National Park are designated under Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) and Special Areas of Conservation (SAC), which provides them additional protection. Like many grasslands, upland calcareous grasslands are primarily maintained through livestock grazing, and face issues of both overgrazing and under grazing, which can ultimately result in succession to woodlands. Additionally, increasingly severe climatic change will impact species compositions of this habitat.

77.condition:
There are six SSSIs in the Peak District with upland calcareous grassland as a feature, which can be used to indicate the condition of this feature. However, only three of these sites has a current condition assessment of this feature, where two sites were in favourable condition and the other in unfavourable condition with no change since last assessment. This gives little indication of the overall condition of this feature due to the paucity of the data available[160].

The condition of this habitat is likely to decline without intervention in the future, due to the fragmented nature of the sites, which reduce their resilience. Overgrazing and land management practices can pose threats to these grasslands; however, without a certain level of grazing they run the risk of succession into mixed ash woods. Therefore, it can be challenging to strike the right balance, especially with different sites falling on different land owners’ property. The species composition of different sites is also likely to change with a changing climate, because, as it becomes hotter and drier (as is the most likely scenario in models), less adaptable and tolerant species will disappear as the conditions for this habitat type become increasingly scarce.

76.distribution:
There are only 219ha of upland calcareous grassland in the Peak District, predominantly in the White Peak and along its borders with other Landscape Character Areas. The largest stretches are found the south of the region around Dovedale and Biggin dale. It is worth noting that the Peak District National Park Authority’s internal ecological data for this area does not contain any records of upland calcareous grassland, with only records from the Priority Habitat Inventory showing areas of this habitat type. These records overlap with those of lowland calcareous grassland from the internal records; this also occurs in other areas of the National Park[158],[159]. Therefore, there is low certainty over the extent and location of this habitat type in the Peak District.

Example site – Dovedale  

Dovedale is a popular visitor destination in the south of the White Peak, which is famous of its steep sided limestone valley and scree slopes. Along the altitudinal gradient of the steep dale sides, the grassland communities change significantly, with upland calcareous grasslands being found in the highest parts where the soil is thin and leeched of nutrients. The species assemblage present includes nationally scarce species such as the limestone bedstraw (Galium sterneri)[178].

15.title: Good quality semi-improved grassland
15.key_data: There are roughly 10,161ha of good quality semi-improved grassland in the Peak District. This is not considered to be a priority habitat type and therefore does not undergo condition assessments as part of designated sites. Its condition is also relative to the priority habitats it could be transformed in to and its ability to act as a habitat corridor between these sites. This means there is no condition data available for this habitat type in the Peak District.

family.description: Ecological and geological features

36.description:
Good quality semi-improved grassland occurs where grassland has experienced a degree of agricultural “improvement”; i.e. the promotion of fast-growing grazing crops such as perennial ryegrass (Lolium perenne) and white clover (Trifolium repens) through grazing regimes, seeding, and the application of fertilisers. This habitat type is therefore not considered a priority habitat in its own right, however that fact it is only semi-improved means it can retain floral diversity and has the potential to be managed back towards a more ecological significant condition. Although less biodiverse than priority habitats, sites still host species such as skylarks (Alauda arvensis) and meadow pipits (Anthus pratensis). Such grasslands are abundant across the Peak District, generally outside of protected sites. As a result, this habitat type can act as a corridor between more higher quality grasslands which also makes it important to consider alongside the priority habitats.

This grassland type relies on certain land management actions and therefore is susceptible to changes in this which could cause it to either increase or decrease in extent and species composition. This is likely to be impacted by the policy and funding opportunities available to land managers, which can shift to promote both more intensive farming and more environmentally sustainable methods. Climate change could also impact this grassland type, for example the increased likelihood of grassland wildfires as temperature and precipitation patterns change.

78.condition:
As this habitat types is not a priority or protected feature there is less condition information than for other habitat types. It is also likely to be greatly variable between sites as it can occur across a wide variety of conditions and will be subject to different land management practices. These conditions will affect the ability for this habitat to be transformed into a higher priority habitat type or to act as a habitat corridor between priority sites, which means that it would be useful to have an understanding of this habitats condition in this regard.

The condition of good quality semi-improved grasslands could be improved by altering land management practices, such as reducing grazing intensity and removing artificial drainage. This is influenced by who owns and manages land, the social and cultural practices of land managers and the farming subsidy schemes that most land managers rely on. Therefore, a wide variety of factors could either positively or negatively impact the condition of this habitat type.

77.distribution: This habitat type is widespread and abundant in the Peak district, with roughly 10,161ha recorded. It occurs primarily in a mosaic with other grassland habitat types, but also moorland and heath, wetland, and woodland habitats[158],[159].

28.introduction:
The Peak District’s grasslands can be some of the most biodiverse habitats, with internationally important habitat and species such as the calcareous grasslands of the White Peak. Grasslands are also almost always farmed landscapes, relying on grazing  often by sheep or cattle to maintain their diversity. This makes them cultural as well as ecological habitats; places where people make their living and produce food. As a result, historic pressure to increase agricultural productivity has led to the loss of much of the Peak District’s historic species rich grassland, in favour of agriculturally “improved” grasslands, which require higher nutrient input in order to produce more grazing for livestock.

As a result, understanding what remains of the Peak District’s current priority grasslands is of vital importance. Much priority grassland is within protected areas, such as Sites of Special Scientific Interest, Special Areas of Conservation or Special Protected Areas. These can give an insight into the condition of grasslands through their condition monitoring record. However, this is only a sample from which to understand the condition of all of the Peak District’s priority grasslands and what factors may be causing them to change. Climate change will have a huge impact on grasslands, altering the climatic conditions in which they currently survive. Governance and legislation will have a significant impact on grasslands, with historic farming policy having driven much of the improvement of grasslands which exists today. The Farming Roadmap 2050 and the Land Use Framework will set this direction, while further land use and farming policy and funding will emerge over the coming years.

16.distribution: Priority grasslands are often highly fragmented in the Peak District, forming mosaics with other habitat types including non-priority grasslands as well as other priority habitats. The Dark Peak is dominated by lowland dry acid and semi-improved grasslands as a result of its acid soils. In the limestone areas of the White Peak upland and lowland calcareous grasslands can be found, while the Southwest Peak contains the largest extents of purple moor grass and rush pasture. The White Peak and Southwest Peak Landscape Character Areas also contain the most meadows due to the techniques of grazing and hay cutting in these areas that support this habitat type.

7.importance:
Grassland habitats contribute to a wide range of benefits alongside other ecological features. These include the provision of food and fibre as part of farmed systems, with the livestock that graze the Peak District’s grasslands going on to produce meat, dairy products and wool. This also supports the livelihoods and economy of rural communities. Good quality grasslands are also essential for healthy soils and controlling erosion; grassland species support natural soil carbon and nutrient cycle, alongside binding and stabilising soils. Grassland soils are also important carbon stores, often underestimated in comparison to woodland or peat-soil habitats.

For people, grasslands are also an important social and cultural side of the Peak District. The aesthetic quality of grasslands contributes to the tranquillity and beauty that benefits people in the Peak District. People benefit from health and wellbeing when they visit grassland areas to walk, wheel or cycle. This supports a sense of connection to place and cultural belonging.

8.quality: • Relying on SSSI condition data to understand the condition of these habitats will only give a partial picture as it does not account for sites outside of protected areas. Additionally, SSSI condition data is very often out of date, with many records not having been updated for 10-20 years or more. This means that the condition assumptions presented in this report are of very low certainty.

24.likelihood_text: It is possible that this impact will occur. The result of governance and legislation driving how land is managed make these both key factors. As grasslands rely on grazing to be maintained, and farming policy impacts how and where animals are put to graze, this has a key impact on grassland extent and condition. Legislation may push for more intensive farming which will reduce the condition of priority grasslands, but it may also push towards less intensive grazing which could allow tree succession; in either case, priority grasslands are reduced. This may be slightly compensated if current non-priority grasslands can be brought into a higher quality condition.
24.severity: This impact has the potential to be severe for grassland habitats as either agricultural improvement or reduced grazing pressure can alter grassland habitats very quickly. However, the full extent of this impact may not affect all areas across the National Park and is more likely to have localised impacts, reducing its overall severity. For example, a single wildfire may have a devastating impact but only over a specific area of grassland.
24.impact: Reduction in extent and condition of priority grasslands

3.impact:
Climate change has compound impacts on other factors. These are briefly laid out below with more detail on each of the relevant factor pages.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Due to climate change having unequal impacts globally, as a result of both physical and socio-economic conditions, international migration of people may increase the UK population and/or change the character of the UK population as a whole. Additionally, there may be increased demand for housing in rural areas as a result of disproportionate population growth and warming in urban areas. As a result, the Peak District may experience changes to the demographic character of both its residents and its visitors due to global and local population changes. There is little research into exactly what these changes may look like, however projections do indicate that current migration trends are likely to be amplified as a result of climate change[64].

Ecological change

The projected impacts of climate change are intrinsically linked to potential ecological changes. As the physical conditions which define species’ niches shift, both spatially and temporally, species distribution and phenology (timing of biological events) will change.

Cooke et al. (2026) model biodiversity change in the UK under a range of climate scenarios up to 2080[61]. They project “extensive community reorganisation” under any scenario with “the disappearance of current bioclimates and emergence of novel ones”. In the Peak District, this is likely to contribute to the local extinction of species, colonisation by novel species, changes to composition of biological communities, increase likelihood of invasive alien species and increased likelihood of pathogens.

Formulating and setting habitat and species targets, as has been the practice for many years, will need to be carefully re-examined as an approach.

Land management practices

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

4.impact:
Climate change

As outlined on the Climate change factor page, Representative Concentration Pathway modelling accounts for different future greenhouse gas emissions scenarios that result from different responses to climate change. These responses are profoundly shaped by social trends and demographic characteristics. Therefore, all climate change scenarios are intrinsically linked to demographic and sociocultural changes.

Governance and legislation

Potential changes to governance and legislation that impact the National Park are in turn impacted by social trends. For example, the changes in social attitudes to outdoor recreation discussed above could contribute to changes in access legislation if more people demand and campaign for an increased right to countryside access for recreation.

Land management practices

The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways discussion on the Land management practises factor page exemplify how demographic and sociocultural change could impact land management. Under different socio-economic scenarios, these pathways can be used to describe different possible future land use scenarios in the UK.

Visitation and access

Patterns and trends of visitation and access in the National Park are likely to be impacted by changes in the demographic and sociocultural character of both Peak District resident and visitors. This could result in impacts such as change to visitor numbers and changes in the behaviour of visitors due to changing attitudes to outdoor recreation.

6.impact:
Governance and legislation have the potential to impact all other factors due to the legislation and governance frameworks that underlie all action carried out in the UK. This could be drawn together in an almost infinite number of links, however certainty about what impacts are likely is very low, and many relevant ways in which governance and legislation impacts other factors have already been outlined above. Therefore, these are briefly summarised below with some additional impacts that have not yet been noted.

Factor

Possible impacts from governance and legislation

Climate change

Stronger commitments to emissions reduction and carbon sequestration and storage could help to reduce likelihood of global climate change impacts, e.g. changes to the Climate Change Act 2008 or additional global agreements.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Impacts on communities from changes to planning regulation (NFFP, local plan making process etc) could alter housing development in communities, potential knock-on impact to composition of communities.

Ecological change

Possibility for strengthened or weakened environmental protections, e.g. through BNG and biodiversity credits, changes to National Park legislation and governance, etc. Land use framework, LNRSs and 30x30 target may introduce stronger requirements and spatial planning for land to be managed for ecology.

Economy and industry

Changes to farm subsidy schemes may positively or negatively impact he viability of farm businesses. More NSIPs to support low carbon energy and transport infrastructure could support construction and operation jobs.

Land management practices

Farm subsidies and land management grants may incentivise changes to land uses and management actions. Land use framework may change how land use is determined. Changes to land ownership resulting in changed land management may result from enhance community right to buy to England[98].

Possible changes to legislation relating to driven grouse shooting, including further changes to moorland burning regulation about and an ongoing campaign to ban on driven grouse shooting[99], may result to changes in moorland management.

Pollution

Changes to the regulation of sewage waste outflow into freshwater would reduce freshwater pollution. Legislation relating to land management outline above could change agricultural pollution e.g. lower input farming reducing nutrient pollution.

Visitation and access

New access legislation could strength right to access, including permitted activities and areas with open access. Combined authorities may use visitor levies which could impact visitor access by presenting financial barrier, may cause inequality in access.

7.impact:
Climate change

As described above, land can be managed to mitigate the impacts of climate change by sequestering or preventing the further emission of fossil fuels. If the Peak District was managed to maximise this, it could help remove CO2 from the atmosphere to slow future climate change. However, on the scale of the Peak District this would have a relatively small impact on global climate change.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Where land management and ownership change, this could have consequences for the demographics of rural and farming communities, based on who is able to live and work in the Peak District. If land is consolidated under fewer ownership, this could mean that fewer people live and work on the land. However, changes to farming or conservation land management practices may result in more rural jobs. Therefore, it is difficult to make projections about exactly what these changes may look like.

Pollution

Certain land management practices can either result in or reduce pollution. Fertiliser run off from agricultural land can cause polluting effects in freshwater systems, and therefore moving toward lower input agricultural land management can reduce this pollution. Land management practices which stabilise soils, for example peatland restoration, can result in reduced top soil runoff and therefore less sediment contaminated with pollutants from industrial air pollution ending up downstream.

Visitation and access

The Peak District is widely known among visitors for its landscapes under their current management regimes, which promote people to visit the area and participate in different recreational activities. If land was managed differently, this could change people’s perception of the landscape and alter their visiting behaviour, as well as possible changes to access infrastructure which would need to adapt around changing land use.  This could be in the direction of reduced access and declining visitation, for example under agriculture intensification, or it could be increased visitation through ecotourism.

9.impact:
Ecological Change

Visitation and access has the potential to affect ecological change if it leads to impacts such as soil compaction and habitat degradation. Roadside verges have been identified as agricultural settings that may be rich in wildflowers and meadow species can be prone to invasion of more dominant ruderal species due to the nature of disturbance and additional nitrogen that occurs alongside roads and higher levels of traffic[71].

Pollution

If there are changes to visitor numbers, the current prevalence of car travel in how people access the National Park could have an effect on pollution: contributing to carbon emissions as well as noise and light pollution. The knock on demand for car or public transport related infrastructure could also therefore generate further embedded carbon and generate emissions during production.

There is little research into exactly what these changes may look like, however projections do indicate that current migration trends are likely to be amplified as a result of climate change[64].

Ecological change

The projected impacts of climate change are intrinsically linked to potential ecological changes. As the physical conditions which define species’ niches shift, both spatially and temporally, species distribution and phenology (timing of biological events) will change.

Cooke et al. (2026) model biodiversity change in the UK under a range of climate scenarios up to 2080[61]. They project “extensive community reorganisation” under any scenario with “the disappearance of current bioclimates and emergence of novel ones”. In the Peak District, this is likely to contribute to the local extinction of species, colonisation by novel species, changes to composition of biological communities, increase likelihood of invasive alien species and increased likelihood of pathogens.

Formulating and setting habitat and species targets, as has been the practice for many years, will need to be carefully re-examined as an approach.

Land management practices

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

Climate change

Change in ecological communities could alter the potential for carbon storage in biomass, which will impact the possibility for land-based mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions as is accounted for in net zero targets. For example, changes to blanket bog communities could result in less accumulation of peat soil, reducing carbon storage potential, and in the possible release of additional carbon from soil due to runoff, resulting in enhanced climate change. Ecological communities may also experience non-linear shifts, for example a sudden collapse in function in single biome, which could in turn provoke non-linear climatic impacts due to the impact on water, carbon and nutrient cycling.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Ecological change could impact on the demography and sociocultural practices of both residents and visitors to the Peak District due to the connections between people and their wider ecologies. Shifts in ecological communities could invoke changes to the composition of rural communities, as the possibility for agricultural livelihoods changes and people’s connection to and sense of belonging in the landscape shifts. Additionally, visitors to the Peak District come in part to interact with the ecology of the landscape, from foraging to taking in the view. Changes to these communities may result in different people visiting in different ways.

Land management practices take place in relation to the underlying ecological communities. Therefore, changes to this ecology are likely to result in changed land management practices. For example, in the Peak District, uplands currently managed for grouse moors may be managed differently if the red grouse experiences population decline and the composition upland moorland habitats shift to make this form of moorland management no longer sustainable. Similarly, agricultural practices may have to change if different compositions of agri-ecological systems emerge, pests and diseases impact on crops and livestock, etc.

Pollution

The potential destabilisation of moorland soils as a result of changes to upland vegetation communities could resulting in the wash out of heavy metal pollution stored in these soils from industrial revolution. This would have downstream consequences as this pollution is spread, potentially having further ecological impacts as well as impacting agricultural land and drinking water.

26.likelihood_text: This impact is likely, partly as a result of the wide range of causes that may lead to it. Shifts in species composition in habitats is a feature of ongoing background ecological change, but this is likely be exacerbated by anthropogenic causes. Climate change, in combination and related to other factors such as changes in land management practices, will further this as the underlying conditions on which species assemblages are constructed continue to move further away from the baseline.
26.severity: This impact may only be minor over the next ten years, but will become increasingly severe over time as the impacts of climate change develop. It is also possible that the negative consequences of this impact could be mitigated, for example by managing changes in species composition to support the continuation of the overall functioning of ecosystems, so that benefits like clean water or climatic regulation continue to be provided. This would reduce the overall severity of the impact in some ways.

6.impact:
Governance and legislation have the potential to impact all other factors due to the legislation and governance frameworks that underlie all action carried out in the UK. This could be drawn together in an almost infinite number of links, however certainty about what impacts are likely is very low, and many relevant ways in which governance and legislation impacts other factors have already been outlined above. Therefore, these are briefly summarised below with some additional impacts that have not yet been noted.

Factor

Possible impacts from governance and legislation

Climate change

Stronger commitments to emissions reduction and carbon sequestration and storage could help to reduce likelihood of global climate change impacts, e.g. changes to the Climate Change Act 2008 or additional global agreements.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Impacts on communities from changes to planning regulation (NFFP, local plan making process etc) could alter housing development in communities, potential knock-on impact to composition of communities.

Ecological change

Possibility for strengthened or weakened environmental protections, e.g. through BNG and biodiversity credits, changes to National Park legislation and governance, etc. Land use framework, LNRSs and 30x30 target may introduce stronger requirements and spatial planning for land to be managed for ecology.

Economy and industry

Changes to farm subsidy schemes may positively or negatively impact he viability of farm businesses. More NSIPs to support low carbon energy and transport infrastructure could support construction and operation jobs.

Land management practices

Farm subsidies and land management grants may incentivise changes to land uses and management actions. Land use framework may change how land use is determined. Changes to land ownership resulting in changed land management may result from enhance community right to buy to England[98].

Possible changes to legislation relating to driven grouse shooting, including further changes to moorland burning regulation about and an ongoing campaign to ban on driven grouse shooting[99], may result to changes in moorland management.

Pollution

Changes to the regulation of sewage waste outflow into freshwater would reduce freshwater pollution. Legislation relating to land management outline above could change agricultural pollution e.g. lower input farming reducing nutrient pollution.

Visitation and access

New access legislation could strength right to access, including permitted activities and areas with open access. Combined authorities may use visitor levies which could impact visitor access by presenting financial barrier, may cause inequality in access.

7.impact:
Climate change

As described above, land can be managed to mitigate the impacts of climate change by sequestering or preventing the further emission of fossil fuels. If the Peak District was managed to maximise this, it could help remove CO2 from the atmosphere to slow future climate change. However, on the scale of the Peak District this would have a relatively small impact on global climate change.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Where land management and ownership change, this could have consequences for the demographics of rural and farming communities, based on who is able to live and work in the Peak District. If land is consolidated under fewer ownership, this could mean that fewer people live and work on the land. However, changes to farming or conservation land management practices may result in more rural jobs. Therefore, it is difficult to make projections about exactly what these changes may look like.

Pollution

Certain land management practices can either result in or reduce pollution. Fertiliser run off from agricultural land can cause polluting effects in freshwater systems, and therefore moving toward lower input agricultural land management can reduce this pollution. Land management practices which stabilise soils, for example peatland restoration, can result in reduced top soil runoff and therefore less sediment contaminated with pollutants from industrial air pollution ending up downstream.

Visitation and access

The Peak District is widely known among visitors for its landscapes under their current management regimes, which promote people to visit the area and participate in different recreational activities. If land was managed differently, this could change people’s perception of the landscape and alter their visiting behaviour, as well as possible changes to access infrastructure which would need to adapt around changing land use.  This could be in the direction of reduced access and declining visitation, for example under agriculture intensification, or it could be increased visitation through ecotourism.

8.impact:
Climate change

Particulate pollution can contribute towards climate change as a result of airborne particulates absorbing heat and light, contributing to atmospheric warming and cloud formation[118].

Ecological changes

Water pollution alters the chemical environment for aquatic life, impacting species’ abilities to reproduce. Excess nutrients or changes to pH cause imbalance with some species thriving at the expense of others, resulting changes to the diversity and composition of aquatic ecosystems. This can also have knock on impacts on terrestrial ecosystems which interact with polluted water sources[119].

Nitrogen air pollution alters lichen community composition, with some species being nitrogen-tolerant and others nitrogen-sensitive. In this was lichens can be used as indicators of nitrogen air pollution[120].

45.title: Lowland fens
45.key_data: There is approximately 163ha of lowland fen habitat in the Peak District, widely distributed across the whole National Park. There are twelve lowland fen features in the National Park recorded in the SSSI condition inventory. Only 3 of these twelve features have recorded condition data, with one in favourable condition and two in unfavourable but recovering condition.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

20.description:
Lowland fens are waterlogged wetland habitats that typically form on mineral rich and peaty soils. They receive water and nutrients from multiple sources, including groundwater, surface run-off and rainfall, and normally display vegetation structures formed of tall herbs, reeds and tussocky grass. The structure and diversity of lowland fens varies with location and hydrology, and they can be separated into two main categories: poor fens and rich fens. Poor fens are found where the underlying geology is more acidic, namely in the uplands of the Dark Peak, whereas rich fens are typically found in more calcareous areas in the lowlands of the White Peak. Rich fens are, as the name suggests, often more biodiverse habitats, supporting a variety of invertebrates – for example, beetles, moths and flies.

In the Peak District, lowland fens are a rare habitat, with most examples small and fragmented. The majority are found in the White Peak. The fragmented nature means resilience of this habitat is lowered, and at risk of factors such as pollution and land management practices. As a wetland habitat, lowland fens are susceptible to polluted groundwater and run-off of fertilisers from agricultural land. Additionally, as they need saturated land, any changes to the water table in the local area can lead to drying out and the collapse of the habitat – a situation that will likely become more frequent with the increase in drought periods due to climate change.

62.condition:
Lowland fen habitat-types are recorded as three distinct features in the SSSI record;

  • Lowland fens, including basin, flood-plain, open water transition and valley fens
  • Lowland wetland including basin fen, valley fen, floodplain fen, waterfringe fen, spring/flush fen and raised bog lagg
  • Spring/flush fen (lowland)

These habitats are presents as a feature of nine Sites of Special Scientific Interest in the Peak District, with 12 individual features accounting for sub-types of this habitat. Condition records show that one of these 12 lowland fen features is deemed to be in favourable condition, and two others are in an unfavourable but recovering condition. The remaining nine features fen do not have a current condition assessment[160]. Therefore, while available data suggests that condition is stable or improving, more thorough condition assessment is required to improve the certainty of this assumption.

With appropriate management, the condition of lowland fens could be maintained and improved. However, climate change – as well as land management practices and pollution – are likely to have an impact on this habitat’s extent and condition. Changes in nutrient levels as a result of fertiliser run-off, and pollution in groundwater and rainfall, can all determine the species assemblage of lowland fens. Nutrient increases may lead to influxes of more generalist species, which may outcompete the local populations. Climate change is already creating longer and more intensive hot weather and drought periods, which could have lasting impacts on the water table and saturation of the land.

60.distribution: Lowland fens in the Peak District are fragmented and small, with approximately 163 hectares across the whole National Park. This habitat type is widespread across the Peak District and is present in all Landscape Character Areas, and is predominantly found in mosaics with other habitats including other freshwater and wetland habitats as well as woodland, grassland and moorland. While widespread, this habitat type is less present in both the fertile lowlands of the White Peak, probably as a result of this habitat being improved for agriculture, and the upland moors of the Dark Peak likely due to their altitude[158],[159].

46.title: Blanket bog
46.key_data: There is approximately 29,780ha of blanket bog in the Peak District, primarily in the Dark Peak, Eastern Moors and South West Peak landscape character areas. Too little condition information regarding blanket bogs in SSSI sites is available to indicate the condition of this habitat type. Outcomes of restoration work on blanket bog suggest that recovery can be quick (within ~10 years) where restoration work is applied.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

21.description:
Blanket bog occurs in areas where the soil and rocks are of an acidic nature, and the terrain is flat or gently sloping. This allows water to accumulate and create waterlogged conditions, which along with the acidic, nutrient poor conditions, allow dead plant material to build up and turn into peat. These habitats, when active and in good condition, are extremely important stores of carbon, and although nutrient poor, can support a range of species. Blanket bogs in good condition also improve water quality of the surrounding areas. Bog mosses such as Sphagnum grow in the most wet areas, along with cross-leaved heath (Erica tetralix) and cotton grass (Eriophorum angustifolium). Drier areas that are transitioning to other moorland and heathland types host heather (Calluna vulgaris), bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus), and purple moor grass (Molinia caerulea). The majority of blanket bog in the Peak District is found in the Dark Peak, as well as the Eastern Moors and South West Peak, and much is protected within Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) and Special Areas of Conservation (SACs). Many bird species are found around blanket bog, such as: golden plover (Pluvialis apricaria), merlin (Falco columbarius), dunlin (Calidris alpina), meadow pipit (Anthus pratensis), red grouse (Lagopus lagopus), curlew (Numenius arquata), twite (Linaria flavirostris), ring ouzel (Turdus torquatus), wheatear (Oenanthe oenanthe) and whinchat (Saxicola rubetra).

The blanket bog in the Peak District has experienced many years of degradation as a result of peat cutting and drainage, intentional burning and wildfires, overgrazing, and historical industrial pollution. This has meant what was once stores of carbon now act more as sources, releasing carbon into the atmosphere. These processes have also dried out these wetlands, and allowed the encroachment of heather and purple moor grasses – and even bare, exposed peat in the worst affected areas – alongside the reduction of Sphagnum mosses. However, many restoration projects have been working to reverse these situations, in particular those carried out by the Moors for the Future Partnership. These efforts work to revegetate the exposed peat and raise the water table, so areas can become more waterlogged again, at which point Sphagnum mosses are planted to establish an active bog.

Only two sites have available condition information, with both sites in unfavourable condition but one recovering while the other is declining[160]. This does not support any overall condition assessment of blanket bog in the Peak District.

Moors for the Future Partnership work to restore degraded blanket bog across the Peak District and wider South Pennine area. In their 2022 assessment of restoration sites, it was reported that “at the bare peat sites, vegetation cover returned to almost 100% within 5–7 years after initial revegetation work” and “indicator species succeeded seeded and natural pioneer species, developing ~100% cover within 10 years”. This indicates that where restoration work is underway, blanket bog can recover its condition fairly rapidly[162].

However, going forward, climate change is likely to significantly impact the capacity for blanket bogs to both recover into or maintain favourable condition. Changing temperature and precipitation patterns will impact these areas due to their reliance on precipitation for water and nutrient input. This will also increase the likelihood of wildfires which, combined with ignition risks from land management practices and visitor behaviour, could have widespread impacts on the vegetation in this habitat type.

61.distribution: Blanket bog is the predominant habitat across the high uplands of the Dark Peak, South West Peak and Eastern Moors, with other fragmented areas where conditions allow, with a total area of approximately 29,780ha across the whole National Park. This is the largest area of any of the priority habitats in the Peak District[158],[159]. Significant examples of blanket bog include the Kinder Plateau, the highest area in the Peak District at 636m above sea level. This area is characterised by deep peat intersected by erosion gullies, and is an important catchment for drinking water[161].

47.title: Upland flushes, fens and swamps
47.key_data: There is approximately 1,095ha of upland flushes, fens and swamps in the Peak District, and while widely distributed are predominantly found in the higher areas including the Dark Peak, Eastern Moors and South West Peak. Limited condition data is available for this habitat type, but of the three sites which are recorded they are all in either favourable or unfavourable but recovering condition.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

22.description:
Upland flushes, fens and swamps occur in waterlogged, often peaty areas where the water table is extremely high – in plenty of places even rising to above the surface. They receive water and nutrients from multiple sources including groundwater, surface water and rainfall. In the Peak District these habitats are found in small patches usually along valley sides in the South West Peak, Dark Peak and associated landscape character areas. The composition of species in each location can vary depending on pH, mineral content, water source and hydrology, with some example species including lesser skullcap (Scutellaria minor), round-leaved sundew (Drosera rotundifolia) and ivy-leaved bellflower (Wahlenbergia hederacea). These in turn support diversity of invertebrate and vertebrate species, including snipe (Gallinago gallinago).

As areas of upland flushes, fens and swamps in the Peak District are very small and found within other moorland habitats, they can often be overlooked and affected by land management processes intended for other habitats. Their small size increases their vulnerability to other factors as well, such as climate change – along with the increased droughts, floods and more extreme weather associated with it. These changes in weather patterns and water availability will impact the water table, which in turn will affect upland fens, flushes and swamps and will likely lead to some locations drying out.

64.condition:
Upland flushes, fens and swamps are recorded across three different feature-types in the Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) record for the Peak District;

  • Short sedge acidic fen (upland)
  • Spring-head, rill and flush (upland)
  • Transition mire, ladder fen and quaking bog (upland)

There are nine records of these features across six different SSSIs in the National Park. Out of the nine features recorded, only three have condition information available, with two features in favourable condition and one in unfavourable but recovering condition[160]. Therefore, where the data is available this indicates upland flushes, fens and swamps are in a relatively good condition, however the lack of data makes this very uncertain.

The extent and species assemblages present in this habitat can vary between sites across the National Park due to the hydrology, geology and mineral composition of each location. For example, in the SSSI record there are three habitat sub-types that have been grouped under upland flushes, fens and swamps for this report: short sedge acidic fen (upland), spring-head, rill and flush (upland), and transition mire, ladder fen and quaking bog (upland)[160]. As there is variation in the species composition across sites, this could mean that certain sub-types of these habitats are more vulnerable to factors than others, and so may be lost in the future. However, this could also mean that the habitat type as a whole is more resistant due to its diversity, which could support adaptation to change climatic conditions.

The isolation and fragmentation of this habitat type can mean that it is at greater risk from impact by factors including climate change, land management practices, and pollution. Climate change, and the increased length, frequency and severity of drought periods it will result in, will affect the height of the water table; as these habitats need waterlogged conditions, and without a steady supply of rainfall, surface run off and groundwater, they will dry out. Additionally, land management practices, and pollution as fertiliser run off from agriculture, can lead to nutrient enrichment and encroachment from generalist species, which changes the species assemblage of the area.

62.distribution: While identified in all Landscape Character Areas of the Peak District, upland flushes, fens and swamps are predominantly found in the higher areas of the National Park in the Dark Peak, Eastern Moors and South West Peak. There is roughly 1,065ha of this habitat overall in the Peak District, however this is highly fragmented and tends to occur in a mosaic alongside other wetland and grassland habitat types. It can occur as a marginal transition zone between lowland fen and lowland dry acid grassland, and extensive blanket bog areas. Larger areas in the South West Peak can be seen to occur alongside purple moorgrass and rush pasture[158],[159].

48.title: Ponds
48.key_data: There are approximately 3065 ponds in the Peak District, with 477 of these recorded as “priority habitat”. Ponds occur in all Landscape Character Areas of the Peak District but are most highly concentrated in the White Peak, which includes many artificially created dew ponds. Around one quarter of priority habitat ponds are rated A for condition (the highest condition rating category).

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

23.description:
Ponds are small, at under 2ha, permanent or seasonal bodies of freshwater that can be natural or artificially made. Ponds can vary greatly in size and location, and as a result can support very different species assemblages from one another. These bodies of water are found across the Peak District, but the highest concentrations are found in the White Peak – where there are many dew ponds. These pond types are artificially made, and primarily used as water sources for livestock. Beyond dew ponds there are naturally formed ponds, moorlands ponds, fish ponds and ponds associated with industrial workings, including former coal and mineral works. The ponds found in the National Park support a variety of life, with examples of many different types of fish and aquatic invertebrates being seen, but one of the most well-known species seen in the White Peak especially is the great crested newt (Triturus cristatus).

The number of ponds in the Peak District has declined over the decades due to neglect and land management changes. Dew ponds as well have suffered from being filled in or damaged from livestock trampling and lack of maintenance. Additionally, those that do remain have sometimes experienced management that – although retains the functionality of the pond – destroys historic aspects of its structure. Ponds as aquatic habitats are particularly vulnerable to pollution and intensive farming practices that result in fertiliser and pesticide run off. As these increase in concentration in the habitat they can lead to eutrophication, which allows the unrestrained growth of algae, which then limits the amount of oxygen available for other species. As a result of these habitats being static bodies of water, land management practices can have particularly harmful impacts.

65.condition:
Ponds are not a feature of any Sites of Special Scientific interest in the Peak District[160]. The Peak District National Park Authority’s internal ecological data identifies 477 ‘priority habitat’ ponds and a further 2512 non-priority habitat ponds[159]. Using a condition rating of A-C, this data shows that priority ponds tend to be in better condition, with nearly a quarter being rating A, while non-priority habitats are more likely to be rated C. However, for both priority and especially non-priority ponds, the majority of records have no associated condition rating and even for those that do, this may not have been updated for as much as 25 years and so has low certainty.

63.distribution: Ponds are widely distributed across the whole of the National Park, with approximately 3065 ponds in total. These are most highly concentrated in the White Peak scattered throughout agricultural land especially artificial dew ponds. Contrastingly, the White Peak has the lowest concentration of rivers across the Peak District due to the porous underlying limestone geology, and as such ponds in this area are a vital freshwater source both agriculturally and within the wider ecology systems[158],[159].

49.title: Rivers and streams
49.key_data: There are over 867km of rivers and streams in the Peak District, more highly concentrated in the uplands of the Dark and Southwest Peak but present across the National Park. The overall condition of rivers across 93.4% of records was moderate, while the ecological condition assessment of the same records showed 31.1% in good condition and 62.3% in moderate condition.

24.description:
There are six river catchments across the Peak District: the Dove, Derbyshire Derwent, Don and Rother, and Aire and Calder, which flow into the Humber; and the Upper Mersey and Weaver Gowy, which flow into the Mersey. Because of the linear nature of rivers as a habitat, they can cross through many other habitat types and many flow through protected sites including Sites of Special Scientific interest and Special Areas of Conservation. Many stretches also show evidence of human interference including straightening, drainage, and disconnection from flood plains as a result of historical land management practices.

 Different stretches host different species, with rivers and streams in the White Peak tending to possess greater biodiversity. Notable species include white-clawed crayfish (Austropotamobius pallipes), brook lamprey (Lampetra planeri), brown trout (Salmo trutta), and dipper (Cinclus cinclus). Invasive species threaten native river and riparian ecosystems, for example crayfish plague from American signal crayfish (Pacifastacus leniusculus) and Himalayan balsam (Impatiens glandulifera). Climate change will have multiple impacts across rivers and streams, from increased temperatures in rivers and streams, to drought and permanent drying pout of some streams, to flood risks and increased sedimentation. Healthy freshwater ecosystems are an essential part of providing clean drinking water both in and beyond the park. Peatland restoration work can support the protection of good water quality and raise the water table to help prevent water shortages.

Ecological condition shows a more mixed picture, with 100% records from the Weaver Gowy being in good ecological condition however this is based on only three records. 64.distribution: There are roughly 867km of rivers across the Peak District in all Landscape Character Areas. The characteristics of the rivers and streams within these vary greatly across the National Park depending on the underlying geology. Smaller rivers and streams are concentrated in the high moorlands of the Dark and Southwest Peak where headwaters begin in acidic, boggy regions conditions before flowing into the characteristic cloughs and valleys towards the lowlands. The Derwent Valley Landscape Character Area is defined by containing the larger river Derwent which is fed by many of these headwaters. A small number of streams rise out of caves in the limestone regions of the White Peak but this area generally contains fewer waterways due to the porous nature of the underlying limestone, which can also result in the seasonality of those streams which can be found in this area[163].

8.introduction:
The Peak District experiences a high level of rainfall as a result of its elevation, which creates conditions for the National Park’s significant wetland and freshwater habitats. These support a wide diversity of plant, animal and fungal species as well as contributing to the character of the landscape which is known and loved by many. Starting at the highest reaches in blanket bogs, water flows off the moorlands into the variety of rivers and streams within the six catchments that the National Park feeds, flowing eventually into either the Humber to the east or the Mersey to the west. Along the way, these waters feed the thousands of ponds as well as other wetland habitat types, from the flushes, fens and swamps of the uplands to the lowland fens. This interconnected water system is of vital benefit to the communities in a wide area surrounding the Peak District, by supplying clean and plentiful water to millions of homes in the north of England.

Many of these freshwater and wetland habitats are protected as Sites of Special Scientific Interest, which help to protect their priority habitat features as well as supporting an understanding of condition where monitoring data is available. Other sites may be protected under other designations, including Special Areas of Conservation or Special Protected Areas. These support the protection of freshwater and wetland sites to mitigate against the factors which may impact them, which range from climate change, to changes in land management practices, to pollution. The changes in seasonal temperature and precipitation patterns that will result from climate change will have huge impacts on freshwater and wetland habitats, by altering water cycling and effecting the conditions that wetland species need to thrive. The drying out of land can also result from land management practices, for example, where draining land is practiced to increase the areas of land in cultivation. Pollution can also have greater impacts in wet habitats compared to others, as water can transport pollutants far from their site of release to impact these habitats downstream.

15.distribution: The distribution of the different priority freshwater and wetland habitat types is uneven across the National Park. The gritstone areas of Dark Peak and its fringes, the Eastern Moors and the Southwest Peak contain the majority of the blanket bog, upland flushes, fens and swamps, and lowland fens, as well as many rivers and streams. The Derwent Valley Landscape Character Area (LCA) is significantly shaped by the upper reaches of the river Derwent that flow through it. The White Peak LCA is significant in containing very few wetland habitats or rivers, as a result of its porous underlying limestone geology, but does have this highest concentration of ponds within the National Park, many of which are associated with historic farming practices, such as dew ponds, and provide a vital habitat for aquatic and semi-aquatic species in this otherwise often dry landscape.

6.importance:
Freshwater and wetland habitats make a vital contribution to a wide range of the Peak District’s benefits. Healthy and functioning wetland ecosystems are essential to the provision of clean and plentiful water, with blanket bogs able to store water in the uplands like a sponge. This also contributes to flood protection, reducing the rate that water flows off the uplands and thereby protecting communities downstream in times of heavy rain. Wetlands across the Peak District also help to prevent fires, with wetter habitats less likely to catch light and spread uncontrolled fires.

The Peak District’s freshwaters and wetlands are also often farmed areas, contributing to the National Park’s output of food and fibre. Ponds are essential to this, providing drinking water and respite from heat to farm animals. Finally, wetlands are some of our most culturally significant habitats, contributing towards people’s connection to the landscape and the tranquillity and beauty visitors and residents experience. The history of the Peak District’s extensive blanket bogs, being restored from their damaged condition as a result of industrial pollution, is a national success story that should be celebrated for generations to come.

7.quality: • Relying on SSSI condition data to understand the condition of these habitats will only give a partial picture as it does not account for sites outside of protected areas. Additionally, SSSI condition data is very often out of date, with many records not having been updated for 10-20 years or more. This means that the condition assumptions presented in this report are of very low certainty.

27.likelihood_text:
This impact is likely to continue, as land management practices have already significantly altered the water table in some places by processes of artificial drainage.
In addition, climate change projections indicate that seasonal precipitation patterns are rapidly changing, which could be exacerbated by ecological changes. For example, if areas become more populated by trees this may impact the water table. While summers will be drier, winters may also become wetter which could cause dramatic fluctuations in the water table annually as well as an overall drop in the water table.
27.severity: Over the period of the next management plan (up to 2033) this impact may be moderate, however, its severity is likely to continue to increase over time unless significant climate change mitigation measures are implemented. Land management practices have the potential to mitigate some of this impact by removing artificial drainage and promoting re-wetting, for example the gully-blocking carried out to help restore blanket bogs. This could be supported by changes in land ownership and by funding allocation to support such measures.
