3.impact:
Climate change has compound impacts on other factors. These are briefly laid out below with more detail on each of the relevant factor pages.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Due to climate change having unequal impacts globally, as a result of both physical and socio-economic conditions, international migration of people may increase the UK population and/or change the character of the UK population as a whole. Additionally, there may be increased demand for housing in rural areas as a result of disproportionate population growth and warming in urban areas. As a result, the Peak District may experience changes to the demographic character of both its residents and its visitors due to global and local population changes. There is little research into exactly what these changes may look like, however projections do indicate that current migration trends are likely to be amplified as a result of climate change[64].

Ecological change

The projected impacts of climate change are intrinsically linked to potential ecological changes. As the physical conditions which define species’ niches shift, both spatially and temporally, species distribution and phenology (timing of biological events) will change.

Cooke et al. (2026) model biodiversity change in the UK under a range of climate scenarios up to 2080[61]. They project “extensive community reorganisation” under any scenario with “the disappearance of current bioclimates and emergence of novel ones”. In the Peak District, this is likely to contribute to the local extinction of species, colonisation by novel species, changes to composition of biological communities, increase likelihood of invasive alien species and increased likelihood of pathogens.

Formulating and setting habitat and species targets, as has been the practice for many years, will need to be carefully re-examined as an approach.

Land management practices

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

5.impact:
Climate change

Change in ecological communities could alter the potential for carbon storage in biomass, which will impact the possibility for land-based mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions as is accounted for in net zero targets. For example, changes to blanket bog communities could result in less accumulation of peat soil, reducing carbon storage potential, and in the possible release of additional carbon from soil due to runoff, resulting in enhanced climate change. Ecological communities may also experience non-linear shifts, for example a sudden collapse in function in single biome, which could in turn provoke non-linear climatic impacts due to the impact on water, carbon and nutrient cycling.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Ecological change could impact on the demography and sociocultural practices of both residents and visitors to the Peak District due to the connections between people and their wider ecologies. Shifts in ecological communities could invoke changes to the composition of rural communities, as the possibility for agricultural livelihoods changes and people’s connection to and sense of belonging in the landscape shifts. Additionally, visitors to the Peak District come in part to interact with the ecology of the landscape, from foraging to taking in the view. Changes to these communities may result in different people visiting in different ways.

Land management practices

Land management practices take place in relation to the underlying ecological communities. Therefore, changes to this ecology are likely to result in changed land management practices. For example, in the Peak District, uplands currently managed for grouse moors may be managed differently if the red grouse experiences population decline and the composition upland moorland habitats shift to make this form of moorland management no longer sustainable. Similarly, agricultural practices may have to change if different compositions of agri-ecological systems emerge, pests and diseases impact on crops and livestock, etc.

Pollution

The potential destabilisation of moorland soils as a result of changes to upland vegetation communities could resulting in the wash out of heavy metal pollution stored in these soils from industrial revolution. This would have downstream consequences as this pollution is spread, potentially having further ecological impacts as well as impacting agricultural land and drinking water.

6.impact:
Governance and legislation have the potential to impact all other factors due to the legislation and governance frameworks that underlie all action carried out in the UK. This could be drawn together in an almost infinite number of links, however certainty about what impacts are likely is very low, and many relevant ways in which governance and legislation impacts other factors have already been outlined above. Therefore, these are briefly summarised below with some additional impacts that have not yet been noted.

Factor

Possible impacts from governance and legislation

Climate change

Stronger commitments to emissions reduction and carbon sequestration and storage could help to reduce likelihood of global climate change impacts, e.g. changes to the Climate Change Act 2008 or additional global agreements.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Impacts on communities from changes to planning regulation (NFFP, local plan making process etc) could alter housing development in communities, potential knock-on impact to composition of communities.

Ecological change

Possibility for strengthened or weakened environmental protections, e.g. through BNG and biodiversity credits, changes to National Park legislation and governance, etc. Land use framework, LNRSs and 30x30 target may introduce stronger requirements and spatial planning for land to be managed for ecology.

Economy and industry

Changes to farm subsidy schemes may positively or negatively impact he viability of farm businesses. More NSIPs to support low carbon energy and transport infrastructure could support construction and operation jobs.

Land management practices

Farm subsidies and land management grants may incentivise changes to land uses and management actions. Land use framework may change how land use is determined. Changes to land ownership resulting in changed land management may result from enhance community right to buy to England[98].

Possible changes to legislation relating to driven grouse shooting, including further changes to moorland burning regulation about and an ongoing campaign to ban on driven grouse shooting[99], may result to changes in moorland management.

Pollution

Changes to the regulation of sewage waste outflow into freshwater would reduce freshwater pollution. Legislation relating to land management outline above could change agricultural pollution e.g. lower input farming reducing nutrient pollution.

Visitation and access

New access legislation could strength right to access, including permitted activities and areas with open access. Combined authorities may use visitor levies which could impact visitor access by presenting financial barrier, may cause inequality in access.

7.impact:
Climate change

As described above, land can be managed to mitigate the impacts of climate change by sequestering or preventing the further emission of fossil fuels. If the Peak District was managed to maximise this, it could help remove CO2 from the atmosphere to slow future climate change. However, on the scale of the Peak District this would have a relatively small impact on global climate change.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Where land management and ownership change, this could have consequences for the demographics of rural and farming communities, based on who is able to live and work in the Peak District. If land is consolidated under fewer ownership, this could mean that fewer people live and work on the land. However, changes to farming or conservation land management practices may result in more rural jobs. Therefore, it is difficult to make projections about exactly what these changes may look like.

Pollution

Certain land management practices can either result in or reduce pollution. Fertiliser run off from agricultural land can cause polluting effects in freshwater systems, and therefore moving toward lower input agricultural land management can reduce this pollution. Land management practices which stabilise soils, for example peatland restoration, can result in reduced top soil runoff and therefore less sediment contaminated with pollutants from industrial air pollution ending up downstream.

Visitation and access

The Peak District is widely known among visitors for its landscapes under their current management regimes, which promote people to visit the area and participate in different recreational activities. If land was managed differently, this could change people’s perception of the landscape and alter their visiting behaviour, as well as possible changes to access infrastructure which would need to adapt around changing land use.  This could be in the direction of reduced access and declining visitation, for example under agriculture intensification, or it could be increased visitation through ecotourism.

28.likelihood_text: This impact is unlikely to occur in full over the period of the 2028-33 National Park Management Plan. However, it is likely that it will worsen, with populations starting to decrease and become more fragmented. Therefore, while species may not be completely lost in the next 10 years, they may in the next 20 or 30 years, with tipping points – points of no return where management actions cannot rebuild the population - occurring on this shorter timeframe.
28.severity: This could be a moderate to severe impact; the reason for the range in this rating is that in some cases, the function that a species plays in a habitat or ecosystem may be replaced by a novel species, reducing the overall severity. However, this will not be possible in all cases and would only be possible under certain conditions or with human intervention, e.g. to support colonisation of new species through translocation.

29.likelihood_text: It is likely that this impact will occur. There are many factors which have historically led to the current extent of blanket bog, and present and future factors are likely to work in combination to reduce its extent. This is primarily as a result of climate change, which is leading to drying out and change in the water table that are fundamental to blanket bog conditions. Land management practices can positively impact this habitat by supporting its regeneration, but it is likely that in places this will become less effective over time as the underlying climatic conditions shift.
29.severity: Over the next ten years this impact is expected to be moderate. The scale of the reduction in blanket bog extent is hard to determine, partly due to the fact that conservation practices may support the recovery of this habitat. Conversely increasingly large wildfire could cause the major and rapid loss of large areas of this habitat, which takes a long time and intense management to be restored. Over a longer timescale this impact is going to become more severe, as the impacts of climate change worsen and tipping points area reached.
29.impact: Reduction in blanket bog condition and extent

The projected impacts of climate change are intrinsically linked to potential ecological changes. As the physical conditions which define species’ niches shift, both spatially and temporally, species distribution and phenology (timing of biological events) will change.

Cooke et al. (2026) model biodiversity change in the UK under a range of climate scenarios up to 2080[61]. They project “extensive community reorganisation” under any scenario with “the disappearance of current bioclimates and emergence of novel ones”. In the Peak District, this is likely to contribute to the local extinction of species, colonisation by novel species, changes to composition of biological communities, increase likelihood of invasive alien species and increased likelihood of pathogens.

Formulating and setting habitat and species targets, as has been the practice for many years, will need to be carefully re-examined as an approach.

Land management practices

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

5.impact:
Climate change

Change in ecological communities could alter the potential for carbon storage in biomass, which will impact the possibility for land-based mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions as is accounted for in net zero targets. For example, changes to blanket bog communities could result in less accumulation of peat soil, reducing carbon storage potential, and in the possible release of additional carbon from soil due to runoff, resulting in enhanced climate change. Ecological communities may also experience non-linear shifts, for example a sudden collapse in function in single biome, which could in turn provoke non-linear climatic impacts due to the impact on water, carbon and nutrient cycling.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Ecological change could impact on the demography and sociocultural practices of both residents and visitors to the Peak District due to the connections between people and their wider ecologies. Shifts in ecological communities could invoke changes to the composition of rural communities, as the possibility for agricultural livelihoods changes and people’s connection to and sense of belonging in the landscape shifts. Additionally, visitors to the Peak District come in part to interact with the ecology of the landscape, from foraging to taking in the view. The potential destabilisation of moorland soils as a result of changes to upland vegetation communities could resulting in the wash out of heavy metal pollution stored in these soils from industrial revolution. Demographic and sociocultural change

Where land management and ownership change, this could have consequences for the demographics of rural and farming communities, based on who is able to live and work in the Peak District. If land is consolidated under fewer ownership, this could mean that fewer people live and work on the land. Shifts in species composition in habitats is a feature of ongoing background ecological change, but this is likely be exacerbated by anthropogenic causes. 50.title: Fragmented heath
50.key_data: There are roughly 452ha of fragmented heath which can be found mostly in the upland areas of the Peak District. No condition data is available for these sites as they are not a priority habitat, however by nature fragmented heath in is relatively ecologically poor condition.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

37.description:
Fragmented heath is a non-priority habitat which is in degraded condition, often relict upland heath in a mosaic with acid grassland. While it is not considered to be a conservation priority, it may still be of ecological importance due to its interconnectivity with other priority habitats, while certain areas may also have the potential to be restored to priority heathlands habitats. As a form of heathland, this habitat grows on acidic and peaty soils, often in moorland areas, with the highest concentrations in the Peak District occurring in the Dark Peak. Due to the degraded nature of fragmented heath, it is not particularly species rich, although this could vary between individual sites. The most common species seen will likely be heather (Calluna vulgaris) with some other species potentially being hosted, especially where it occurs in a mosaic with species-rich heathland and acid grassland.

Land management practices will determine the future of fragmented heath sites in the National Park. In some locations there is potential for restoration and increased network connectivity, which would result in the increase of priority heathland seen. However, without intervention this habitat could continue to degrade. Overgrazing, drainage and historical pollution can all impact heathland habitats and lead to reduced biodiversity, drying out and encroachment form invasive species, as well as potential succession to other habitat types, such as woodland or acid grasslands. Atmospheric pollution from past industrial activities has caused nitrogen deposition on these upland sites, which has historically encouraged more generalist species due to improved soil fertility.

79.condition:
There is no specific condition information associated with this habitat type as it is not protected in designated sites such as Sites of Special Scientific Interest where condition data is recorded. By definition, it is in a relatively poor ecological condition, due to it being quite species poor and fragmented. Its value comes from its capacity to be managed towards a more high-quality condition and to act as connecting corridors for wildlife to move between more high quality habitat types. Therefore, recorded condition data in this regard would be useful to help inform management.

Management actions could be taken to support the development of this habitat type towards a better condition, however factors also pose a risk towards further degradation. Management regimes to alter grazing and draining have the potential to support these sites to become more biodiverse, but overgrazing could further reduce diversity of these sites, while lack of grazing could lead to its succession by woodland. While this may potentially be desirable in some locations, it also reduces fragmented heath’s potential to be managed back towards a higher quality of moorland or heath habitat. Other management actions such as rotational burning and cutting could further reduce biodiversity and encourage heather domination. Climate change will also affect this habitat type due to changing precipitation and temperature patterns impacting soil quality and plant growth.

78.distribution: The roughly 452ha of fragmented heath in the Peak District are located primarily in the Dark Peak and its surrounding fringe Landscape Character Areas, as well as in the Southwest Peak LCA. It is by definition fragmented and therefore often occurs in small patches, although it can be found in mosaics with other heathland types and grassland habitats, such as upland heath and grass moorland. A large patch occurs alongside Ladybower reservoir beneath Whinstone Lee Tor, in enclosed fields used for grazing which is bordered on its uphill side by upland heathland[158],[159].

51.title: Grass moorland
51.key_data: There is approximately 4467ha of grass moorland in the Peak District, which is widespread and occurs in every Landscape Character Area although is less abundant in the White Peak and Derwent Valley. As this habitat type is not considered a priority, no condition data is currently available however by nature it is considered to be species poor and of relatively low ecological value.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

38.description:
Grass moorland is an upland habitat dominated by grasses and is generally species-poor. Generally, within an acid grassland there may be patches of more species-rich grassland in mosaics within the grass moorland-dominated areas. Although not a priority habitat, it has the potential to be managed into better condition using the right land management techniques, and as a result has ecological value. Due to the nature of the soils grass moorland grows upon, it is predominantly found in the South West Peak as well as the Dark Peak and its associated landscape character areas.

As grass moorland is not a priority habitat and so not monitored, it can be harder to know how sites have been or are going to be affected by various different factors. This habitat is likely affected by land management practices that impact other types of grassland – particularly acid grassland – such as overgrazing from livestock. Land management in general has a great effect on this habitat, as it is through land management decisions that grass moorland sites may be transformed into more species rich habitats, or alternatively degrade further.

80.condition:
As this habitat type is not considered to be a priority habitat, it is not a designated feature within protected areas such as Sites of Special Scientific Interest and therefore does not have the same condition data associated with it. By nature, this habitat is considered to be species poor and in relatively low ecological condition; its value comes from its capacity to be managed back towards a more high-priority grassland (or other) habitat type. Assessing the condition of such grasslands in the Peak District with this focus would be a useful process to support land management actions.

While already species poor, factors could impact this habitat to further reduce its quality while with suitable management it may be improved. Grazing is a key factor in both the current state of this habitat and its potential for future regeneration. Overgrazing will maintain or further reduce the ecological value of these sites but suitable grazing, for example using different grazing species and rotations, could support its recover. Management of surrounding areas, for example tree planting, could also impact grass moorland by altering soil drainage regimes and encouraging woodland recruitment. Finally as with all habitats, future climate change will impact grass moorland by altering the fundamental conditions in which this habitat grows. The future impacts of this are not yet clear and will have to be responded to be land managers as they develop and more modelling data becomes available.

79.distribution: The Peak District’s 4467ha of grass moorland can technically be found across all Landscape Character Areas, however it is much less common in the lower-altitude and more limestone rich areas of the White Peak and Derwent Valley. On the Eastern Moors, extensive sites can be found between Curbar and Froggatt edges and White Edge, an areas which is both intentionally grazed with cattle but also by a large deer population[158],[159].

52.title: Lowland heathland
52.key_data: There are 462ha of lowland heath in the Peak District, found across all Landscape Character Areas but predominantly in the Dark Peak and Southwest Peak areas. Only two condition records are available for lowland heath in Sites of Special Scientific Interest, which both indicate this habitat is in favourable condition however the confidence rating for these records is low.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

39.description:
Lowland heath can occur in either wet or dry soils, resulting in different species assemblages. Significantly less abundant than upland heath in the Peak District, lowland heath can be found in similar areas but at a lower altitude. Lowland dry heath forms on free draining, acidic soils below 300 metres above sea level. Lowland wet heath forms on similarly acidic and peaty soils which do not drain freely and are instead waterlogged seasonally or permanently. Lowland heath is often found in mosaics with upland heath, as well as blanket bogs and acid grasslands. Species that make up this habitat include: common heather (Calluna vulgaris), bell heather (Erica cinerea) and cross-leaved heath (Erica tetralix), alongside purple moor grass (Molinia caerulea) and gorse (Ulex europaeus). Species richness fluctuates depending on the land management of the area. Lowland heath habitats in mosaics with other habitats can help host many animal species, such as merlins (Falco columbarius) and meadow pipits (Anthus pratensis).

Heathland condition in the Peak District is heavily affected by land management practices, which determine the extent and biodiversity of the habitat. Lowland heath is regularly burnt and cut as a form of management for grouse shooting, as well as being grazed, predominately by sheep. These practices cause the biodiversity of the habitat to decrease, resulting in domination by one species, such as common heather or purple moor grass, rather than a complex mosaic of species. Fluctuations in grazing levels can also see the succession of heathland to woodland or acid grassland. Industrial pollution, mainly historical, can increase the nitrogen in the soil and lead to the invasion of more generalist species which outcompete the ones typical of lowland heath. Lowland wet heath is vulnerable to drying out from drainage, in addition to drought – a situation that will become more frequent as a result of climate change.

81.condition:
Much of the lowland heath in the National Park is found within the boundaries of Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs). Condition assessments within these protected sites varies in how up to date they are, but they can provide some indication of the condition of lowland heath. SSSI recorded lowland wet heath and lowland dry heath, so the below figure combines the recorded those these two feature-types. There are four records of these features across four sites in the Peak District, and only two of these sites have a condition record, both of which have a low confidence rating as they were carried out over a decade ago. Both recorded are of favourable condition, however, due to the scarcity and uncertainty of the data this reveals little about the general condition of this habitat type[160].

The future condition and abundance of both wet and dry lowland heath depends on a variety of factors. Perhaps the most influential are land management practices, including grazing levels, as these determine how biodiverse the heath is, and can prevent or cause heathland to succeed to woodland or acid grassland. Additionally, historical pollution and nitrogen levels can affect whether generalist species have the ability to invade and colonise. Wet heath is more vulnerable to pollution due to its need for more saturated ground, which increases the leeching of heavy metals through the soil. Wet heath is also more vulnerable to changes in the water table as a result of droughts and flooding due to climate change.

80.distribution:
There are 462ha of lowland heath in the Peak District, which is highly fragmented and can be found in all Landscape Character Areas but is most commonly found in a mosaic with other moorland and heath, or grassland, habitat types in the Dark Peak, its fringes, the Eastern Moors and the Southwest Peak. This is due to the domination of acid soils in these areas as result of the underlying gritstone geology. As it is a fairly fragmented habitat, there are no examples of large swathes, however, some lowland heath can be found in areas such as the Roaches in the South West Peak[158],[159].

Example site - The Roaches

The Roaches is a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and is also part of the South Pennine Moor Special Area of Conservation (SAC). Popular with walkers and climbers, the moorlands here are also important habitats for specialist birds such as curlew (Numenius Arquata), red grouse (Lagopus scotica) and tree pipit (Anthus trivialis)[179].

53.title: Upland heathland
53.key_data: Upland heath is the second most abundant priority habitat in the National Park after blanket bog, with around 20,196ha occurring widely across all LCAs, but occurs less in the White Peak. The three records of condition for upland heath in Sites of Special Scientific Interest report its condition to be unfavourable but recovering, however the confidence in these records is low.

family.title: Landscape
family.description: Ecological and geological features

40.description:
Upland heath is an abundant priority habitat in the Peak District and includes both upland dry heath and upland wet heath. Upland heathlands form on acidic and peaty soils, that are often fairly thin in nature, with wet heath forming in the areas which are more waterlogged. These habitats are commonly found alongside lowland heath, blanket bog and acidic grasslands in moorland landscapes. Common heather (Calluna vulgaris) is the dominant species seen, but other species typically found include bell heather (Erica cinerea), cowberry (Vaccinium vitis-idaea), crowberry (Empetrum nigrum), bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus) and wavy hair grass (Deschampsia flexuosa). Wet heath areas tend to contain a higher percentage of plants such as cross-leaved heath (Erica tetralix) and cotton grass (Eriophorum angustifolium), as well as sphagnum mosses (Sphagnum spp.) indicating a transition to blanket bog in the wettest areas. Upland heath is host to many vertebrate and invertebrate species, but red grouse (Lagopus scotica) is the main bird species seen here, as a result of land management decisions, although other species such as merlin (Falco columbarius) and meadow pipit (Anthus pratensis) are also present.

Land management practices play a huge role in the structure and extent of upland heath in the Peak District. Some areas are subject to rotational burning or cutting as used in traditional grouse moor management, and grazing with sheep is common. These actions can decrease biodiversity in the habitat, as burning – whilst it can regenerate heather – causes damage to more vulnerable species, such as lichens and bryophytes. Overgrazing can lead to the loss of heather and expansion of acid grasslands; although under grazing can result in the succession of heathlands to woodlands. Drainage and fluctuating water tables can cause wet heath to dry out, which is increasingly a concern with the hotter, drier summers that will occur due to climate change. Atmospheric pollution, both historical and current, can cause increased nitrogen levels in the soil, which allows different plant species to colonise which outcompete the heathland species. In a place such as the Peak District, where there is a lot of cultural value attached to the upland heath, it can be difficult to balance traditional views and customs with management techniques that are more ecologically beneficial.

82.condition:
A substantial amount of upland heath in the Peak District is located within Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs). SSSI records for the National Park record the feature-type wet heath (upland) at four sites, three of which record condition assessments. One of these has a medium confidence rating in its assessment, which was carried out in 2012, while the other two have low confidence ratings. All three records are for unfavourable but recovering features meaning they show indications of returning to healthy, biodiverse and stable conditions. However, whether land management of the areas has, or will, return them to fully favourable condition remains to be seen.  These unfavourable but recovering sites are found in these SSSIs of the Dark Peak, Eastern Peak District Moors, and the Goyt Valley[160].

Upland heath condition and extent is heavily impacted by both past and present influences. As heathlands occur on fairly nutrient poor soils, nitrogen deposition from historical industrial practices means other plants can colonise and invade into the heath. High nitrogen levels in the soil can also damage heather roots and make them more vulnerable to invertebrate infestation. Land management practices, namely livestock grazing as well as heather burning and cutting, often lower biodiversity and can result in either heathland where few species other than heather are present – or in some circumstances succession to woodland or acid grassland.

81.distribution:
Upland heathland is an extensive habitat type in the Peak District and second only to blanket bog in total area of a priority habitat, with 20,196 ha found in all Landscape Character Areas (LCAs). However, this habitat is predominately associated with the Dark Peak and Eastern Moors, with more fragmented examples in other areas[158],[159].

Example site - Eastern Moors

Situated on the western edge of Sheffield, the Eastern Moors encapsulates a variety of habitats and wildlife, as well as history dating back to the Bronze age. Beyond the heathland, meadows and woodland habitats are present, all of which host a variety of different fauna. Eastern Moors is an important site for adder (Vipera berus) populations, as well as short eared owls (Asio flammeus), winchats (Saxicola rubetra) and skylarks (Alauda arvensis)[180].

29.introduction:
The Peak District’s moorlands and heaths, especially in the uplands, are some of its most iconic habitats that draw in visitors from around the world. While the White Peak contains almost no moorland or heath habitats, in the other Landscape Character Areas of the National Park, especially the Dark Peak and Eastern Moors these habitats can be some of the most continuous and extensive. As well as the priority habitat types of lowland and upland heath, this report also considers the extent and condition of two non-priority habitats; fragmented heath and grass moorland. While these habitats are less ecological diverse, they have the potential to be managed back into a higher quality condition and, therefore, it is useful to have an understanding of their condition and extent alongside the priority habitats.

Together with other ecological features, moorland and heath habitats provide important benefits through their functions in the landscape. These include the stabilisation of soils and their role in the flow and cycling of water and nutrients. However, these habitats and the benefits they provide are at risk from a number of factors. Land management practices, including grazing, cutting and burning, play a large role in both maintaining and changing the condition of moorland and heaths. This is as a result of these habitats requiring some vegetation reduction to not be succeeded by trees, however, too much can lower the diversity and reduce the quality of the habitats. Climate change will also play an increasing role in driving change to these habitats, with warmer wetter winters and drier hotter summers altering the conditions within which their key species can survive.

18.distribution: Moorland and heaths are extensively present in the Dark Peak, its fringes and the Eastern Moors Landscape Character areas. Here, upland heath especially dominates extensive areas where blanket bog is not present. In the White Peak and the Derwent Valley, there is very little moorland or heath habitat, while in Southwest Peak these habitats are found in a patchy mosaic with grassland and wetland habitats.

9.importance:
Moorland and heath habitats contribute to the ecological and social benefits provided by the National Park. These include ecosystem services the support the conditions for life, such as protecting from floods and providing clean water by supporting water cycling. Good quality heathland can also help to control erosion and provide good quality soil by supporting nutrient cycling and acting to physically stabilise soils. These habitats can also support diverse species, with higher quality habitat helping to control pests and diseases such as heather beetle.

These habitats are also culturally and socially significant; they are often farmed or managed for grouse moors, which while not loved by all has played a vital role in shaping the Peak District’s uplands and is greatly important to some of the Peak District’s rural communities. This means that these habitats provide livelihoods as well as opportunities for leisure and recreation. The landscapes created by management for grouse moors are also culturally distinctive, providing a sense of connection and belonging for residents and visitors.

9.quality: • Relying on SSSI condition data to understand the condition of these habitats will only give a partial picture as it does not account for sites outside of protected areas. Additionally, SSSI condition data is very often out of date, with many records not having been updated for 10-20 years or more. This means that the condition assumptions presented in this report are of very low certainty.

32.likelihood_text: It is almost certain that this impact will occur, as it has been increasingly occurring over the last 15 years. The summer of 2026 saw widespread fires across the Peak District damaging large areas of moorland and heath habitats. Going forward, this is only going to become more likely in all areas of the National Park.
32.severity: This impact will be severe, especially if it occurs repeatedly in the same areas and so not allowing vegetation the ability to recover. Over time, this could result in completely revegetated areas.

3.impact:
Climate change has compound impacts on other factors. These are briefly laid out below with more detail on each of the relevant factor pages.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Due to climate change having unequal impacts globally, as a result of both physical and socio-economic conditions, international migration of people may increase the UK population and/or change the character of the UK population as a whole. Additionally, there may be increased demand for housing in rural areas as a result of disproportionate population growth and warming in urban areas. As a result, the Peak District may experience changes to the demographic character of both its residents and its visitors due to global and local population changes. There is little research into exactly what these changes may look like, however projections do indicate that current migration trends are likely to be amplified as a result of climate change[64].

Ecological change

The projected impacts of climate change are intrinsically linked to potential ecological changes. As the physical conditions which define species’ niches shift, both spatially and temporally, species distribution and phenology (timing of biological events) will change.

Cooke et al. (2026) model biodiversity change in the UK under a range of climate scenarios up to 2080[61]. They project “extensive community reorganisation” under any scenario with “the disappearance of current bioclimates and emergence of novel ones”. In the Peak District, this is likely to contribute to the local extinction of species, colonisation by novel species, changes to composition of biological communities, increase likelihood of invasive alien species and increased likelihood of pathogens.

Formulating and setting habitat and species targets, as has been the practice for many years, will need to be carefully re-examined as an approach.

Land management practices

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

7.impact:
Climate change

As described above, land can be managed to mitigate the impacts of climate change by sequestering or preventing the further emission of fossil fuels. If the Peak District was managed to maximise this, it could help remove CO2 from the atmosphere to slow future climate change. However, on the scale of the Peak District this would have a relatively small impact on global climate change.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Where land management and ownership change, this could have consequences for the demographics of rural and farming communities, based on who is able to live and work in the Peak District. If land is consolidated under fewer ownership, this could mean that fewer people live and work on the land. However, changes to farming or conservation land management practices may result in more rural jobs. Therefore, it is difficult to make projections about exactly what these changes may look like.

Pollution

Certain land management practices can either result in or reduce pollution. Fertiliser run off from agricultural land can cause polluting effects in freshwater systems, and therefore moving toward lower input agricultural land management can reduce this pollution. Land management practices which stabilise soils, for example peatland restoration, can result in reduced top soil runoff and therefore less sediment contaminated with pollutants from industrial air pollution ending up downstream.

Visitation and access

The Peak District is widely known among visitors for its landscapes under their current management regimes, which promote people to visit the area and participate in different recreational activities. If land was managed differently, this could change people’s perception of the landscape and alter their visiting behaviour, as well as possible changes to access infrastructure which would need to adapt around changing land use.  This could be in the direction of reduced access and declining visitation, for example under agriculture intensification, or it could be increased visitation through ecotourism.

9.impact:
Ecological Change

Visitation and access has the potential to affect ecological change if it leads to impacts such as soil compaction and habitat degradation. Roadside verges have been identified as agricultural settings that may be rich in wildflowers and meadow species can be prone to invasion of more dominant ruderal species due to the nature of disturbance and additional nitrogen that occurs alongside roads and higher levels of traffic[71].

Pollution

If there are changes to visitor numbers, the current prevalence of car travel in how people access the National Park could have an effect on pollution: contributing to carbon emissions as well as noise and light pollution. The knock on demand for car or public transport related infrastructure could also therefore generate further embedded carbon and generate emissions during production.

33.likelihood_text: Given current data regarding the condition of protected sites, it is possible that this impact will occur in widespread manner, as many sites are currently in unfavourable condition with no improvement. It is possible that changes in protected site legislation could support an improvement in condition, however this is uncertain.
33.severity: As many protected sites have already been in an unfavourable condition for many years, a lack improvement may not have that much additional impact as it represents no change in state. However, in places this impact could be more severe where protected sites continue to decline and that declining condition is not improved, as it may result in the loss of the key designated features in these sites.

6.impact:
Governance and legislation have the potential to impact all other factors due to the legislation and governance frameworks that underlie all action carried out in the UK. This could be drawn together in an almost infinite number of links, however certainty about what impacts are likely is very low, and many relevant ways in which governance and legislation impacts other factors have already been outlined above. Therefore, these are briefly summarised below with some additional impacts that have not yet been noted.

Factor

Possible impacts from governance and legislation

Climate change

Stronger commitments to emissions reduction and carbon sequestration and storage could help to reduce likelihood of global climate change impacts, e.g. changes to the Climate Change Act 2008 or additional global agreements.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Impacts on communities from changes to planning regulation (NFFP, local plan making process etc) could alter housing development in communities, potential knock-on impact to composition of communities.

Ecological change

Possibility for strengthened or weakened environmental protections, e.g. through BNG and biodiversity credits, changes to National Park legislation and governance, etc. Land use framework, LNRSs and 30x30 target may introduce stronger requirements and spatial planning for land to be managed for ecology.

Economy and industry

Changes to farm subsidy schemes may positively or negatively impact he viability of farm businesses. More NSIPs to support low carbon energy and transport infrastructure could support construction and operation jobs.

Land management practices

Farm subsidies and land management grants may incentivise changes to land uses and management actions. Land use framework may change how land use is determined. Changes to land ownership resulting in changed land management may result from enhance community right to buy to England[98].

Possible changes to legislation relating to driven grouse shooting, including further changes to moorland burning regulation about and an ongoing campaign to ban on driven grouse shooting[99], may result to changes in moorland management.

Pollution

Changes to the regulation of sewage waste outflow into freshwater would reduce freshwater pollution. Legislation relating to land management outline above could change agricultural pollution e.g. lower input farming reducing nutrient pollution.

Visitation and access

New access legislation could strength right to access, including permitted activities and areas with open access. Combined authorities may use visitor levies which could impact visitor access by presenting financial barrier, may cause inequality in access.

34.likelihood_text: It is possible that key species will be lost over the next ten-year period, but this will only be possible for those already at the more extreme edge of their range, for example mountain hare. However, over a longer period it will become increasingly likely that key species are lost as climatic changes effect species’ ranges and the compound impacts of multiple factors result in worsening ecological change and in changing land management practices.
34.severity: This will initially have a moderate impact, however in the longer term the severity of this impact will worsen as more species are lost, causing knock on impacts to ecological functioning and integrity. This impact will not only have ecological implications but also social and cultural costs, as key species, especially larger enigmatic species of birds and mammals, play a key role in the cultural significance of the National Park.

Change in ecological communities could alter the potential for carbon storage in biomass, which will impact the possibility for land-based mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions as is accounted for in net zero targets. For example, changes to blanket bog communities could result in less accumulation of peat soil, reducing carbon storage potential, and in the possible release of additional carbon from soil due to runoff, resulting in enhanced climate change. Ecological communities may also experience non-linear shifts, for example a sudden collapse in function in single biome, which could in turn provoke non-linear climatic impacts due to the impact on water, carbon and nutrient cycling.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Ecological change could impact on the demography and sociocultural practices of both residents and visitors to the Peak District due to the connections between people and their wider ecologies. Shifts in ecological communities could invoke changes to the composition of rural communities, as the possibility for agricultural livelihoods changes and people’s connection to and sense of belonging in the landscape shifts. Additionally, visitors to the Peak District come in part to interact with the ecology of the landscape, from foraging to taking in the view. Changes to these communities may result in different people visiting in different ways.

Land management practices

Land management practices take place in relation to the underlying ecological communities. Therefore, changes to this ecology are likely to result in changed land management practices. For example, in the Peak District, uplands currently managed for grouse moors may be managed differently if the red grouse experiences population decline and the composition upland moorland habitats shift to make this form of moorland management no longer sustainable. Similarly, agricultural practices may have to change if different compositions of agri-ecological systems emerge, pests and diseases impact on crops and livestock, etc.

Pollution

The potential destabilisation of moorland soils as a result of changes to upland vegetation communities could resulting in the wash out of heavy metal pollution stored in these soils from industrial revolution. This would have downstream consequences as this pollution is spread, potentially having further ecological impacts as well as impacting agricultural land and drinking water.

7.impact:
Climate change

As described above, land can be managed to mitigate the impacts of climate change by sequestering or preventing the further emission of fossil fuels. If the Peak District was managed to maximise this, it could help remove CO2 from the atmosphere to slow future climate change. However, on the scale of the Peak District this would have a relatively small impact on global climate change.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Where land management and ownership change, this could have consequences for the demographics of rural and farming communities, based on who is able to live and work in the Peak District. If land is consolidated under fewer ownership, this could mean that fewer people live and work on the land. However, changes to farming or conservation land management practices may result in more rural jobs. Therefore, it is difficult to make projections about exactly what these changes may look like.

Pollution

Certain land management practices can either result in or reduce pollution. Fertiliser run off from agricultural land can cause polluting effects in freshwater systems, and therefore moving toward lower input agricultural land management can reduce this pollution. Land management practices which stabilise soils, for example peatland restoration, can result in reduced top soil runoff and therefore less sediment contaminated with pollutants from industrial air pollution ending up downstream.

Visitation and access

The Peak District is widely known among visitors for its landscapes under their current management regimes, which promote people to visit the area and participate in different recreational activities. If land was managed differently, this could change people’s perception of the landscape and alter their visiting behaviour, as well as possible changes to access infrastructure which would need to adapt around changing land use.  This could be in the direction of reduced access and declining visitation, for example under agriculture intensification, or it could be increased visitation through ecotourism.

24.impact: Changes to conservation land management practices

35.likelihood_text: This impact is likely, partly as a result of the wide range of causes that may lead to it. Shifts in species composition in habitats is a feature of ongoing background ecological change, but this is likely be exacerbated by anthropogenic causes. Climate change, in combination and related to other factors such as changes in land management practices, will further this as the underlying conditions on which species assemblages are constructed continue to move further away from the baseline.
35.severity: This impact may only be minor over the next ten years, but will become increasingly severe over time as the impacts of climate change develop. It is also possible that the negative consequences of this impact could be mitigated, for example by managing changes in species composition to support the continuation of the overall functioning of ecosystems, so that benefits like clean water or climatic regulation continue to be provided. This would reduce the overall severity of the impact in some ways.

3.impact:
Climate change has compound impacts on other factors. These are briefly laid out below with more detail on each of the relevant factor pages.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Due to climate change having unequal impacts globally, as a result of both physical and socio-economic conditions, international migration of people may increase the UK population and/or change the character of the UK population as a whole. Additionally, there may be increased demand for housing in rural areas as a result of disproportionate population growth and warming in urban areas. As a result, the Peak District may experience changes to the demographic character of both its residents and its visitors due to global and local population changes. There is little research into exactly what these changes may look like, however projections do indicate that current migration trends are likely to be amplified as a result of climate change[64].

Ecological change

The projected impacts of climate change are intrinsically linked to potential ecological changes. As the physical conditions which define species’ niches shift, both spatially and temporally, species distribution and phenology (timing of biological events) will change.

Cooke et al. (2026) model biodiversity change in the UK under a range of climate scenarios up to 2080[61]. They project “extensive community reorganisation” under any scenario with “the disappearance of current bioclimates and emergence of novel ones”. In the Peak District, this is likely to contribute to the local extinction of species, colonisation by novel species, changes to composition of biological communities, increase likelihood of invasive alien species and increased likelihood of pathogens.

Formulating and setting habitat and species targets, as has been the practice for many years, will need to be carefully re-examined as an approach.

Land management practices

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

6.impact:
Governance and legislation have the potential to impact all other factors due to the legislation and governance frameworks that underlie all action carried out in the UK. This could be drawn together in an almost infinite number of links, however certainty about what impacts are likely is very low, and many relevant ways in which governance and legislation impacts other factors have already been outlined above. Therefore, these are briefly summarised below with some additional impacts that have not yet been noted.

Factor

Possible impacts from governance and legislation

Climate change

Stronger commitments to emissions reduction and carbon sequestration and storage could help to reduce likelihood of global climate change impacts, e.g. changes to the Climate Change Act 2008 or additional global agreements.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Impacts on communities from changes to planning regulation (NFFP, local plan making process etc) could alter housing development in communities, potential knock-on impact to composition of communities.

Ecological change

Possibility for strengthened or weakened environmental protections, e.g. through BNG and biodiversity credits, changes to National Park legislation and governance, etc. Land use framework, LNRSs and 30x30 target may introduce stronger requirements and spatial planning for land to be managed for ecology.

Economy and industry

Changes to farm subsidy schemes may positively or negatively impact he viability of farm businesses. More NSIPs to support low carbon energy and transport infrastructure could support construction and operation jobs.

Land management practices

Farm subsidies and land management grants may incentivise changes to land uses and management actions. Land use framework may change how land use is determined. Changes to land ownership resulting in changed land management may result from enhance community right to buy to England[98].

Possible changes to legislation relating to driven grouse shooting, including further changes to moorland burning regulation about and an ongoing campaign to ban on driven grouse shooting[99], may result to changes in moorland management.

Pollution

Changes to the regulation of sewage waste outflow into freshwater would reduce freshwater pollution. Legislation relating to land management outline above could change agricultural pollution e.g. lower input farming reducing nutrient pollution.

Visitation and access

New access legislation could strength right to access, including permitted activities and areas with open access. Combined authorities may use visitor levies which could impact visitor access by presenting financial barrier, may cause inequality in access.

Climate change

Particulate pollution can contribute towards climate change as a result of airborne particulates absorbing heat and light, contributing to atmospheric warming and cloud formation[118].

Water pollution alters the chemical environment for aquatic life, impacting species’ abilities to reproduce.
