This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

5.impact:
Climate change

Change in ecological communities could alter the potential for carbon storage in biomass, which will impact the possibility for land-based mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions as is accounted for in net zero targets. For example, changes to blanket bog communities could result in less accumulation of peat soil, reducing carbon storage potential, and in the possible release of additional carbon from soil due to runoff, resulting in enhanced climate change. Ecological communities may also experience non-linear shifts, for example a sudden collapse in function in single biome, which could in turn provoke non-linear climatic impacts due to the impact on water, carbon and nutrient cycling.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Ecological change could impact on the demography and sociocultural practices of both residents and visitors to the Peak District due to the connections between people and their wider ecologies. Shifts in ecological communities could invoke changes to the composition of rural communities, as the possibility for agricultural livelihoods changes and people’s connection to and sense of belonging in the landscape shifts. Additionally, visitors to the Peak District come in part to interact with the ecology of the landscape, from foraging to taking in the view. Changes to these communities may result in different people visiting in different ways.

Land management practices

Land management practices take place in relation to the underlying ecological communities. Therefore, changes to this ecology are likely to result in changed land management practices. For example, in the Peak District, uplands currently managed for grouse moors may be managed differently if the red grouse experiences population decline and the composition upland moorland habitats shift to make this form of moorland management no longer sustainable. Similarly, agricultural practices may have to change if different compositions of agri-ecological systems emerge, pests and diseases impact on crops and livestock, etc.

Pollution

The potential destabilisation of moorland soils as a result of changes to upland vegetation communities could resulting in the wash out of heavy metal pollution stored in these soils from industrial revolution. This would have downstream consequences as this pollution is spread, potentially having further ecological impacts as well as impacting agricultural land and drinking water.

Governance and legislation have the potential to impact all other factors due to the legislation and governance frameworks that underlie all action carried out in the UK. This could be drawn together in an almost infinite number of links, however certainty about what impacts are likely is very low, and many relevant ways in which governance and legislation impacts other factors have already been outlined above. Possible impacts from governance and legislation

Climate change

Stronger commitments to emissions reduction and carbon sequestration and storage could help to reduce likelihood of global climate change impacts, e.g. changes to the Climate Change Act 2008 or additional global agreements.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Ecological change

Possibility for strengthened or weakened environmental protections, e.g. through BNG and biodiversity credits, changes to National Park legislation and governance, etc. Land use framework, LNRSs and 30x30 target may introduce stronger requirements and spatial planning for land to be managed for ecology.

Economy and industry

Changes to farm subsidy schemes may positively or negatively impact he viability of farm businesses. More NSIPs to support low carbon energy and transport infrastructure could support construction and operation jobs.

Farm subsidies and land management grants may incentivise changes to land uses and management actions. Land use framework may change how land use is determined. Changes to land ownership resulting in changed land management may result from enhance community right to buy to England[98].

Possible changes to legislation relating to driven grouse shooting, including further changes to moorland burning regulation about and an ongoing campaign to ban on driven grouse shooting[99], may result to changes in moorland management.

Changes to the regulation of sewage waste outflow into freshwater would reduce freshwater pollution. Legislation relating to land management outline above could change agricultural pollution e.g. lower input farming reducing nutrient pollution.

7.impact:
Climate change

As described above, land can be managed to mitigate the impacts of climate change by sequestering or preventing the further emission of fossil fuels. If the Peak District was managed to maximise this, it could help remove CO2 from the atmosphere to slow future climate change. However, on the scale of the Peak District this would have a relatively small impact on global climate change.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Where land management and ownership change, this could have consequences for the demographics of rural and farming communities, based on who is able to live and work in the Peak District. If land is consolidated under fewer ownership, this could mean that fewer people live and work on the land. However, changes to farming or conservation land management practices may result in more rural jobs. Therefore, it is difficult to make projections about exactly what these changes may look like.

Pollution

Certain land management practices can either result in or reduce pollution. Fertiliser run off from agricultural land can cause polluting effects in freshwater systems, and therefore moving toward lower input agricultural land management can reduce this pollution. Land management practices which stabilise soils, for example peatland restoration, can result in reduced top soil runoff and therefore less sediment contaminated with pollutants from industrial air pollution ending up downstream.

Visitation and access

The Peak District is widely known among visitors for its landscapes under their current management regimes, which promote people to visit the area and participate in different recreational activities. If land was managed differently, this could change people’s perception of the landscape and alter their visiting behaviour, as well as possible changes to access infrastructure which would need to adapt around changing land use.  This could be in the direction of reduced access and declining visitation, for example under agriculture intensification, or it could be increased visitation through ecotourism.

28.title: Myths, legends and oral traditions
28.key_data: Due to their intangible nature, it is difficult to link myths, legends and oral traditions to geographic distribution although this can be done through detailed project work. Some are connected to particular places. Examples of projects that support the continuation of this feature include the Derbyshire Folklore website, Bella Hardy's The Dark Peak and the White album, and Studio Skai's project FOLKS: Peak District Folk Tales.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

14.description:
Oral traditions passed down through story and song connect the present to the past through a lineage of proverbs, riddles, myths and legends. These often connect to particular places, people or times of year and pass on local knowledge, moral lessons and social memories. A storied and varied landscape such as the Peak District has a multitude of tales connected to its historic and natural places, which often are connected to or retold through the myths, legends and oral traditions of the National Park. With links to folk heroes such as Robin Hood, or people persecuted for their difference like Hulac Warren, these folk tales are some of the strongest ways that visitors and residents have to connect to the people, communities and places of the Peak District that have gone before.

However, as an intangible feature of the Peak District's heritage, myths, legends and oral traditions are at risk of being lost or disconnected from the people and places that are part of their importance. This is likely to be a result of demographic and sociocultural change; changing populations in villages, with aging residents and more interest in technology, may result in oral traditions not being passed down to the next generation. This could be furthered by the factor of governance and legislation, if policy and, subsequently, funding does not recognise the importance of this aspect of our cultural heritage. Additionally, ecological changes associated with climate change and changing land management practises may result in changes to the ecologies and landscapes that connect to the Peak Districts myths and legends, which could disrupt their transmission or cause them to shift and change to adapt to these new conditions.

16.condition:
It is very challenging to provide a full condition assessment of the Peak District's myths, legends and oral traditions given their nature as an intangible aspect of cultural heritage and the paucity of information that traces the historical linage of these traditions and could indicate their survival. It is likely that some of the material conditions for how myths and legends are passed on - the structure of the oral traditions - has been lost or has evolved as society has changed. This is discussed further in Local traditions and events. However, there are present-day projects that aim to retell traditional myths and legends to continue this heritage and keep the stories alive which can be used as examples as to where this feature is in good condition.

Website: Derbyshire Folklore
Curated by the Derbyshire born-and-bred Simon Unsworth, the website Derbyshire Folklore catalogues many stories, myths and legends relating to the Peak District. The site aims to "fill in that 'Derbyshire-shaped hole' that exists in so many books about English and British folklore, myths and legends"[20].

Music: The Dark Peak and the White, Bella Hardy, 2012
Combining revived content from a songbook from 1867 and new material, this album captures stories from the Peak District in song. Edale-born Bella Hardy retells, in the style of the contemporary revival of folk music, a number of traditional stories from across the National Park including of the plague in Eyam, murders in Winnats pass and the "drowned village" of Derwent[23].

Art: FOLKS: Peak District Folk Tales, Studio Skai, 2025
Studio Skai-artist Joe Winstanley is Peak District-based, and uses his creative practice to "explor[e] folklore, landscape, and memory through miniature model-making and storytelling"[18]. The two books of "Folks" beautifully capture Winstanley's thoughtful and eerie retellings whilst exploring what truth means in relation to folk stories, and whether it matters[28].

44.distribution: Due to their intangible nature, it can be difficult to link myths, legends and oral traditions to geographic distribution, although some are very closely tied to place. Therefore, for the purpose of management planning it is useful to understand this feature as linking to all parts of the Peak District, and therefore in this report it is being considered as present in all Landscape Character Areas.

29.title: Local traditions and events
29.key_data: While it is hard to account for, local traditions and events are believed to be widespread across the Peak District. For example, well dressings are taking place in 2026 across 6 of the 8 Landscape Character Areas in the Peak District. It is very difficult to estimate the condition of these traditions and events, but some initiatives aim to record them such as the National Folklore Survey for England which may reveal more detail after research is complete.

15.description:
The towns and villages across the PDNP hold a wide range of events throughout the year that are attended by local people as well as visitors from the surrounding communities and further afield. Many have origins dating back over a hundred years, while others are so ancient that their origin is not fully known. The wide range of events include carnivals, fell races, village fetes, sheep dog trials, and country shows are held in various locations including Hope, Chatsworth and the Manifold Valley. Many of these include within them traditional activities, which may be widespread or particular to the individual community or location. Examples include Castleton Garland Day and Winster Pancake Run. These types of events are often tied to a particular date in the year. Well dressings are popular and are held on various dates between May and September and feature intricate designs created by pressing natural materials into clay boards. One of the earliest and well known is held in Tissington.

These traditions and events are one of the most active ways that residents and visitors participate in the cultural heritage of the Peak District. They therefore greatly contribute to people's sense of connection to the place, and its cultural significance in the wider region. However as with other intangible aspects of heritage, these traditions and events are at risk from demographic and sociocultural change, where changes to communities may result in the loss of such traditions if they go out of fashion or knowledge of them is lost. Climate change and other changes relating to ecology and land management may also have an impact, as many traditions and events are tied to place and activities relating to land management.

17.condition:
Throughout the Peak District a vast range of events takes place during the course of the year; it would be impossible to catalogue them all here, but websites such as Visit Peak District and Derbsyhire[46] and Let's Go Peak District[37] capture many of the year's events, both traditional and more recent.

Local traditions and events are also an important part of the oral traditions through which Myths, legends and oral traditions are retold in the Peak District. Examples of these include the Eyam bonfire night tradition of burning a rat effigy, which contributes to transmitting the memory of the impact of the plague in Eyam[24]. However, while some such examples survive, it is likely that as the Peak District's population is declining (see the Demographics page) and contemporary culture has spread which relies more on digital storytelling, that many of the events which helped to relay oral traditions are at risk of being changed or lost.

It is very difficult to account for this within just the Peak District, however at a national level emerging initiatives are aiming to catalogue not just the stories but also the local traditions and events that continue their retelling. This includes the work of the National Folklore Survey for England, which aims to capture what it describes as "our cultural DNA...includ[ing] the art, stories, knowledge, and practices of a people"[48]. Such initiatives provide hope for the future condition of this intangible aspect of our heritage.

Many events are reliant on the weather, and poor conditions such as successive wet summers can have a negative impact and contribute to events suffering financial losses. A number have been lost in recent years such as the Hartington Steam Rally, while Bakewell Show was not held at all in 2018 and was scaled back in 2019 due to damage caused to the showground and revenue being lost. However, nationally, rural events such as agricultural shows are thought to be "booming" as seven million people visit agricultural shows per year[21].

45.distribution:
Due to their intangible nature, it can be difficult to link some local traditions and events to geographic distribution, although many have a place-based focus. Using well dressings as an example of a popular local tradition, research shows that over 30 well dressings are due to happen in the Peak District in 2026[46],[37], with 18 in the White Peak, four in each the Derwent Valley and Dark Peak, two in the South West Peak and one in each of the Dark Peak West and the Derbyshire Peak Fringe Landscape Character Areas.

This shows a fairly wide distribution of this particular local tradition across the Peak District, however, many other traditions take place which may be differently distributed. For the purpose of management planning, it is useful to understand this feature as linking to all part of the Peak District, and therefore in this report it is being considered as present in all Landscape Character Areas.

30.title: Cultural and social history
30.key_data: Due to its intangible nature, it is very difficult to link cultural and social history to geographic distribution.  Groups and projects in the Peak District seek to record and celebrate this often under recorded aspect of the National Park's cultural heritage, such as Castleton Historical Society and the Hayfield Kinder Trespass Group. However, in other ways this feature could be seen as in decline due to the loss of traditional skills such as locally important building techniques, which is being seen on a national scale.

family.title: Cultural Heritage
family.description: Archaeology, buildings, landscapes and intangible heritage

16.description:
The cultural and social history of a place is the way of understanding the daily lives, experiences and interrelationships between ordinary people throughout time, and how this shapes their beliefs, practises and interactions with their wider community and environments. This history concerns itself with "real life", and in this context, as a feature of Intangible heritage in the Peak District, it will consider the state of our understanding of, practices related to, and continued experiences of, historical cultural and social traditions and knowledge within the National Park. This could include traditional crafts and activities, such as techniques related to the maintenance of Traditional buildings and settlements, celebrations and remembrances of important social events such as the Kinder Trespass, and the knowledge and celebration of the lives and experiences of the Peak District's farming communities, amongst other aspects.

This feature is of course related to many others outlined in the Cultural Heritage section, as features such as Cultural monuments, Traditional buildings and Farmed landscapes have important interrelationships with ways that people have lived over the centuries in this special landscape. Together, these connect visitors and residents to the ordinary people that have shaped these landscapes over history, and connect us to this place and its past.

18.condition:
Due to the nature of cultural and social history as relating to the everyday life of ordinary people, this can be one of the most under recorded aspects of our cultural heritage and as a result is very difficult to assess. However, projects and groups exist which seek to celebrate and retain this history in the Peak District. Examples include:

Castleton Historical Society
As well as regular talks with guest speakers, this group has collected archival evidence and materials relating to the lives of Castleton residents over history. In 2021, the group received funding for the project "Lives of the Common People" which aimed to further the understanding of everyday people's lives and work between 1066 and 1642[47].

Hayfield Kinder Trespass Group
The Kinder Trespass was a formative event not just for the Peak District, but for all National Parks in the UK. Hayfield Kinder Trespass Group keep this history alive through an annual festival celebrating the anniversary of the Trespass on 24th April, as well as a website with a project archive and trespass trail walking routes[29].

The Land that Made Us: The Peak District Farmer's Story
This book, released in 2019, is history of 80 years of farming in the South West Peak told through stories collected by Shelia Hine and Christine Gregory. This presentation of farmer's lives and experiences since the Second World War reveals the impacts on real people of histories that are often reported in abstract ways, such as joining the 'Dig for Victory' campaign, or joining the Common Market[42].

The above are examples of how our cultural and social history is remembered well, however in other ways this is declining, although it is challenging to give specific examples of this in the Peak District. On a national scale, it is believed that traditional building skills are being lost, putting Historic buildings at risk due to a lack of skilled workers who can support their upkeep using traditional methods[41]. However, it is possible that National Parks are less at risk of this decline as a result of the first purpose promoting work which supports cultural heritage preservation and enhancement.

Overall, there is not enough evidence to fully account for the condition of this feature in the Peak District.

47.distribution: Due to its intangible nature, it can be difficult to link cultural and social history to geographic distribution, although some elements of this feature can be very closely tied to place. Therefore, for the purpose of management planning it is useful to understand this feature as linking to all part of the Peak District, and in this report it is being considered as present in all Landscape Character Areas.

21.introduction:
Across the Peak District, intangible heritage is alive in the stories, traditions, and skills that, while difficult to measure, contribute towards the Peak District’s special qualities and sense of identity. This feature group includes the myths, legends and oral traditions passed from generation to generation, along with the local events linked to these traditions, such as well dressings and other seasonal celebrations. More recent cultural and social histories are also an important feature of the National Park, with the social heritage of the Kinder Mass Trespass as tightly integrated into the historic environment of the Peak District as Chatsworth House or Peveril Castle.

Therefore, intangible heritage features are important components in delivering the benefits of connection to place and cultural significance that the Peak District provides. When people visit this landscape, it is not just the tangible aspects that shape their experience, but also these untouchable and immeasurable qualities. Despite their intangibility, it is therefore important to consider what may impact the features that make up this group and as a result the important benefits they contribute.

9.distribution: Due to their very nature, intangible heritage features are difficult to link to geographic areas, although many are closely tied to places – villages, ecological or geological features, and historic sites. Therefore, for the purpose of management planning it is useful to understand these feature as linking to all parts of the Peak District, and in this report they are being considered as present in all Landscape Character Areas. As a rough proxy, below are mapped the well dressings occurring across the Peak District in 2026 as an example of a typical local traditional that is widespread across the National Park.

4.importance: Intangible heritage contributes to the ongoing transmission and development of culture and identify in the Peak District. This is a vital contribution towards residents’ and visitors’ connection to the place, as well to the cultural significance of the Peak District beyond its boundaries. Due to the intangible nature of these features, they can be easy to overlook in comparison to more tangible aspects of the National Park. This adds an importance to acknowledging them and attempting to understand their condition, despite this being difficult precisely because of their intangibility.

5.quality: • There is very little record overall of intangible aspects of cultural heritage, therefore it is very difficult to account for what there is, let alone any spatial distribution or condition assessment. Surveying intangible heritage in the Peak District both historically and in the present day could help to understand how this has changed and provide a way to understand condition.

14.likelihood_text: This may be a moderate impact, as some events such as well dressings are in good condition, while others may be lost without resources or protective legislation to support them. The National Park as a visitor destination may have a positive impact on supporting the continuation of local activities and events, compared to other rural places which are less popular with visitors.
14.severity: It is possible that this impact may occur, as a change in population demographics is noticeably occurring. However, this is over a long timescale. Additionally, expert opinion is that to some extent there has been a revival of interest attributed to traditional “folkloric” events, which may support their continuation of the Peak District and mitigate the likelihood of this impact.

3.impact:
Climate change has compound impacts on other factors. These are briefly laid out below with more detail on each of the relevant factor pages.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Due to climate change having unequal impacts globally, as a result of both physical and socio-economic conditions, international migration of people may increase the UK population and/or change the character of the UK population as a whole. Additionally, there may be increased demand for housing in rural areas as a result of disproportionate population growth and warming in urban areas. As a result, the Peak District may experience changes to the demographic character of both its residents and its visitors due to global and local population changes. There is little research into exactly what these changes may look like, however projections do indicate that current migration trends are likely to be amplified as a result of climate change[64].

Ecological change

The projected impacts of climate change are intrinsically linked to potential ecological changes. As the physical conditions which define species’ niches shift, both spatially and temporally, species distribution and phenology (timing of biological events) will change.

Cooke et al. (2026) model biodiversity change in the UK under a range of climate scenarios up to 2080[61]. They project “extensive community reorganisation” under any scenario with “the disappearance of current bioclimates and emergence of novel ones”. In the Peak District, this is likely to contribute to the local extinction of species, colonisation by novel species, changes to composition of biological communities, increase likelihood of invasive alien species and increased likelihood of pathogens.

Formulating and setting habitat and species targets, as has been the practice for many years, will need to be carefully re-examined as an approach.

Land management practices

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

5.impact:
Climate change

Change in ecological communities could alter the potential for carbon storage in biomass, which will impact the possibility for land-based mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions as is accounted for in net zero targets. For example, changes to blanket bog communities could result in less accumulation of peat soil, reducing carbon storage potential, and in the possible release of additional carbon from soil due to runoff, resulting in enhanced climate change. Ecological communities may also experience non-linear shifts, for example a sudden collapse in function in single biome, which could in turn provoke non-linear climatic impacts due to the impact on water, carbon and nutrient cycling.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Ecological change could impact on the demography and sociocultural practices of both residents and visitors to the Peak District due to the connections between people and their wider ecologies. Shifts in ecological communities could invoke changes to the composition of rural communities, as the possibility for agricultural livelihoods changes and people’s connection to and sense of belonging in the landscape shifts. Additionally, visitors to the Peak District come in part to interact with the ecology of the landscape, from foraging to taking in the view. Changes to these communities may result in different people visiting in different ways.

Land management practices

Land management practices take place in relation to the underlying ecological communities. Therefore, changes to this ecology are likely to result in changed land management practices. For example, in the Peak District, uplands currently managed for grouse moors may be managed differently if the red grouse experiences population decline and the composition upland moorland habitats shift to make this form of moorland management no longer sustainable. Similarly, agricultural practices may have to change if different compositions of agri-ecological systems emerge, pests and diseases impact on crops and livestock, etc.

Pollution

The potential destabilisation of moorland soils as a result of changes to upland vegetation communities could resulting in the wash out of heavy metal pollution stored in these soils from industrial revolution. This would have downstream consequences as this pollution is spread, potentially having further ecological impacts as well as impacting agricultural land and drinking water.

7.impact:
Climate change

As described above, land can be managed to mitigate the impacts of climate change by sequestering or preventing the further emission of fossil fuels. If the Peak District was managed to maximise this, it could help remove CO2 from the atmosphere to slow future climate change. However, on the scale of the Peak District this would have a relatively small impact on global climate change.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Where land management and ownership change, this could have consequences for the demographics of rural and farming communities, based on who is able to live and work in the Peak District. If land is consolidated under fewer ownership, this could mean that fewer people live and work on the land. However, changes to farming or conservation land management practices may result in more rural jobs. Therefore, it is difficult to make projections about exactly what these changes may look like.

Pollution

Certain land management practices can either result in or reduce pollution. Fertiliser run off from agricultural land can cause polluting effects in freshwater systems, and therefore moving toward lower input agricultural land management can reduce this pollution. Land management practices which stabilise soils, for example peatland restoration, can result in reduced top soil runoff and therefore less sediment contaminated with pollutants from industrial air pollution ending up downstream.

Visitation and access

The Peak District is widely known among visitors for its landscapes under their current management regimes, which promote people to visit the area and participate in different recreational activities. If land was managed differently, this could change people’s perception of the landscape and alter their visiting behaviour, as well as possible changes to access infrastructure which would need to adapt around changing land use.  This could be in the direction of reduced access and declining visitation, for example under agriculture intensification, or it could be increased visitation through ecotourism.

17.likelihood_text: This be a positive impact on intangible heritage, as continuing to adapt and change makes the continuation of intangible heritage in the Peak District more likely.
17.severity: It is possible that this impact will occur, as intangible heritage is in a constant state of change, however this change is more likely to occur slowly over generations.
17.impact: Emergence of new or adapted customs, events and traditions

16.introduction:
What are heritage assets and how do we record what we know about them? Our ‘tangible’ heritage assets have physical form, and can vary greatly from a commanding Iron-Age hill-fort to a modest roadside milepost or flint tool buried in peat. Our ‘intangible’ heritage of skills, traditions, customs and language is equally important, though perhaps less easy to quantify.

This diversity, as well as the significance of some key features, is what makes cultural heritage a key component of the importance of the Peak District’s landscapes. This contributes towards making the Peak District a place that gives both residents and visitors a sense of connection, as well as lending the landscape cultural significance beyond its borders. Cultural heritage features can also contribute towards providing housing, creating livelihoods, giving opportunities for leisure and recreation which supports health and wellbeing, as well as regulating the sensory and aesthetic environment.

Through their contribution to providing these benefits, and due to their intrinsic significance, we need to understand the condition of cultural heritage features in the Peak District and what factors may be putting them at risk. This is vital to developing plans for how to conserve and enhance these features, as well as the wider landscape.

34.title: Residents
34.key_data: Between 1991 and 2021, the resident population in the Peak District has fallen by 5.8% from roughly 38,100 to 35,901. Dwelling based projections show that the population change over the next 20 years is dependent on the number of houses built per year. The Peak District’s resident population is marginally healthier and less deprived, but also less diverse, than the national population.

family.description: Local communities, visitors and the economy

41.description:
The Peak District National Park is home to over 30,000 residents, with the area inhabited since the Mesolithic era 10,000 years ago. The settlements, the history of industry and the rich cultural heritage produced over thousands of years from the local population are an intrinsic part of the National Park. The people who live in the National Park are a key feature of this living landscape which has and will continue to be shaped by their settlements, livelihoods and land use over time.

As an important feature of the National Park, it is vital to assess the condition of the resident population, based on its size, characteristics and signs of change. This can serve as an indicator of the sustainability of local communities and reveal information regarding aspects such as health, deprivation and diversity. Characteristics of the Peak District’s population will undoubtedly by impacted a range of factors. These include access and visitation, as the visitor economy remains a focus for local government, and climate change, which will have far reaching consequences on many aspects including health.

83.condition:
An ageing and decreasing population

The population size of the Peak District shows a steady downwards trend over time. In 1991, the resident population was 38,100, while in the most recent census in 2021 this had fallen to 35,901[181].

The above data show that the population in the Peak District is older than the national average, with fewer residents under 50 and more over 50 than the overall England and Wales population. The percentage of over-65s has also been rising, with 30% of residents now above the age of 65 compared to 23.1% in 2011[182]. This is likely due to a combination of both the population ageing, and outward migration of younger people.

Population Forecast and Dwelling Led Scenarios

There are no official ONS population forecasts for National Parks, however as part of the evidence base for the Local Plan there are a number of dwelling-based population scenarios that show the population could continue to decline or increase over the next 20 years depending on scale of housing development.

Scenarios with the development of 48 dwellings per annum (dpa) or more show an increase in the resident population, while no dpa development would result in continued population decrease. In these scenarios, population increase is assumed to only occur due to net migration given the low number of births in comparison to the number of deaths that currently occur in the Peak District National Park.

It is important to note that if housing delivery continued as it has over the past 16 years (roughly 73dpa) this does represent a scenario in which the population would be projected to increase by 3,079 by 2045[126].

Ethnicity

The ethnicity of Peak District residents shows a less diverse population compared to England and Wales as a whole, with over 98% of residents classified as White compared to 82% of the national population. This is in line with other National Parks in England and Wales, all of which have disproportionately low proportions of ethnic minority residents compared to the national average[183].

Health

The health of residents in the National Park is mostly consistent with the rest of the country, with 48.7% of residents in very good health compared to 48.4% nationally and 0.9% classified as having very bad health compared to 1.2% nationally[184].

Deprivation

Deprivation, unlike poverty that simply accounts for a lack of money, identifies whether households are also deprived of employment, health, housing and education. The Peak District National Park is less deprived than the wider country, with 55% of households being not deprived in any dimension compared to 48.3% across England and Wales[185]. It also has far less households deprived in multiple dimensions in comparison to national figures.

82.distribution: The resident population is widespread across the landscape with hundreds of small villages, hamlets and rural settlements in the National Park, as well as more isolated farmsteads and houses. The majority of settlements are concentrated towards the south of the National Park, meaning the White Peak is likely to be the most populated region whilst the Dark Peak to the north the sparsest, although data to support this is not available. Bakewell is the National Park’s only town, with over 4000 residents. Whilst there are larger towns in the wider Peak District area such as Buxton, Glossop and Matlock, these all sit just outside the National Park boundary. The maps below, whilst not an exhaustive list, display some of the key settlements across the different Landscape Character Areas.

35.title: Housing
35.key_data: The Peak District has almost twice as many detached houses as the national average and significantly less purpose-built flats or tenement housing. Over half of all households in the Peak District own their property, much higher than across England and Wales, while there is less socially rented housing and less private renting. None of the local authority areas which include parts of the National Park have a median house price that is affordable for the median wage in that area; Barnsley is the most affordable area with house prices 5.4 times above the median salary, and Derbyshire Dales the least affordable with houses 10.24 times the median salary.

family.description: Local communities, visitors and the economy

42.description: The National Park, beyond being a landscape protected for its cultural and natural heritage, is also home to over 140 villages and hamlets with many more dispersed dwellings which the over 30,000 residents call home. Residents have expressed a strong connection to the landscape, to nature, and to their built environment, and visitors come not simply for the sweeping landscapes but also to visit the picturesque villages that remain centres of the community to this day. As a result, housing is still a crucial feature for the National Park, providing vital homes that are necessary to sustain the local population and enable communities to thrive as well as contribution to the cultural significance of the Peak District.

Housing occupancy

Based on 2021 Census data analysed by the Housing Needs Assessment for the PDNPA, there are roughly 2100 vacant dwellings in the Peak District, around 11% of all dwellings2. High numbers of vacant housing can suggest structural weaknesses in the housing market or issues with the housing stock itself, however there isn’t evidence of these issues in the Peak District. Therefore, rather than 11% of Peak District dwellings being complete vacant, this figure is likely inflated by the prevalence of second homes and holiday lets which are not primary residences[126].

There is also a trend towards under-occupancy in houses that are primary dwellings; 45.3% of properties with 2 bedrooms have single occupiers, whilst 21.5% are occupied by couples. Households with dependent children occupy 12.6% of 2-bedroom housing, implying that some overcrowding may be occurring in these houses. Three- and four-bedroom homes are most commonly occupied by households with dependent children and couples, although a higher-than-expected share of larger properties are also occupied by single residents, suggesting a level of under-occupancy[188],[189]. This combination of smaller households in larger housing and larger households in smaller housing is similar to national trends, and can present a barrier to meeting the house needs of larger households.

House Tenure

Type of tenure refers to whether households own or rent their accommodation. For the Peak District, a much higher percentage of households live in dwellings owned outright (51.3%) than nationally (32.8%), and a smaller percentage of dwellings owned with a mortgage or loan (22.8% compared with 28.7%)[187].

To be able to afford an average house in the district you would need an income of £33,330 at the maximum loan-to-income ratio, significantly higher than the median income of £27,799. 83.distribution: Housing in the Peak District is distributed between a range of towns, villages and hamlets while also being dispersed throughout the landscape in more isolated farmsteads and houses. The majority of settlements are concentrated towards the south of the National Park, with the White Peak likely being the most populated region whilst the Dark Peak to the north being the sparsest. Bakewell is the National Park’s only town, with over 4000 residents. Whilst there are larger towns in the wider Peak District area such as Buxton, Glossop and Matlock, these all sit just outside the National Park boundary.

36.title: Travel
36.key_data: Less than 1% of Peak District residents commuted to work using public transport in 2021, and as of 2025 only 12% of visitors used public transport to journey to the National Park. Recreational roads have seen a 30% increase in traffic since 2012 and there’s been a 15% increase overall across all roads.

43.description: The ways in which people travel to and within the National Park, via public transport, active travel, or private vehicle, is a key feature of the landscape. This affects how both residents and visitors interact with the landscape, which is important to monitor to help understand both how to promote sustainable travel and access, and to understand the ways in which traveling in the National Park can impact the landscape. Within this report, travel is placed within the Local Communities feature-group due to its close link to how residents are connected across and beyond rural areas. However, in reality, travel has direct relevance to visitors, tourism, and the economy.

The Peak District has higher levels of home working (39.6%) compared to national levels (31.2%). There are lower levels of residents within the Peak District using public transport or active travel methods to travel to work, with over 50% getting to work via private vehicle[192].

Main Transport to the National Park

The visitor survey from 2025 also queries what was the main transport visitors used to journey to the National Park[136].

A higher proportion of visitors use public transport to travel to the National Park than commuters within the National Park represented in the travel to work data. However, the car remains the dominant form of transport, with only 12% of visitors utilising public transport.

Traffic Flow Data

As part of one the National Park’s core policies to reduce road travel and promote sustainable transport, average annual daily traffic flows (AADT) are monitored. AADT is the actual volume of vehicles crossing a point in the road both ways, totalled up over a year and then divided by 365. This means that AADT doesn’t necessarily describe an average day as it doesn’t take into account seasonality; traffic on any given day may be higher or lower than AADT, depending on the time of year, school holidays, etc.

AADT data for the Peak District shows an increase in traffic flows since 2012 across all road types in the National Park, with a total increase of 15%. Recreational roads have seen the largest increase of traffic at almost 30%, although still remain the least used when looking at overall AADT, whereas A roads have seen the lowest rise of just 6.9% and even falling a few percentage points in between 2024 and 2025[193].

Despite there being a clear increase over the 13-year period, the year-by-year AADT data shows that levels have also fluctuated significantly. 2020 and 2021, in particular, have been adversely affected by the global pandemic. However, since then, 2023 to 2025 have shown higher levels than seen pre-pandemic. 

Whilst in isolation, daily traffic flows don’t provide strong evidence for shifting travel and visitation patterns, it is important to note that post-covid saw a large shift towards homeworking across the country[133]. Therefore, if it is assumed that commuting will likely have decreased in that time period, the higher levels seen may be as a result of increases in other reasons for travelling such as leisure.

85.distribution:
It is very challenging to monitor the spatial distribution of travel across the Peak District; public transport networks are highly spatial, but data as to their specific use is not available, while traffic monitoring data is only collected at specific sites on specific roads. There is a large amount of anecdotal evidence of travel-related issues, especially during holiday seasons and bank holidays. Often cited congested roads include:

  • A619 at Baslow
  • A6 & A619 at Bakewell
  • A6187 Hope Valley
  • Winnats Pass

However, without further monitoring it can be hard to differentiate between parking capacity, overall traffic volume and parking behaviour. Winnats Pass, for example, is likely to face more congestion due to people parking in order to access Mam Tor, rather than necessarily just an increase in traffic volume. However, there is a lack of data available to evidence this.

family.description: Local communities, visitors and the economy

42.title: Visitor numbers and economic impact
42.key_data: The estimated total number of days visitors spent in the Peak District National Park in 2022 was approximately 13.3 million, shared between around 9.5 million individual visitors. This has increased slightly from 9.1 million in 2011. In 2022, the total economic impact from visitors on the local economy of the Peak District was estimated to be £774m, with the largest impact on the shopping and food & drink sectors. Annual trends in number of visitors and their economic impact have become slightly less seasonal, with the peak summer months seeing reduced or stable visitor numbers and economic impact while the winter months show a converse increase.

family.title: People
family.description: Local communities, visitors and the economy

17.description:
The number of visitors and their impact on the local economy are key features of any visitor destination. They are also closely tied to the core purposes of the Peak District; the second statutory purpose of National Parks in England and Wales is to promote opportunities for the understanding and enjoyment of the special qualities by the public. Alongside this sits a statutory duty to seek to foster the economic and social well-being of local communities within the National Park. Visitor numbers and economic impact are therefore important in two ways: they may indicate the extent to which the public is engaging with the National Park, and they provide an estimate of the economic value visitors bring to the area which supports communities’ economic wellbeing.

This section focuses on analysing visitor numbers and economic impact as a feature of the National Park, rather than exploring the impact of visitors on the landscape, local communities and other tourism related pressures. Visitor numbers and their economic impact can themselves be impacted by a variety of factors; shifting seasonal weather patterns could be influencing the peak times of year for visitors, while sociocultural changes in peoples’ relationship to the outdoors may positively or negatively influence the number of visitors to the National Park. To explore the impact of visitors on other features, see the Visitation and access factor page.

22.condition:
Visitor numbers and days per year

It is challenging to estimate the number of visitors to the Peak District as there are no clear entrance or exit points to the National Park, and visits can take many different forms including visits for a partial or full day compared to a multi-day visit. ‘Visitor days’ is used as an estimation of the number of days visitors spend in the Peak District, which accounts for individual visitors that spend more than one day in the National Park during a single visit. Different models result in contrasting estimates of total visitor days per year. The STEAM model, which uses local supply side data and tourism performance, and visitor data collection[147], estimates that the total number of visitor days (visitors spending over 3 hours) in the Peak District National Park and its ‘influence area’ was around 13.31m per year in 2022[148].

For comparison, a 1996 study by the Peak District National Park Authority (PDNPA) estimated in excess of 22-26 million tourist days each year. While this data is much older, the large difference in figures due to the methodology of each study shows that it is important that absolute figures are not taken as an accurate representation of the true number of visitors the National Park receives, but that examining this data over time can help us understand change and trend in visitor numbers.

24.condition:
Using STEAM data from 2011 to 2022, the trend in visitor numbers shows a peak in 2019 before a sharp fall due to the Covid-19 pandemic, and a stable trend towards recovery in 2021/22. Overall, visitor numbers rose by 3.8% between 2011 and 2022, and visitor days by 8.9%. It is important to note that firstly, these figures do not include visitors that stay under 3 hours, and secondly, data is only available up until 2022[148].

Visitor spend and economic impact of visitors

The 2025/26 survey of visitors conducted by the Peak District National Park Authority showed that 90% of respondents spent money on their most recent visit, with 97% of domestic visitors (those living over a 1-hour drive from the National Park) spending money, compared to 87% of locals (those living within a 1-hour drive). Of respondents who spent money, 92% spent money on food and drink, 51% on shopping, 49% on car parking and 39% on accommodation. 39% of those who spent money spent less than £100 in total and 20% spent £500 or more. The estimated average was £300 per visit among those who spent money, or £265 across all respondents (locals £200, domestic visitors £460)[136].

26.condition:
The STEAM model aims to quantify the total impact of visitors on the local economy, including both overnight-stay and day visitors, through analysis and use of a variety of inputs including visitor attraction numbers, tourist accommodation bedstock, events attendance, occupancy levels, accommodation tariffs, macroeconomic factors, visitor expenditure levels, transport use levels and tourism-specific economic multipliers[147].

Accounting for inflation, there was an overall 8.1% growth in visitor economic impact from 2011 to 2022, increasing from £716m to £774m despite the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020. Without data later than 2022, it is hard to say whether the economic impact has continued to stabilise and return to pre-pandemic levels[148].

28.condition: Broken down by sector, the distribution of economic impact from direct expenditure (visitors purchasing goods and services from businesses) is widely distributed, with shopping making up the largest sector at £178m, while food & drink and accommodation are the next largest contributing £144m and £116m respectively. Additionally, a further £200m is contributed via indirect expenditure, this accounts for the wider supply-chain that supports the visitor economy[148].

30.condition:
These sectors have been growing at relatively comparable levels to each other since 2011, with roughly 7-8% overall growth, with the exception of accommodation which has only grown around 4%[148].

Seasonal trends in visitor numbers and economic impact

Both visitor numbers and their economic impact show a clear annual trend, with a consistent peak in the six months between April and September and the six months of October to March clearly showing an off-season. Between 2011 and 2022 data, while this seasonal distribution is still clearly present, it has slightly flattened, with both visitor numbers and economic impact decreasingly or staying the same in the summer peak season and increasing in the winter season[148]. This corroborates anecdotal evidence about an increasing in off-season visitors.

The below graph shows if difference in monthly visitor numbers between 2011 and 2022, which shows an overall reduction in visitors during the peak months of April, July, August and September with a converse increase in visitors in January, February, March, May, November and December. For example, in January 2011 there were roughly 300,000 visitors, increasing by 43.6% to 430,000 by 2022, while there was a 24.3% reduction in August visits from 1,215,000 in 2011 to 919,000 in 2022[148].

It is important to note that visitor numbers overall saw a slight increase between these years, from 9.11m in 2011 to 9.46m in 2022[148]. Therefore, the fact that there was a net decrease in visitors during summer months, as well as an increase in winter months shows that there is a change in seasonality of visitors occurring as well as an overall increase in visitor numbers. As these data come from two years rather than showing trends over time, it is possible that there are specificities between the two years that account for this change, e.g. a wetter summer and warmer winter in 2022 compared to 2011. However, as such factors driving this trend in seasonal visitation (e.g. climate change) are likely to continue, it is expected that this change in visitation will become a trend over time.

properties.caption: STEAM Visitor Numbers by month of the Peak District and influence area between 2011 and 2022. Visitor numbers in millions.

32.condition: Examining the seasonality of the economic impact of visitors shows a similar trend. The off-season winter months show an increasing economic impact between 2011 and 2022, with December seeing the greatest increase, while there is a slight decline in some peak season months, with May showing the biggest decline[148]. This indicates a slight flattening of seasonality in visitator economic impact, which corroborates the conclusion that visitors are becoming slightly more evenly distributed across the year.

34.condition:
National trends in visits to natural spaces

Looking at national data of how people are spending their time outside can also help us understand trends of visitor volume. The previous State of the Park Report looked at data from the Monitor Engagement Natural Environment survey (MENE)[149] which showed a steady rise of adults visiting nature at least weekly from 54% in 2009 to 62% in 2019. After 2019, the People and Nature Survey (PaNS)[150] replaced MENE, they use slightly different methodologies so are not directly comparable but do allow us to track similar metrics.

According to the PaNS survey data there has been a steady rise in adults visiting green and natural spaces since 2020/21, whilst those visiting at least weekly has remained broadly stable.

36.condition: However, the survey did change slightly; there was a further question added to those who responded “don’t know” to the 14-day measure in 2022/23 which may account for this rise. Additionally, 2020/21 and 2021/22 were heavily affected by the Pandemic and the report itself often omits those years in its analysis. When removing the first two years, there is very little change in the percentages of people spending time outdoors in green and natural spaces.

properties.caption: Source: People and Nature Survey (Natural England)

54.distribution: The Peak District is one of the most accessible UK National Parks through its connections to the major urban centres of Manchester, Derby, Sheffield and Stoke-On-Trent. This gives a large section of the UK population easy access to the National Park. Visitor hotspots with easy access to these urban centres via cars and public transport include Chatsworth House and Bakewell, the Hope Valley and Mam Tor, Ladybower and the Upper Derwent Valley, Stanage Edge, and Dovedale. While the precise distribution of visitors across the National Park is difficult to quantify, the most recent visitor survey gives an indication of their destination-type[136].

43.title: Visitor demographics and engagement
43.key_data: 76% of visitors list experiencing beautiful views, scenery and landscape as one of their primary motivations for visiting the National Park. In 2025/26, 50% of visitors had visited the National Park outside of the summer peak (May-August), an increase from 44% in 2024/25. 97% of those who visited in 2025/26 said they were likely to return, with 96% agreeing that the National Park seems well managed and cared for.

family.title: People
family.description: Local communities, visitors and the economy

18.description:
National Parks have a statutory purpose to promote opportunities for the public to understand and enjoy their special qualities. Understanding the demographics of our visitors, where they’re coming from and the purpose of their visit can help us understand whether that purpose is being met and whether the special qualities themselves continue to be relevant in how people engage with the Peak District National Park. Alongside data on visitor volume and value we can begin to build a picture of how people engage with the park and use that to inform decision making.

The figures in this page primarily draw on the Peak District National Park Authority's visitor survey results from 2024/25 and 2025/26. The 2025/26 visitor survey represents 1000 adults who had visited the National Park in the past three years; 750 of whom were “locals” (living within one hour’s drive of the National Park), the other 250 were “domestic” (living further than one hour’s drive). In 2024/25 there were 1,240 respondents, with 799 locals and 441 domestic visitors meaning domestic visitors were a larger share of that sample (36%); the 2024/25 survey also included people who last visited more than three years ago and people visiting for business.

38.condition:
Who visits?

Age:

The age distribution of surveyed Peak District visitors in 2025/26 was relatively broad, with 25-44 representing the largest age distribution. Domestic visitors tend to skew somewhat younger, with almost 1 in 3 visitors being 25-34, whereas locals skew older, with a larger proportion of over 65s[136].

40.condition:
Employment:

2025/26 survey results show that 73% of visitors were employed in either full-time or part-time work, 4% of visitors were students and 15% were retirees. This is broadly in line with national employment statistics, with a slightly reduced portion of those who are retired compared to national data[136].

42.condition:
Income:

There was a large difference in the income distribution of the households of visitors between locals and domestic visitors surveyed in 2025/26; domestic visitors are disproportionately more likely to live in wealthier households, with 34% of those having an annual household income of over £100,000. This is 10% higher than local visitors, and also likely much higher than national figures (although there are not directly comparable national measures of household income available for this timeframe)[136].

44.condition:
Ethnicity:

There are some key differences between the ethnicity of PDNP visitors surveyed in 2025/26 to the England and Wales population. Those who identify as White British take up a larger share of Peak District National Park visitors. Most minority groups are underrepresented except for those who identify as Black or Black British[136].

46.condition:
Travel Groups:

Over the two surveys in 2024/25 and 2025/26, there was an increase in visitors who came with a partner or spouse (36% to 41%) and fewer with a family group with children (33% to 28%). Both changes were present across all respondents. However among domestic visitors, the share travelling alone rose from 7% to 12%[151],[136].

48.condition:
When and how often people visit

Examining seasonality shows that the summer peak months of May to August remain the most likely time of year that surveyed visitors had their most recent visit between the 2024/25 and 2025/26 surveys. Interestingly, when looking at the non-peak months of September to April, there is a shift from a 44% share in 2024/25 up to a 50% share in 2025/26, which would corroborate perceptions of reduced seasonality in the tourism sector in general[151],[136].

50.condition:
Frequency:

The majority of visitors surveyed in 2025/26, including those living over one hour away, have visited the National Park before and are likely to have visited at least twice prior. Predictably, locals are more likely to visit at a higher frequency, with almost 1 in 5 locals having visited over 6 times in the previous 3 years[136].

52.condition:
Length of stay and accommodation

Day and Overnight visits:

In 2025/26, 41% of respondents made a day visit and 59% stayed overnight, almost unchanged compared to 2024/25 (40% and 60%). Among locals, the day visit share was unchanged at 51%. Among domestic visitors, day visits fell significantly from 18% to 8%, and stays of four to six nights rose from 17% to 24%[136].

54.condition:
Accommodation:

Among overnight visitors, hotels were the most common accommodation during both surveys. This were followed by self-catering and guest houses or B&Bs. B&B use fell from 24% overall in 2024/25 to 18% in 2025/26, however "Pub with accommodation" was a new answer option in 2025/26 (5%), which may account for some of this fall. Among domestic visitors, campsite stays fell from 14% in 2024/25 to 7% in 2025/26 and wild camping from 7% to 3%[151],[136].

56.condition:
Why visitors come

Respondents chose up to 3 reasons for visiting. These each align closely with the Peak District National Park’s Special Qualities. These remain largely unchanged between 2024/25 and 2025/26, with a slight increases in responses indicating reasons relating to active pursuits (Adventure activities and General exercise and outdoor recreation).

Health and wellbeing:

98% of visitors surveyed in 2025/26 agreed their visit was good for their mental health, a rise from 96% in 2024/25. The share who strongly agreed rose from 58% to 64%, driven by domestic visitors (54% to 66%). Agreement that the visit was good for general wellbeing (98%) and physical health (94%) was similar to 2024/25[151],[136].

What visitors do

Walking or hiking has remained the most common activity in both years, eating and drinking out (46% to 53%) and visiting an attraction/museum (29% to 35%) have both seen notable increases across the two surveys years.

58.condition:
How visitors travel

How visitors travel has changed very little across the two surveys, the car is by far the dominant mode of transport to the National Park for visitors and, according to a follow up question on the 2025/26 survey, 87% of those who travelled used a car at some point in their journey. Highlighted above you can also see that public transport only makes up 12% of all journeys[136].

60.condition:
Visitor Satisfaction

Visitors surveyed in 2025/26 were highly satisfied when visiting the National Park; 97% were likely to return (68% very likely), 61% were very likely to recommend the National Park with only 6% unlikely to. An overwhelming 96% agreed the National Park seems well managed and cared for and the most common reasons for recommending it were the scenery (34%) and an overall positive experience (28%)[136].
