57.distribution: Visitor demographics and engagement are primarily assessed by surveying visitors; this does reveal the demographic distribution of visitors or their types of engagement across the National Park. Therefore, as visitors are distributed across the whole of the Peak District, it is useful to consider visitor demographics and engagement as a feature of the whole National Park. However, the Peak District National Park Authority’s visitor survey results do provide an overview of the main types of destinations visitors primarily engage with[151],[136].

44.title: Access and rights of way
44.key_data: There are roughly 3000km of public rights of way across the Peak District, and over 500 square kilometres of open access land. Based on the most recent survey conducted on the condition of the public rights of way network in the Peak District National Park, 85.3% of them were found to be easy to use based on a sample. The Manifold track, the Tissington and High Peak Trail, and the Monsal Trail averaged roughly 1065 trips per day in 2025.

family.title: People
family.description: Local communities, visitors and the economy

19.description:
Access and rights of way describes how people are able to reach and move through the National Park, by foot, bike, horseback or mobility aids. They are an essential aspect of the second purpose of National Parks, to promote understand and enjoyment, and underpin two of the Peak Districts special qualities: "an inspiring space for escape, adventure, exploring and quiet reflection" and "vital benefits for millions of people that flow beyond the landscape boundary".

The Peak District also has a special place in the history of access. The 1932 mass trespass on Kinder Scout helped lead to the National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949. Today, the Peak District National Park Authority is the access authority for open access land, and manages its own trails. It works with several highway authorities, which are responsible for recording and maintaining rights of way.

61.condition:
Rights of Way and Ease of Use

There are roughly 3000km of public rights of way across the Peak District, and over 500 square kilometres of open access land. Long distance routes include the Pennine Way National Trail and the Trans Pennine Trail.

A survey of 5% of the rights of way network is conducted every two years by the PDNPA. Rangers and ranger volunteers use a field app to record signposting, waymarking, path surface, structures (gates, stiles, steps, bridges and boardwalks) and obstructions. The latest survey, reported in October 2025, found 85.6% of the network easy to use[152]. The 2022/23 survey found 82%[153], and 2019 showed 81%[128], reflecting an upward trend in condition. However given the small sample, there will be some natural variation in those figures from year to year.

National Park Authority trails

The previous State of the Park Report estimated 519,000 visits on key trail routes in 2017. These included 330,000 on the Monsal Trail (215,129 walkers and 132,991 cyclists) and over 50,000 each on the High Peak, Tissington and Upper Derwent routes. Cyclists at the Hassop Station counter rose by 112% between 2015 and 2017[128].

The PDNPA also has a number of permanent counters set up on trails including the Monsal Trail at Hassop Station, the High Peak and Tissington trails at Parsley Hay and the Manifold Track at Waterhouses. Based on a report in 2025, the PDNPA reported that its three permanent counters averaged 1,056 movements a day in total, with August being the busiest month[154].

There was also a trail user survey conducted in the autumn of 2024 with a handful of key headlines:

  • walking was the most common activity (54%)
  • the main reasons for visiting were to experience nature (25%) or take part in a recreational activity (23%)
  • users rated facilities 9 out of 10 on average
  • users spent an average of £42.06 per visit
  • 48% said more off-road routes would make them walk, wheel or cycle more[154]

Accessibility improvements

Defra's Access for All programme has funded a series of improvements since 2022/23:

  • 2023/2024 (announced February 2023, £130,000): upgraded trail routes, more Miles without Stiles routes, and the motorised Tramper fleet increased from three to nine[155].
  • 2024/25 (£155,800, plus £26,200 from the Peak District National Park Foundation): a Changing Place at Parsley Hay, improvements at North Lees campsite, and fast charging for e-bikes. Surfacing nearly doubled the length of the Goyt Miles without Stiles route, and a new route with gates for cyclists and horse riders was started at Fernilee Reservoir[156].
  • 2025/26 (£255,900): a Changing Place at Trentabank (Macclesfield Forest), Accessible Bakewell, interactive mapping of Miles without Stiles routes, and trikes, wheelchair bikes and e-bikes for hire[157].

The PDNPA’s own Access Fund, set up in 2014 and run by the Foundation since 2021, has paid for new access points, new access land, permissive paths, signs and leaflets[157].

Walking, Wheeling, Cycling and Horse-riding Infrastructure Plan

The Authority's Walking, Wheeling, Cycling and Horse-riding Infrastructure Plan sets out proposed new and improved routes. A business case prepared with the Yorkshire Dales National Park Authority in March 2025 estimated that the proposed routes could add 2,268 walking and cycling trips a day. It also estimated around £65.5 million a year in extra visitor spending, close to a 10% increase on the £774 million a year that visitors already bring in[154]. Work is continuing on the White Peak Loop, including a possible link between the Monsal Trail and Coombs Road[156].

59.distribution: Access routes and rights of way can be found in all Landscape Character Areas of the National Park. Open access land is mostly on the high moorland of the Dark Peak, the eastern gritstone edges and the moors of the South West Peak. The limestone White Peak is mostly enclosed farmland, so open access land there is less extensive and more scattered. Multi-user trails are mainly located in the White Peak, on former railway lines: the Monsal, High Peak and Tissington Trail, the Manifold Track and the Thornhill Trail. The Trans Pennine Trail crosses the north of the Park through Longdendale. Miles without Stiles routes are spread across the Park. They include several routes around the Dark Peak reservoirs and routes across the White Peak trails and Dales. The others are on the eastern edges (Curbar Gap and Longshaw), at Castleton and Mam Tor, and in the west (Goyt and Lyme Park). Green lanes with a Traffic Regulation Order are Chapel Gate and The Roych near Edale and Chapel-en-le-Frith, Long Causeway near Stanage, Leys Lane at Little Longstone, Derby Lane at Monyash, Washgate at Hollinsclough, and Wetton Hills.

22.introduction:
Visitors are a key feature of the Peak District; the National Park was established in 1951 with the dual purposes of protecting the landscape, and providing opportunities for visitors to enjoy and benefit from this special place. To this day, the number of people who come to visit, who they are, how they engage with the landscape and contribute to the local economy, and how they access the Peak District are all key features of the National Park that should be assessed and understood to ensure that the landscape is being managed to fulfil these purposes. Visitors can, in turn, have an impact on other features of the National Park, however, this page discusses visitors as a feature in themselves, which, as a result of this statutory purpose of National Parks, should be positively managed. To understand more about the impact visitors can have on the landscape, see the Visitation and access  factor page.

The benefits of visitors to the National Park are numerous, from their economic impact which allows local communities to thrive, to the benefits that visiting has on people’s health and wellbeing. However, the ability for people to visit the National Park can be impacted by a range of factors. Climate change, due to its impact on the seasonality of weather as well as physical impact on the landscape, may be altering how and when people visit the Peak District as well as their ability to enjoy their visit. This, in combination with how land is managed, may be increasing the risk of tick- and mosquito-borne diseases which could have impacts on the health of visitors. However, overall, both the number of and enjoyment of visitors seem to be relatively stable to the National Park, indicating that visitors as a feature are in relatively favourable condition.

11.distribution:
While visitors are not evenly distributed across the whole National Park, it is useful to understand visitors as a feature that can occur in all Landscape Character Areas of the Peak District. This is in part due to the big areas of open access land across the National Park, where visitors are able to widely access the landscape, as well as the fact that the Peak District is in the centre of a large network of urban areas, including Manchester, Stoke-on-Trent, Derby and Sheffield.

There are, however, ways to assess the uneven distribution of visitors. The Peak District National Park Authority’s visitor survey results show the destination types that visitors are distributed between.

13.distribution: Visitors can also be concentrated into specific ‘hot spot’ areas, which include places like Chatsworth House and Bakewell, the Hope Valley and Mam Tor, Ladybower and the Upper Derwent Valley, Stanage Edge, and Dovedale. The rights of way network can also show where visitors are accessing the wider landscape.

5.importance: Visitors are important to the Peak District because a core part of the purpose of National Parks is to support people to visit this special landscape. The Peak District National Park came into being in part as a result of the Kinder Mass Trespass, in which people living in the urban centres surrounding the now-National Park asserted their right to enjoy the countryside for the benefit of their health and wellbeing. Since then, this has been a well-visited landscape which supports millions of people to learn about, care for and protected the cultural heritage and natural beauty of the landscape. Visitors also make an important economic contribution to the landscape, which supports other features to be conserved. For example, in 2022, the economic impact of visitors to the Peak District was £774 million, which supports the local economy through providing jobs and income as well as supporting the upkeep of features such as country houses and stately homes.

6.quality:
• Accurately assessing visitor numbers and behaviour is very challenging as there are no totalising ways to understand these indicators. The different data presented in this report should only ever be taken as estimates and the trends across different methodologies are the most useful elements to understand rather than total figures, for example ‘total number of visitors’ which is almost impossible to accurately assess.
  • There is a lack of evidence of the condition of most access points and rights of way in the Peak District due to there be no fully aligned methodologies of condition assessment or regular schedule of assessment across the different land owners and authorities responsible of rights of way. As a result, the condition data present is only taken from a sample.

18.likelihood_text: The likelihood of this impact is possible, as experts have identified that these causes are occurring, for example data showing that fly camping and littering is frequently reported. However, according to a visitor survey, 98% of visitors continue to believe that the National Park seems well managed and cared for, so there is currently not evidence that visitor enjoyment is being impacted in a measurable way.
18.severity: Overall this impact could be minor. While they may cause more severe localised impacts, specific events such as wildfire and noise pollution are likely to be unevenly distributed across space and time. Therefore, where this impact does occur it will not be widespread across the National Park. Additionally, whilst the causes of this impact (i.e. damage and disruption to the landscape) have identified as occurring, the impact of this on visitor enjoyment has not been evidenced.
18.impact: Visitor enjoyment of the Peak District National Park is diminished

3.impact:
Climate change has compound impacts on other factors. These are briefly laid out below with more detail on each of the relevant factor pages.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Due to climate change having unequal impacts globally, as a result of both physical and socio-economic conditions, international migration of people may increase the UK population and/or change the character of the UK population as a whole. Additionally, there may be increased demand for housing in rural areas as a result of disproportionate population growth and warming in urban areas. As a result, the Peak District may experience changes to the demographic character of both its residents and its visitors due to global and local population changes. There is little research into exactly what these changes may look like, however projections do indicate that current migration trends are likely to be amplified as a result of climate change[64].

Ecological change

The projected impacts of climate change are intrinsically linked to potential ecological changes. As the physical conditions which define species’ niches shift, both spatially and temporally, species distribution and phenology (timing of biological events) will change.

Cooke et al. (2026) model biodiversity change in the UK under a range of climate scenarios up to 2080[61]. They project “extensive community reorganisation” under any scenario with “the disappearance of current bioclimates and emergence of novel ones”. In the Peak District, this is likely to contribute to the local extinction of species, colonisation by novel species, changes to composition of biological communities, increase likelihood of invasive alien species and increased likelihood of pathogens.

Formulating and setting habitat and species targets, as has been the practice for many years, will need to be carefully re-examined as an approach.

Land management practices

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

4.impact:
Climate change

As outlined on the Climate change factor page, Representative Concentration Pathway modelling accounts for different future greenhouse gas emissions scenarios that result from different responses to climate change. These responses are profoundly shaped by social trends and demographic characteristics. Therefore, all climate change scenarios are intrinsically linked to demographic and sociocultural changes.

Governance and legislation

Potential changes to governance and legislation that impact the National Park are in turn impacted by social trends. For example, the changes in social attitudes to outdoor recreation discussed above could contribute to changes in access legislation if more people demand and campaign for an increased right to countryside access for recreation.

Land management practices

The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways discussion on the Land management practises factor page exemplify how demographic and sociocultural change could impact land management. Under different socio-economic scenarios, these pathways can be used to describe different possible future land use scenarios in the UK.

Visitation and access

Patterns and trends of visitation and access in the National Park are likely to be impacted by changes in the demographic and sociocultural character of both Peak District resident and visitors. This could result in impacts such as change to visitor numbers and changes in the behaviour of visitors due to changing attitudes to outdoor recreation.

8.impact:
Climate change

Particulate pollution can contribute towards climate change as a result of airborne particulates absorbing heat and light, contributing to atmospheric warming and cloud formation[118].

Ecological changes

Water pollution alters the chemical environment for aquatic life, impacting species’ abilities to reproduce. Excess nutrients or changes to pH cause imbalance with some species thriving at the expense of others, resulting changes to the diversity and composition of aquatic ecosystems. This can also have knock on impacts on terrestrial ecosystems which interact with polluted water sources[119].

Nitrogen air pollution alters lichen community composition, with some species being nitrogen-tolerant and others nitrogen-sensitive. In this was lichens can be used as indicators of nitrogen air pollution[120].

9.impact:
Ecological Change

Visitation and access has the potential to affect ecological change if it leads to impacts such as soil compaction and habitat degradation. Roadside verges have been identified as agricultural settings that may be rich in wildflowers and meadow species can be prone to invasion of more dominant ruderal species due to the nature of disturbance and additional nitrogen that occurs alongside roads and higher levels of traffic[71].

Pollution

If there are changes to visitor numbers, the current prevalence of car travel in how people access the National Park could have an effect on pollution: contributing to carbon emissions as well as noise and light pollution. The knock on demand for car or public transport related infrastructure could also therefore generate further embedded carbon and generate emissions during production.

19.likelihood_text: The likelihood of this is possible, as the climate change-related causes are very certain, however there is less certainty on whether they will change rights of way features in a significant way at a landscape scale. Current surveys  conducted every 2 years of 5% of the public rights of way network to ascertain condition currently show no downward trend.
19.severity: This impact could be moderate due to the possible compounding effects of the causes have. However, this impact is still likely to be relatively localised in nature and extreme change is not likely to occur within the next 10 years. Impacts may also be manageable provided resources are available.

6.impact:
Governance and legislation have the potential to impact all other factors due to the legislation and governance frameworks that underlie all action carried out in the UK. This could be drawn together in an almost infinite number of links, however certainty about what impacts are likely is very low, and many relevant ways in which governance and legislation impacts other factors have already been outlined above. Therefore, these are briefly summarised below with some additional impacts that have not yet been noted.

Factor

Possible impacts from governance and legislation

Climate change

Stronger commitments to emissions reduction and carbon sequestration and storage could help to reduce likelihood of global climate change impacts, e.g. changes to the Climate Change Act 2008 or additional global agreements.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Impacts on communities from changes to planning regulation (NFFP, local plan making process etc) could alter housing development in communities, potential knock-on impact to composition of communities.

Ecological change

Possibility for strengthened or weakened environmental protections, e.g. through BNG and biodiversity credits, changes to National Park legislation and governance, etc. Land use framework, LNRSs and 30x30 target may introduce stronger requirements and spatial planning for land to be managed for ecology.

Economy and industry

Changes to farm subsidy schemes may positively or negatively impact he viability of farm businesses. More NSIPs to support low carbon energy and transport infrastructure could support construction and operation jobs.

Land management practices

Farm subsidies and land management grants may incentivise changes to land uses and management actions. Land use framework may change how land use is determined. Changes to land ownership resulting in changed land management may result from enhance community right to buy to England[98].

Possible changes to legislation relating to driven grouse shooting, including further changes to moorland burning regulation about and an ongoing campaign to ban on driven grouse shooting[99], may result to changes in moorland management.

Pollution

Changes to the regulation of sewage waste outflow into freshwater would reduce freshwater pollution. Legislation relating to land management outline above could change agricultural pollution e.g. lower input farming reducing nutrient pollution.

Visitation and access

New access legislation could strength right to access, including permitted activities and areas with open access. Combined authorities may use visitor levies which could impact visitor access by presenting financial barrier, may cause inequality in access.

There is little research into exactly what these changes may look like, however projections do indicate that current migration trends are likely to be amplified as a result of climate change[64].

Ecological change

The projected impacts of climate change are intrinsically linked to potential ecological changes. As the physical conditions which define species’ niches shift, both spatially and temporally, species distribution and phenology (timing of biological events) will change.

Cooke et al. (2026) model biodiversity change in the UK under a range of climate scenarios up to 2080[61]. They project “extensive community reorganisation” under any scenario with “the disappearance of current bioclimates and emergence of novel ones”. In the Peak District, this is likely to contribute to the local extinction of species, colonisation by novel species, changes to composition of biological communities, increase likelihood of invasive alien species and increased likelihood of pathogens.

Formulating and setting habitat and species targets, as has been the practice for many years, will need to be carefully re-examined as an approach.

Land management practices

Climate change is likely to drive significant and rapid change in land management practices as a result of how land managers and society respond to climate change. Projections from the European Environment Agency indicate that agricultural land value is likely to fall by as much as 80% in southern European and rise by up to 60% northern Europe by 2100, while the UK may see a 20% rise, possibly up to 40% in Scotland[62]. This is indicative of the change in agricultural productivity in these areas; in the UK, land value increase could result in increased arable agriculture to replace lost crop land in southern Europe.

Brown et al. (2022) detail how under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios, different types of land use change may result, however under all scenarios change is projected[63]. This research indicates that while it is difficult to predict the exact change that may occur, changing land management practise are likely in the Peak District, in part as a response to climate change.

Pollution

The understanding of effect of climate change on pollution is beginning to be better understood, with research in to heavy metal pollution, particulates, sewage release and chemical interactions in their infancy. Uncontrolled vegetation fires, so called ‘wildfire’, is however better understood and a present and growing problem. The increased incidence of wildfires that is likely to result from climate change will cause the emission of more airborne particulate pollution as a result of burnt vegetation. Recent vegetation burning demonstrates that airborne particulate pollution travels large distances and has health impacts beyond the boundary of the Peak District[118] as well as direct impacts on ecosystem services and benefits such as water supply.

Visitation and access

Climate change may directly contribute to increased visitor numbers in the Peak District National Park during heatwave events. As extremes of temperature and humidity are projected to be greater in urban areas[52], people may seek cooler outdoor spaces during these events. Additionally, domestic tourism may increase if the popularity of overseas destinations declines due to extreme heat in countries at lower latitudes, an emerging trend observed in recent warmer years. A study of the impact of heat waves on Spanish tourism showed that during heatwaves, UK tourist number significantly declined, which could indicate that these tourists will increasingly seek domestic tourist destinations like the Peak District during these events[60].

Additionally, it is possible that climate change may result in changes to visitor behaviour, such as a longer peak tourist season and changes to visitor hotspots, as visitors seek out respite from extremes of temperature and humidity. Data, and anecdotal reports from European protected areas and popular tourist destinations around the world, including UK protected areas, are showing extended visitor seasons. Consistent reports indicate a change from traditional seasonal peaks to ‘flatter’ year round visitation patterns, an overall increase in visitor days, and the consequent positive and negative impact on the environment, local communities and local economies.

5.impact:
Climate change

Change in ecological communities could alter the potential for carbon storage in biomass, which will impact the possibility for land-based mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions as is accounted for in net zero targets. For example, changes to blanket bog communities could result in less accumulation of peat soil, reducing carbon storage potential, and in the possible release of additional carbon from soil due to runoff, resulting in enhanced climate change. Ecological communities may also experience non-linear shifts, for example a sudden collapse in function in single biome, which could in turn provoke non-linear climatic impacts due to the impact on water, carbon and nutrient cycling.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Ecological change could impact on the demography and sociocultural practices of both residents and visitors to the Peak District due to the connections between people and their wider ecologies. Shifts in ecological communities could invoke changes to the composition of rural communities, as the possibility for agricultural livelihoods changes and people’s connection to and sense of belonging in the landscape shifts. Additionally, visitors to the Peak District come in part to interact with the ecology of the landscape, from foraging to taking in the view. Changes to these communities may result in different people visiting in different ways.

Land management practices

Land management practices take place in relation to the underlying ecological communities. Therefore, changes to this ecology are likely to result in changed land management practices. For example, in the Peak District, uplands currently managed for grouse moors may be managed differently if the red grouse experiences population decline and the composition upland moorland habitats shift to make this form of moorland management no longer sustainable. Similarly, agricultural practices may have to change if different compositions of agri-ecological systems emerge, pests and diseases impact on crops and livestock, etc.

Pollution

The potential destabilisation of moorland soils as a result of changes to upland vegetation communities could resulting in the wash out of heavy metal pollution stored in these soils from industrial revolution. This would have downstream consequences as this pollution is spread, potentially having further ecological impacts as well as impacting agricultural land and drinking water.

7.impact:
Climate change

As described above, land can be managed to mitigate the impacts of climate change by sequestering or preventing the further emission of fossil fuels. If the Peak District was managed to maximise this, it could help remove CO2 from the atmosphere to slow future climate change. However, on the scale of the Peak District this would have a relatively small impact on global climate change.

Demographic and sociocultural change

Where land management and ownership change, this could have consequences for the demographics of rural and farming communities, based on who is able to live and work in the Peak District. If land is consolidated under fewer ownership, this could mean that fewer people live and work on the land. However, changes to farming or conservation land management practices may result in more rural jobs. Therefore, it is difficult to make projections about exactly what these changes may look like.

Pollution

Certain land management practices can either result in or reduce pollution. Fertiliser run off from agricultural land can cause polluting effects in freshwater systems, and therefore moving toward lower input agricultural land management can reduce this pollution. Land management practices which stabilise soils, for example peatland restoration, can result in reduced top soil runoff and therefore less sediment contaminated with pollutants from industrial air pollution ending up downstream.

Visitation and access

The Peak District is widely known among visitors for its landscapes under their current management regimes, which promote people to visit the area and participate in different recreational activities. If land was managed differently, this could change people’s perception of the landscape and alter their visiting behaviour, as well as possible changes to access infrastructure which would need to adapt around changing land use.  This could be in the direction of reduced access and declining visitation, for example under agriculture intensification, or it could be increased visitation through ecotourism.

38.title: Economic output
38.key_data: The Peak District produces around 11% of the total Gross Value Added (GVA) of all English National Parks. Wholesale is the sector with the largest share of business turnover within the National Park, accounting for over 20% of all business turnover. Business turnover in the Peak District National Park grew by 45% from 2022 to 2025, before adjusting for inflation.

family.title: People
family.description: Local communities, visitors and the economy

44.description:
As a lived- and worked-in landscape, the Peak District’s economic output is a key feature of the National Park. In this context, economic output refers to the economic value generated within the Peak District. While some of the sectors generating economic value might be more obviously linked to the National Park as a landscape, such as agriculture and tourism, other less obvious sectors such as wholesale and production make significant contributions to the Peak District’s economy.

Assessing the condition of the economy is important when considering the overall state of the National Park, as it contributes to understanding the prosperity of the Peak District’s communities. Sustainable economic output contributes to the health and wellbeing of communities as well as livelihoods for those living in and around the National Park. However, the conditions for secure economic output may be impacted by a number of factors, such as climate change altering the conditions for agricultural production or changes to legislation and policy, such as planning rules and agricultural subsidy schemes.

85.condition:
Gross Value Added in English National Parks

Gross Value Added (GVA) is the total value generated by all businesses and organisations in a sector or area, after subtracting the cost of the goods and services they buy in to produce it. GVA is regarded as an effective method of measuring the economic contribution of different sectors of the economy. The data on this page is taken from a report produced by Cumulus, the most recent of which is from 2022[190].

As of 2022, using a turnover-based estimate, nine of the ten English National Parks (excluding the Broads) support roughly a GVA of £6.6bn per annum, making up roughly 0.4% of the total GVA in England. This represents a 34% increase in GVA since 2012, adjusted for inflation, showing that as a sector, English National Parks are growing in economic value. They are also growing at a faster than National GVA; UK GVA grew by roughly 13% over the same time frame adjusted for inflation. 

Breaking down National Park GVA by broad industry groups there is a clear picture of uneven growth distribution. Wholesale has remained the largest sector by GVA and grown substantially; a 96% increase in GVA between 2012 and 2022. The professional, scientific and technical sector also greatly increased by almost 200% over the same period. Agriculture also grew but with notably slower, by 50%. Additionally, accommodation and food services had grown very little since 2012 and the health sector has even decreased over that period.

Whilst these figures may give us an indication of changes in GVA across all National Parks, it is important to note these use Inter-Departmental Business Register (IDBR) data for turnover, which does omit smaller data sets in certain instances to ensure individuals or businesses cannot be identified. As a result, turnover figures will likely be underestimated for National Parks.

Gross Value Added and IDBR Turnover Data for the Peak District National Park

The Peak District National Park in 2022 had an estimated GVA of roughly £734 million, accounting for around 11% of the total GVA across all English national Parks. The Cumulus report does not breakdown GVA by sector for each individual National Park, or give comparative data over the 2012-2022 period for each individual National Park.

However, the most recent IDBR data[195] gives a break down turnover figures for each sector for the Peak District National Park. This is not as accurate for discerning the condition of economic output, as unlike GVA it won’t take into account cost of production, it only shows the total gross income a business generates, but it will provide some indication of how economic output is distributed and changing overtime. This shows that total turnover in the Peak District has been increasing overall since 2022 although stagnating between 2024 and 2025. Most sectors still saw relative levels of growth between 2024 and 2025 and the plateauing figures can be explained by a sharp 20% reduction in the wholesale sector as well as the information and communication sector not featuring in the 2025 figures.

The above chart shows the current sectoral distribution of turnover in the Peak District, as of 2025. Wholesale and production produce the largest shares of turnover, with agriculture and accommodation & food services being the next largest. It is important to note economic output only builds part of the picture of the structure of a local economy, for example agriculture still remains the largest sector by business count in the Peak District.

Similar to changes in GVA across all English National Parks, growth has not been distributed evenly amongst economic sectors:

  • Wholesale and production have seen substantial increases in what were already dominant sectors in economic output.
  • Transport & Storage and Construction have grown comparatively slowly compared to other sectors
  • Agriculture has continued to grow in economic output however is being outpaced by other sectors, on the current trajectory accommodation & food Services is likely to over take it as the 3rd largest sector in coming years. 84.distribution: Economic output is generated across the whole of the National Park from a wide variety of business activities and the data presented on this page hare not geographically delineated across the National Park. Therefore, for the purpose of this report it is useful to consider economic output as a feature existing in all Landscape Character Areas.

39.title: Employment
39.key_data: 55.2% of Peak District National Park residents are economically active, meaning they are either in or seeking employment, compared to 58.3% nationally. Almost one fifth of working people in the Peak District are in the highest socio-economic band when ranked by occupation type. Since 2010 workplace earnings have increased by 41% compared to 48% for resident earnings, these both trail behind the UK at large which has increased by 55% over the same time period.

family.title: People
family.description: Local communities, visitors and the economy

45.description:
Employment is an important feature of the Peak District National Park; it can give us an indication of the health of the local economy, as well as the sustainability of the National Park’s resident communities. Therefore, assessing the condition of employment in the Peak District as one key feature of this diverse landscape will support the development of management actions that fulfil the National Park’s duty to foster the economic and social wellbeing of local communities within the Peak District.

Employment as a feature of the National Park provides the benefit of livelihoods for both residents within the National Park and the wider area, with local people relying on stable employment to be able to support themselves, their families and their wider communities within the National Park. However, a number of factors could impact on the sustainability of employment in the Peak District; for example, demographic and sociocultural change leading to an aging population may result in a skew towards older residents, with less working-age people and a change in the types of employment available within the National Park.

87.condition:
Working population

2021 census data reveals that there were 17,115 economically active people in the Peak District, making up 55.2% of the whole National Park population[196]. This is comparable to other National Parks but lower than the 58.3% across all England and Wales. Earlier census data from 2011 shows a wider gap between the national proportion of economically active people in the population compared to the Peak District, suggesting this disparity is reducing over time.

With a total working age population of 20,259, the labour force participation rate (the ratio between the number of people in work divided by the total working-age population) in the Peak District is 84.48%. This is higher than the participation rate across England, which as of January 2026 is 81.5%. However, the Peak District does have higher levels of economic inactivity when accounting for the whole population, compared to the rest of the country, with around 43.5% regarded as inactive as opposed to 39.5% across England and Wales. This is in part due to a much higher level of retirees; 33.1% of the PDNP resident population is retired compared to 21.6% in England and Wales.

Employment status

Accounting for employment status, Peak District residents are less likely to be in full time employment than the rest of the country. However, this is reversed for self-employment, where there are higher levels[196]:

Professional Occupation Distribution

Analysing the high-level occupational categories of employed residents, the Peak District broadly aligns with other National Parks in the UK but differs in some areas from national levels. This includes both skilled trade occupations and managerial roles which are particularly higher in the National Park compared to England and Wales[197].

Socio-economic classification

Breaking down occupation by socio-economic classification also shows that Peak District residents are disproportionately in highly skilled and managerial positions compared to both other National Parks, and England and Wales[198].

The rates of those who have never worked or are long-term unemployed are also lower in the Peak District than other National Parks and England and Wales as a whole. However, this share has more than doubled since the 2011 census, which had rates as low as 2% in the Peak District. This reflects a national trend in rising long-term joblessness.

Resident hours and earnings vs workplace hours and earnings

The national annual survey of hours and earnings does not record results specifically for National Parks, therefore for the purpose of this report the local government districts of Staffordshire Moorlands, High Peak and Derbyshire Dales will be taken as representative of the “wider Peak District area”[199].

Since 2010 in this wider Peak District area there has been uneven growth. Both resident earnings and workplace earnings declined between 2010 and 2015. Workplace earnings show the average annual pay for workplaces inside the defined area as opposed to resident earnings which will include residents who commute out of the wider Peak District area. This is an important distinction as rural areas often have higher resident earnings in comparison to workplace earnings as many residents will commute into urban areas for higher paid skilled work. This may be especially prevalent in the Peak District which is surrounded by several major urban centres.

Earnings have generally recovered post-2015, however it is important to note that workplace earnings in the Peak District have increased at a slightly lower rate as well as starting from a lower baseline in 2010. Since 2010, workplace earnings have increased by 41% compared to 48% for resident earnings; these both trail behind the UK at large which has increased by 55% over the same period.

87.distribution: People are employed across the whole of the Peak District National Park, and as such for this report it is useful to consider employment as a feature of all Landscape Character Areas. However, there are some key sites for employment in the National Park which are protected as Safeguarded Employment Sites in the Peak District National Park Authority’s Local Plan.

40.title: Businesses
40.key_data: There were 6,575 businesses in the National Park in 2025, 2% fewer than 2020, a slightly larger fall than across England’s National Parks and the UK (both 1%). 98% of business sites employ fewer than 50 people in the Peak District, and 88% employ fewer than 10. Agriculture, forestry and fishing accounts for 23% of all businesses in the National Park.

family.title: People
family.description: Local communities, visitors and the economy

46.description:
The Peak District National Park is home to thousands of businesses in a diverse range of sectors. These provide jobs, income, and service provision to residents, visitors and the wider region. The agricultural sector remains the dominant industry by number of businesses in the Peak District, however a wide variety of other businesses that are less directly related to the Peak District as a protected landscape are also present.

These businesses provide livelihoods to those who work in them, as well as contributing to a diverse range of products and services that support leisure and recreation, mining and quarrying for useful minerals, and food, fuel, fibre and timber production and processing. As a result of this diversity, business in the Peak District may also be impacted by diverse factors, including climate change alternating the conditions for food production and governance and legislation impacting businesses in the tourism sector.

88.condition:
Overview

It is difficult to assess the overall condition of business, but taking a given area such as the Peak District and comparing this to all English National Parks and the UK as a whole can give some indication of this relative to other parts of the country. In general, trends in business count from 2020-2025 are roughly comparable to both English National Parks and the UK, but with a slightly lower turnover in the Peak District (lower business birth and death rate). The structure of business type within the National Park has also changed very little over time, with the majority of businesses relating to agriculture as may be expected. Within the agricultural sector, the type of farm businesses has changed since 2010, with a sharp rise in crop growing and a fall in dairy farming. This may indicate that while business overall is stable in the Peak District, the character of businesses are changing. The evidence for this is explored in more detail below.

Business Count

88.distribution: Businesses are found in every Landscape Character Area but official business data are not published at a detailed enough level to map them within the National Park. There will be some obvious clustering for example retail and tourism businesses will be often centred around urban centres such as Bakewell, the only town in the National Park, as well as the larger villages such as Hathersage and Castleton.
